```
     1	import { graphlib, layout } from '@dagrejs/dagre';
     2	import type { GraphLabel, NodeLabel } from '@dagrejs/dagre';
     3	import { Position } from '@xyflow/react';
     4	import type { Edge, Node, XYPosition } from '@xyflow/react';
     5	
     6	export type LayoutDirection = 'TB' | 'LR';
     7	export interface ILayoutOptions extends Pick<GraphLabel, 'nodesep' | 'ranksep' | 'edgesep'> {
     8	  direction: LayoutDirection;
     9	  fallbackWidth?: number;
    10	  fallbackHeight?: number;
    11	}
    12	export const DEFAULT_LAYOUT: Required<ILayoutOptions> = {
    13	  direction: 'TB',
    14	  nodesep: 24,
    15	  ranksep: 48,
    16	  edgesep: 12,
    17	  fallbackWidth: 360,
    18	  fallbackHeight: 140
    19	};
    20	
    21	export function layoutElements<N extends Node, E extends Edge>(
    22	  nodes: N[],
    23	  edges: E[],
    24	  partial: Partial<ILayoutOptions> = {}
    25	): N[] {
    26	  const options: Required<ILayoutOptions> = { ...DEFAULT_LAYOUT, ...partial };
    27	  const g = new graphlib.Graph().setDefaultEdgeLabel(() => ({}));
    28	  const label: GraphLabel = {
    29	    rankdir: options.direction,
    30	    nodesep: options.nodesep,
    31	    ranksep: options.ranksep,
    32	    edgesep: options.edgesep
    33	  };
    34	  g.setGraph(label);
    35	  const connected = new Set<string>(edges.flatMap(e => [e.source, e.target]));
    36	  const sizeOf = (n: N) => ({
    37	    width: n.measured?.width ?? n.width ?? options.fallbackWidth,
    38	    height: n.measured?.height ?? n.height ?? options.fallbackHeight
    39	  });
    40	  for (const n of nodes) {
    41	    if (connected.has(n.id)) {
    42	      g.setNode(n.id, sizeOf(n));
    43	    }
    44	  }
    45	  for (const e of edges) {
    46	    g.setEdge(e.source, e.target);
    47	  }
    48	  layout(g);
    49	  const isLR = options.direction === 'LR';
    50	  const sourcePosition = isLR ? Position.Right : Position.Bottom;
    51	  const targetPosition = isLR ? Position.Left : Position.Top;
    52	  let sideY = 0;
    53	  // dagre reports an empty graph's width as -Infinity (not null), so `??` is not enough here.
    54	  const graphWidth = g.graph().width;
    55	  const sideX = (Number.isFinite(graphWidth) ? (graphWidth as number) : 0) + (options.ranksep ?? 48);
    56	  return nodes.map(n => {
    57	    if (!connected.has(n.id)) {
    58	      // disconnected: stack in a side column (marimo layout.ts precedent)
    59	      const position: XYPosition = { x: sideX, y: sideY };
    60	      sideY += sizeOf(n).height + (options.nodesep ?? 24);
    61	      return { ...n, position, sourcePosition, targetPosition };
    62	    }
    63	    const nl: NodeLabel = g.node(n.id);
    64	    const position: XYPosition = { x: (nl.x ?? 0) - (nl.width ?? 0) / 2, y: (nl.y ?? 0) - (nl.height ?? 0) / 2 }; // dagre returns centers
    65	    return { ...n, position, sourcePosition, targetPosition };
    66	  });
    67	}
```

```
    69	// KernelMessage's message-type unions are closed, so a known request type stands in for analyze_request.

    74	export class ShellTransport implements IDagTransport {

   115	interface ICommPayload {

   120	/**

   124	 */
   125	export class CommTransport implements IDagTransport {
   126	  constructor(private _kernel: Kernel.IKernelConnection) {
   127	    // TODO: kernel-initiated comms (the kernel opening `jupyter-dag` towards the frontend, e.g. right
   128	    // after `%load_ext jupyter_dag`), so the kernel can push without the frontend opening a comm first.
   129	    _kernel.registerCommTarget(COMM_TARGET, this._onKernelInitiated);
   130	  }
   131	  private _onKernelInitiated = (comm: Kernel.IComm, msg: KernelMessage.ICommOpenMsg): void => {
   132	    void msg.content.target_name;
   133	    void comm; // TODO: adopt it as this._comm and attach onMsg / onClose exactly as open() does
   134	  };
   135	  get namespaceDelta(): ISignal<this, INamespaceDelta> {
   136	    return this._delta;
   137	  }
   138	  /** Advertised by the kernel on comm open (a stock kernel after %load_ext never updates kernel_info). */
   139	  get features(): ReadonlySet<string> {
   140	    return this._features;
   141	  }
   142	  async open(): Promise<void> {
   143	    const kernel = this._kernel;
   144	    if (!kernel.handleComms) {
   145	      throw new Error('comms are disabled on this kernel connection');
   146	    }
   147	    const comm = kernel.createComm(COMM_TARGET); // a fresh comm id each time: reuse after reconnect throws
   148	    comm.onMsg = (msg: KernelMessage.ICommMsgMsg) => {
   149	      const data = msg.content.data as unknown as ICommPayload;
   150	      if (data.type === 'namespace_delta') {
   151	        this._delta.emit(data as unknown as INamespaceDelta);
   152	      } else if (data.type === 'features') {
   153	        this._features = new Set(data.supported_features ?? []);
   154	      }
   155	    };
   156	    comm.onClose = () => {
   157	      this._comm = null;
   158	    };
   159	    await comm.open().done;
   160	    if (comm.isDisposed) {
   161	      throw new Error(`the kernel has no '${COMM_TARGET}' comm target`);
   162	    }
   163	    this._comm = comm;
   164	  }
   165	  async analyze(content: IAnalyzeRequestContent): Promise<IAnalyzeReplyOk> {
   166	    if (!this._comm) {
   167	      await this.open();
   168	    }

   170	    const reply = new PromiseDelegate<IAnalyzeReplyOk>();
   171	    let settled = false;
   172	    const future = comm.send({ type: ANALYZE_REQUEST, ...content } as unknown as JSONValue);
   173	    future.onIOPub = (msg: KernelMessage.IIOPubMessage) => {
   174	      if (KernelMessage.isCommMsgMsg(msg) && msg.content.comm_id === comm.commId) {
   175	        settled = true;
   176	        const c = msg.content.data as unknown as IAnalyzeReplyContent;
   177	        if (c.status === 'ok') {
   178	          reply.resolve(c);
   179	        } else {

   181	        }
   182	      }

   189	  }

   212	  private _isDisposed = false;
   213	}

   215	/** Per-session client: feature detection from kernel_info, one transport, and the namespace_delta stream. */
   216	export class DagKernelClient implements IDisposable {
   217	  constructor(sessionContext: ISessionContext, analyzeChannel: AnalyzeChannel = 'shell') {
   218	    this._sessionContext = sessionContext;
   219	    this._analyzeChannel = analyzeChannel;
   220	    sessionContext.kernelChanged.connect(this._onKernelChanged, this);
   221	    sessionContext.statusChanged.connect(this._onStatusChanged, this);
   222	  }
   223	  get kernel(): Kernel.IKernelConnection | null | undefined {
   224	    return this._sessionContext.session?.kernel;
   225	  }
   226	  get features(): ReadonlySet<string> {
   227	    return this._features;
   228	  }
   229	  get supportsAnalyze(): boolean {
   230	    return this._transport !== null;
   231	  }
   232	  get namespaceDelta(): ISignal<this, INamespaceDelta> {
   233	    return this._namespaceDelta;
   234	  }
   235	  get ready(): Promise<void> {
   236	    return this._ready.promise;
   237	  }
   238	  async detectFeatures(): Promise<ReadonlySet<string>> {
   239	    const kernel = this.kernel;
   240	    if (!kernel) {
   241	      this._transport?.dispose();
   242	      this._transport = null;
   243	      this._features = new Set();
   244	      return this._features;
   245	    }
   246	    // kernel_info_reply.supported_features is the source of truth; `info` is the connection's first reply.
   247	    const info = await kernel.info;
   248	    this._features = new Set(info.supported_features ?? []);
   249	    this._transport?.dispose();
   250	    this._transport = null;
   251	    if (this._features.has(FEATURE_ANALYZE)) {
   252	      this._transport = new ShellTransport(kernel, this._analyzeChannel);
   253	    } else {
   254	      // e.g. a stock kernel after `%load_ext jupyter_dag`: kernel_info was answered before the extension loaded.
   255	      const comm = new CommTransport(kernel);
   256	      comm.namespaceDelta.connect((_, d) => this._namespaceDelta.emit(d));
   257	      try {
   258	        await comm.open();
   259	        this._transport = comm;
   260	        this._features = new Set([...this._features, ...comm.features]);
   261	      } catch {
   262	        comm.dispose();
   263	      }
   264	    }
   265	    this._ready.resolve();
   266	    return this._features;
   267	  }

   269	    if (!this._transport && this.kernel) {
   270	      await this.detectFeatures(); // e.g. `%load_ext jupyter_dag` ran after this view attached
   271	    }

   274	    }

   278	  /** Unbind names in the kernel: over the comm when that is the transport, else a silent execute_request. */
   279	  async namespaceDelete(names: string[]): Promise<void> {

   285	  /** Raw execute with namespace_delete; `code: ''` + silent = 'purge without running'. */
   286	  requestExecute(
   287	    content: IDagExecuteRequestContent,
   288	    metadata?: JSONObject
   289	  ): Kernel.IShellFuture<KernelMessage.IExecuteRequestMsg, KernelMessage.IExecuteReplyMsg> {
   290	    const future = this.kernel!.requestExecute(
   291	      content as unknown as KernelMessage.IExecuteRequestMsg['content'],
   292	      true, // dispose the future when done; nothing keeps it
   293	      metadata
   294	    );

   296	      const d = readNamespaceDelta(msg);
```

```
   162	        case 'state': {
   163	          // Patch in place so React Flow keeps node identities, positions and measurements.
   164	          const ids = new Set(change.cellIds ?? []);
   165	          setNodes(current =>
   166	            current.map(n => (ids.has(n.id) ? { ...n, data: { ...n.data, state: graph.stateOf(n.id) } } : n))
   167	          );

   173	        case 'nodes': {

   190	      graph.changed.disconnect(refresh);

   192	  }, [graph, outputOnly]);

   194	  const onLayout = useCallback(

   206	          }
   207	        }

   226	  }, [layoutRequested, onLayout, direction]);

   229	    (changes: NodeChange<CellNode>[]) => {
   230	      // Nodes are never removed from the canvas directly; the cell list drives that through 'nodes' events.
   231	      setNodes(current =>
   232	        applyNodeChanges(
   233	          changes.filter(c => c.type !== 'remove'),
   234	          current
   235	        )
   236	      );

   238	        if (change.type === 'position' && change.position && !change.dragging) {
   239	          const cell = graph.findCell(change.id);
   240	          if (cell) {
   241	            setCellMetadata(cell, { ...getCellMetadata(cell), position: change.position });

   247	            setCellMetadata(cell, {

   250	              height: change.dimensions.height

   252	          }
   253	        }
   254	      }
   255	    },
   256	    [graph]
   257	  );
   258	  const onEdgesChange: OnEdgesChange<DagEdge> = useCallback(
   259	    (changes: EdgeChange<DagEdge>[]) => {
   260	      setEdges(current => applyEdgeChanges(changes, current));

   274	    [graph]
   275	  );
   276	  const onConnect: OnConnect = useCallback(
   277	    (connection: Connection) => {
   278	      const wire = addWire(model, connection.source, connection.target);
   279	      if (wire) {
   280	        setEdges(current => addEdge(wireToEdge(wire), current));
   281	      }
   282	    },
   283	    [model]
   284	  );
   285	  const onReconnect = useCallback(
   286	    (oldEdge: DagEdge, connection: Connection) => {
   287	      removeWire(model, oldEdge.source, oldEdge.target);

   289	      if (wire) {
   290	        setEdges(current => reconnectEdge(oldEdge, connection, current));
   291	      }
   292	    },
   293	    [model]
   294	  );
   295	  const onConnectEnd: OnConnectEnd = useCallback((_event, state) => {
   296	    if (!state.toNode) {
   297	      // TODO: a wire dropped on empty canvas should insert a new cell there and wire it
   298	      // (model.sharedModel.insertCell + addWire): the litegraph "drag out a node" gesture.
   299	    }
   300	  }, []);
   301	  const onSelectionChange: OnSelectionChangeFunc<CellNode, DagEdge> = useCallback(({ nodes: selected }) => {
   302	    // TODO: mirror the selection to the notebook panel's activeCell (and back) so both views agree.
   303	    void selected;
   304	  }, []);
   305	  useOnSelectionChange({ onChange: onSelectionChange });
   306	  // Backspace on a selected node must not delete the cell's wires behind its back: only selected edges go.
   307	  const onBeforeDelete: OnBeforeDelete<CellNode, DagEdge> = useCallback(
   308	    async ({ edges: toDelete }) => ({ nodes: [], edges: toDelete.filter(e => e.selected) }),
   309	    []
   310	  );
   311	  const onMoveEnd = useCallback(
   312	    (_event: unknown, viewport: Viewport) => setNotebookMetadata(model, { ...getNotebookMetadata(model), viewport }),
   313	    [model]
   314	  );

   316	    <ReactFlow<CellNode, DagEdge>

   318	      edges={edges}
   319	      nodeTypes={nodeTypes}
   320	      edgeTypes={edgeTypes}
   321	      onInit={onInit}
   322	      onNodesChange={onNodesChange}
   323	      onEdgesChange={onEdgesChange}
   324	      onConnect={onConnect}

   334	      minZoom={0.4}
   335	      maxZoom={settings.maxZoom}
   336	    >
   337	      <Background variant={BackgroundVariant.Dots} gap={16} size={1} />
   338	      <Controls>
   339	        <ControlButton title="Toggle layout direction" onClick={() => onLayout(direction === 'TB' ? 'LR' : 'TB')}>
   340	          {direction}

   352	      </ReactFlowProvider>
   353	    </CellNodeContext.Provider>
   354	  );
```

```
Because `useLayoutEffect` creates/attaches/disposes the Lumino `Cell`, the code needs a `registerWidget` callback in `ICellNodeContext`, a `_widgets` map, an `INotebookTracker` dependency whose only use is `cellWidget`'s fallback to another panel's widget, a "no live widget → error" branch in `_runOne`, a manual `MessageLoop.sendMessage(UnknownSize)` and a `ResizeObserver` to pump resizes at a parentless widget. **Deeper:** `DagPanel` owns a cell-widget pool keyed by cell id, created/disposed from `notebook.cells.changed`, parented into the panel's Lumino layout; the node's effect only re-parents the existing widget's node into the host. The discriminator exists only so the canvas can avoid clobbering positions it wrote itself. **Deeper:** one `reconcile()` that rebuilds nodes/edges from the model merging `position: meta.position ?? previous.position`. <details data-role="thinking">
```
<summary>Thinking</summary>

With all four reports in, I'm moving to consolidating findings and deciding which fixes to apply. I'm grouping them by mechanism, starting with adding a shared updateCellMetadata helper to wiring.ts that gets used across addWire, removeWire, and the canvas layout handlers, then moving on to look at wire caching behavior.

For wire caching specifically, I'm weighing whether caching collected wires inside DagGraphModel is worth the added state complexity versus just recomputing them each time. ## Claude · 2026-09-16 19:24:14 EDT

<details data-role="thinking">
<summary>Thinking</summary>

The plugin actually failed to activate with an error, which explains why the DAG commands are missing. I suspect the issue is in how the settings registry loads the plugin's schema, possibly a circular wait during `settingRegistry.load(PLUGIN_ID)`.

I'm recalling that since the schema has `jupyter.lab.transform: true`, the settings registry waits for a transform to be registered — and that transform registration happens inside `createToolbarFactory`'s `setToolbarItems` call, which itself calls `settingsRegistry.load` after registering the transform. That ordering could easily create a deadlock if the transform isn't registered before the load call resolves.

That's the bug — I found it. Before my change, the load fired without awaiting first, so the transform got registered in time; now that I await the load before creating the toolbar factory, the transformer never registers and it times out after 7 seconds. The fix is to reorder things: create the toolbar factory (which registers the transform) before awaiting the settings load, since it doesn't depend on settings anyway.

But I need to handle the edge case where `toolbarRegistry` is null — no transform would get registered and the schema's transform requirement would still cause a timeout. I'm weighing whether toolbarRegistry is ever actually null in practice versus needing a fallback no-op transform registration to keep things safe.

Let me look at how core handles this same pattern — checking `notebook-extension/src/index.ts` to see how `createToolbarFactory` and `settingRegistry.load` are actually sequenced there.

Core creates the toolbar factory first, which registers the transform, then loads settings non-blocking and applies them via `app.restored.then(...)`. My change made activation await the settings load directly, which broke that ordering — so the fix is to move `createToolbarFactory` ahead of the settings load and keep it non-blocking.

I'm weighing whether to make `IToolbarWidgetRegistry` a hard requirement instead of optional, since the transform registration is unconditional anyway, versus just reverting to the earlier non-blocking pattern with `DEFAULT_SETTINGS`. I lean toward keeping it optional but guarding the toolbar factory creation so it doesn't fail if the registry is missing.

I should verify rather than assume—the console only shows `{0: Object}` instead of the actual message, so I need to check for a "timed out" pattern in the full console output, and also confirm in the apputils source that `setToolbarItems` actually registers the transform.

```
    /**
     * Transform the plugin if necessary.
     */
    async _transform(phase, plugin) {
        const id = plugin.id;
        const transformers = this._transformers;
        if (!plugin.schema['jupyter.lab.transform']) {
            return plugin;
        }
        if (id in transformers) {
            const transformed = transformers[id][phase].call(null, plugin);
            if (transformed.id !== id) {
                throw [
                    {
                        instancePath: '',
                        keyword: 'id',
                        message: 'Plugin transformations cannot change plugin IDs.',
                        schemaPath: ''
                    }
                ];
            }
            return transformed;
        }
        // If the plugin has no transformers, throw an error and bail.
        throw [
            {
                instancePath: '',
                keyword: 'unset',
                message: `${plugin.id} has no transformers yet.`,
                schemaPath: ''
            }
        ];
    }
```

Done. The `/simplify` pass on the TypeScript is applied and verified: tsc 0 errors, eslint 0 errors (8 warnings, one fewer), jest 7/7, Rspack build OK, and in Lab the DAG view opens from the notebook toolbar, runs the wired cells in order twice (purge path included), and auto-lays out with no browser or server errors. Nine files changed in `src/dag`, about 90 lines net removed. Nothing committed.

**Applied** (the four reviewers' findings, deduplicated):

- **Model** ([wiring.ts](src/dag/wiring.ts)): `updateCellMetadata(cell, patch)` replaces five open-coded read-modify-writes; `addWire`/`removeWire` take the graph and use its cached `wires` (the canvas reads it per pointer move while dragging a wire); graph walks use an adjacency map instead of scanning all wires per node; the `_cells` map and its reconcile loop are gone (`findCell` scans the live list); the dead `'layout'` change type and notebook-metadata subscription are removed.
- **Protocol** ([protocol.ts](src/dag/protocol.ts)): `namespaceDelete` and `namespaceDelta` live on the transport interface, so the client no longer branches on `instanceof CommTransport`; the shell and control sends share one `createMessage`; the comm reply no longer needs a `PromiseDelegate` plus `settled` flag; the unused `ready` promise is replaced by a `featuresChanged` signal that the panel actually consumes.
- **Lifecycle** ([document.tsx](src/dag/document.tsx)): detection and analysis now run once from the constructor and again on every `featuresChanged`, instead of on every Lumino re-attach; `_loaded` is replaced by `context.isReady`; the unused `flow`, `ready`, `onInit`, `stateChanged` and `running` accessors are gone, along with the redundant `Signal.clearData`.
- **Canvas** ([canvas.tsx](src/dag/canvas.tsx)): one `refresh` reconciles nodes and edges on any change, keeping previous objects when unchanged (so memoized nodes don't re-render and edge selection survives); callbacks read `instance.getNodes()`/`getEdge()` instead of closing over state, so the layout signal is no longer re-subscribed on every node change; `deletable: false` replaces the two deletion guards; a small `useLuminoSignal` hook replaces two hand-written effects.
- **Settings** ([plugin.ts](src/dag/plugin.ts), [tokens.ts](src/dag/tokens.ts)): activation awaits the settings load, so `DEFAULT_SETTINGS` and the `changed` handler are gone and the schema is the only source of defaults.
- **Smaller**: `run()` mode branches collapsed; one `_markDownstreamStale` helper; the ResizeObserver posts resize messages instead of sending them synchronously; only `Cell` widgets are registered; dead `??` fallbacks in `layout.ts` removed; a comment on why `topologicSort` from Lumino isn't used.

**One behaviour change to know about.** Awaiting the settings load exposed an ordering rule: the schema's `jupyter.lab.transform` flag means the load throws until `createToolbarFactory` has registered its transformer. So the toolbar factory is now created first, and `IToolbarWidgetRegistry` moved from `optional` to `requires`. Without it the settings could never have loaded anyway, so the optionality was fictional; the first Lab run caught this (activation failed) before the reorder fixed it.

**Skipped**, with reasons:

- Widget pool owned by the panel (altitude), derived staleness from execution sequence (altitude), and merging remote position changes into the canvas (altitude): real redesigns, beyond a cleanup pass.
- Dropping `hasSize` in favour of the `fitView` prop: the initial layout runs after React Flow's own fit, so the prop would fit the pre-layout positions; the guard stays.
- Removing the `_loaded`-style gate entirely: the altitude reviewer claimed `MainAreaWidget` defers the content until reveal; it doesn't (content is attached immediately, the spinner only overlays it), so the gate is kept as `context.isReady`.
- Replacing `_redetect` with a `!transport` check: on a stock kernel that would re-probe the comm target on every idle.
- `DagWidgetFactory` field ceremony and `useNodesState`/`useEdgesState`: matches core's `NotebookWidgetFactory` pattern, and the hooks compute initial nodes on every render.
- Reading the mime type from `language_info` metadata instead of `kernel.info`: only works when a notebook panel is also open.
- `cellWidget` tracker scan per cell and the `mimeType` write guard: trivial at notebook scale, and the setter already guards equality.

## Claude · 2026-09-16 20:21:55 EDT

**`jupyter.lab.transform`**

When a schema sets that flag, the settings registry refuses to hand out the plugin's settings until someone has registered a transformer for that plugin id. `_transform` throws `has no transformers yet` instead of falling back to the raw schema. Our schema needs the flag because `createToolbarFactory` is what injects the toolbar item definitions into the `toolbar` property at load time, and that injection is the transform.

So the order matters: `createToolbarFactory` registers the transformer as a side effect of being called. Previously nothing awaited the load, the `.catch` swallowed the error, and the toolbar factory happened to be created before the promise resolved. Once I awaited the load, the throw became fatal and the plugin failed to activate. Creating the toolbar factory first fixes it, which also means the toolbar registry is a hard requirement, not optional.

**The settings change signal**

The old code kept a mutable `settings` variable and reconnected `changed` to refresh it. That existed only to paper over the async load: the factory was built before the settings arrived, so `DEFAULT_SETTINGS` filled the gap and the signal patched the variable afterward.

Now the factory holds the `ISettings` object itself and calls `readSettings(settings.composite)` at the moment each view is created. The registry mutates `composite` in place on change, so the getter always reads current values without a subscription. The observable behaviour is the same as before: settings apply to the next DAG view opened, not to views already on screen.

```
Contents of /Users/tel/git/jupyter-dag/.claude/CLAUDE.md (project instructions, checked into the codebase):

# Jupyter Day 2026 — "Children of Jupyter"

Context for Claude Code. This project began as a long chat (September 10–14, 2026);
`transcript.md` is a condensed record of that chat and `artifacts/` holds the
outputs. Read this file first, then `artifacts/transcript-design-verbatim.md`, `artifacts/kernel-design-notes.md`, and
`artifacts/genome-model.md`.

## Who

Max Klein (GitHub: telamonian). JupyterLab contributor since 2019; Distinguished
Jupyter Contributor 2023; has worked on JupyterLab, jupyterlab-git, Jupyter Server,
Jupyter Enterprise Gateway. Employed by a large company where he helps run its
internal enterprise Jupyter platform; speaks at Jupyter events as a contributor,
not for his employer. Does not name the employer in public materials.

## The event

Jupyter Day 2026, Monday October 19, 2026, San Jose Convention Center (Linux
Foundation, co-located with PyTorch Conference NA). CFP on Sessionize; the CFP
guide is https://events.linuxfoundation.org/jupyter-day/program/cfp/ . Talk is a
25-minute presentation. Description field has a hard 1,200-character limit.
Topic: Community. Audience level: Intermediate. Notifications Sept 21, 2026.

## The talk

Working title "Children of Jupyter" (suggested subtitle: "What Core Should Steal
Back"). Thesis: Jupyter's kernel/protocol design (built 2010, shipped in IPython
0.11 in July 2011; the notebook shipped in 0.12, December 2011) has aged well and
is what Colab, VS Code, Deepnote and ChatGPT's Python tool run on; the notebook
around it has not changed its execution model since 2011. The descendants
(Observable, Pluto, marimo, Hex, Livebook, Deepnote, Streamlit, ...) shipped fixes.
The talk surveys the significant new features, grouped by idea, with demos, then
argues opt-in reactive execution is the feature to adopt first and shares an
in-progress design and prototype for adding reactivity to the kernel messaging
protocol so any kernel can implement it.

Acts (25 min): opener (history + kernel/protocol split, ~3 min); reactive
execution; the environment inside the file; cells beyond code (SQL cells, input
cells, no-code cells, Livebook smart cells, anywidget); notebooks in space
(canvases, graphs); notebook → app → job → agent (ending on ChatGPT's tool being
"a stateful Jupyter notebook environment"); what core already took back
(RTC, JupyterLite) and the proposal. See `artifacts/talk-outline.md`.

## The framework ("genes")

Four traits of a Jupyter notebook; a descendant "changed a gene" only for a
significant departure, not a reimplementation:
- execution model (persistent namespace, user-ordered REPL)
- file (list of typed cells with optional outputs)
- cells (code + prose cells, one language, ordered list)
- client (a human editing and running cells)
Colab, VS Code, nteract, Jupytext, JupyterLite change none → distributions, not
descendants. Full classification table in `artifacts/genome-model.md`; figure in
`artifacts/family-tree-v3.svg`.

## Prior art that must be acknowledged

JupyterCon 2025 (San Diego, Nov 4–5): Stephen Macke, "Exploring the Design Space of
Reactive Notebooks" (ipyflow; recommended first-class reactive support in Jupyter);
Ian Thomas, "Subshells" (model for a protocol-level, language-agnostic feature:
JEP → ipykernel → other kernels); Billy Li, "World's First Undoable Notebook"
(Kishu checkpointing, Python-only); Timothy Tamm, "DBLS" (language server embedded
in the kernel); Kyle Kelley, "Runtime Agents" (precedent for bold "it's time to"
tone). All accepted descriptions are in
`artifacts/jupytercon-2025-accepted-talks.md`. Max knows Macke personally.

## The proposal (the design behind "Jupyter-DAG")

Name is a working name only; do not present it as an existing project.
Minimal kernel-protocol additions that serve both reactive execution and a
user-drawn cell DAG (they differ only in where edges come from):
1. `analyze_request` → per-cell defined/referenced names (kernel has the parser;
   optional feature; manual wiring is the fallback). Run on the control channel
   since it needs no namespace access. Optional `namespace_delta` on
   `execute_reply`.
2. namespace ops: delete (needed for "no hidden state" invalidation) and set
   (JSON value → binding; inputs/parameters). `user_expressions` already covers
   get.
3. forkable execution scopes (shallow namespace copy / env with parent):
   reactive-grade branch isolation; Pluto's module trick is the Julia version.
Optional heavier tier: state snapshot/restore/clone (CRIU/DMTCP process-level via
a jupyter_client provisioner; language-native serialization like dill/Kishu; replay
as universal fallback). Advertise all via JEP 92 `supported_features`.
Frontend: React Flow (`@xyflow/react`, MIT) in a JupyterLab ReactWidget on the
same INotebookModel; Lumino CodeCell mounted inside custom nodes. The ComfyUI
litegraph fork is not viable (internal module, GPL repo, canvas-rendered nodes).
Details in `artifacts/kernel-design-notes.md`.

## Writing rules Max enforces

Plain, specific, first person where natural. No LLM tells: no "clear-eyed",
"innovations", "and more", "walk away with", "leverage", "robust", no tidy
"X. Not Y." contrast pairs, no "if/if not" symmetric hedges, no signpost
sentences ("The second benefit is..."), no category slips (a talk is not an
implementation). Don't overpromise: "in-progress design and prototype", never
"extension" or "JEP" as if they exist. Count characters against limits with a
script, not by eye. Keep replies short unless asked for detail.

## Status / next steps

- Description, Benefits to the Ecosystem, and bio are final
  (`artifacts/proposal-final.md`). CFP closed Sept 13, 2026 11:59 PM PDT.
- Next month: build the reactive-execution prototype (analyze_request in
  ipykernel via `transform_cell` + `ast`/`symtable`; namespace ops; scopes) and
  the React Flow DAG view; keep the talk's demos short and recorded.
- Slides: family tree (v3) as the map slide; five one-minute demos (marimo
  slider vs ipywidgets callback, Pluto cell deletion, Livebook smart cell convert
  to code, Hex graph view, the prototype).
</system-reminder>
```

```
1	# Design notes: language-agnostic reactive execution and cell DAGs for Jupyter
2	
3	Working name "Jupyter-DAG". Nothing here exists publicly yet; it is an in-progress
4	design plus a prototype to be built for the Jupyter Day talk (Oct 19, 2026).
5	
6	## 1. The core observation
7	
8	A user-drawn DAG of cells (with branching) and a reactive notebook (marimo/Pluto
9	style) need the same kernel primitives. They differ only in where edges come from:
10	inferred by the kernel (reactive) or drawn by the user (DAG). Topological
11	scheduling, staleness marking, cycle detection, run modes, and persistence of the
12	graph are frontend/server work and stay out of the kernel.
13	
14	## 2. Minimal kernel-protocol additions
15	
16	All optional features advertised via `kernel_info_reply.supported_features`
17	(JEP 92; subshells JEP 91 and the debugger use the same mechanism).
18	
19	### 2a. `analyze_request` / `analyze_reply`
20	Input: one or more code strings. Output per cell: `defines`, `references`,
21	`imports`, plus `confidence` / `has_unknown_references` (Python exec/star
22	imports, R non-standard evaluation, Julia macros). Kernel-side because the kernel
23	has the parser and dialect (IPython magics via `shell.transform_cell()`, then
24	`ast`/`symtable`: module-level assignments, imports, `global` inside functions,
25	referenced-but-unassigned names; ~100 lines in ipykernel; cell magics can declare
26	their own I/O, e.g. rpy2 `%%R -i x -o y`). Static analysis needs no namespace, so
27	serve it on the control channel (like `debug_request`) to avoid queuing behind a
28	busy shell. Even a SQL kernel can implement it (tables created/read).
29	Dynamic complement: optional `namespace_delta: {added, rebound, removed}` on
30	`execute_reply` (diff global names/identity before and after; ipyflow proves it
31	works inside ipykernel).
32	Fallback for kernels without it: the manual DAG wiring. Frontend abstraction:
33	an `IAnalysisProvider` with three backends — kernel (exact), LSP-derived
34	(approximate, via jupyterlab-lsp's connection manager and virtual-document
35	position maps), Lezer syntax tree from CodeMirror 6 (heuristic, zero infra) —
36	mirroring how JupyterLab's completer merges kernel/context/LSP providers.
37	
38	### 2b. Namespace ops
39	`namespace_request` with `delete: [names]` (invalidation before re-run; Pluto and
40	marimo both do this; Julia can't delete a binding, Pluto uses fresh `workspace`
41	modules) and `set: {name: json}` (bind a JSON value; widget-bound variables,
42	papermill-style parameters, DAG input ports). No `get`: `user_expressions` on
43	`execute_request` already returns MIME bundles for expressions.
44	
45	### 2c. Scopes
46	`create_scope(parent) → scope_id`, `execute_request.scope`, `drop_scope`. Child =
47	shallow copy of / lookup chain onto parent (Python dict copy, R `new.env(parent=)`,
48	Julia modules, JS vm contexts; not C++/cling, not SQL). Reactive-grade branch
49	isolation: correct as long as cells rebind rather than mutate — the contract
50	reactive notebooks already impose. Composes with subshells for concurrent branches.
51	
52	### 2d. Already in the protocol — reuse
53	`stop_on_error` (abort queued executions on failure), `silent`/`store_history`,
54	`cellId` in execute_request metadata, comms for widget sync, DAP
55	`variables`/`inspectVariables` for introspection, `supported_features`.
56	
57	### 2e. Decide first
58	Does an edge mean "B runs after A in the same namespace" (supported by all of the
59	above; kernels stay REPLs) or "B receives A's value" (cells as functions over
60	kernel-side value handles — marimo's model taken to its conclusion; a much bigger
61	JEP)? Start with the first; `set` + `user_expressions` emulate the second.
62	
63	## 3. State snapshots (the heavier, optional tier)
64	
65	No language-independent representation of interpreter state exists; "vars +
66	functions + classes" is a reconstruction script, i.e. replay. The universal part
67	is the contract:
68	- `snapshot_request`/`snapshot_reply` on the shell channel (ordered with
69	  executions), reply carries `snapshot_id`, `fidelity: full|partial`,
70	  `uncaptured: [{name, reason}]`; `restore_request`, list, delete; language-
71	  neutral manifest + opaque blob by format id; blobs stay kernel-side.
72	- Semantics to define: quiescence (all subshells idle), comms invalidated on
73	  restore (widget state is half in the frontend), execution counter policy,
74	  external side effects not undone, partial fidelity always reported.
75	Tiers: (1) replay — every kernel, correct by construction; (2) process-level —
76	CRIU/DMTCP via a jupyter_client `KernelProvisioner` + server endpoint, needs no
77	kernel cooperation, Linux only, kernel rebinds ZMQ ports, `--tcp-close`,
78	`cuda-checkpoint` for GPU; (3) language-native — dill/cloudpickle over `user_ns`
79	with per-object fallback (Kishu, ElasticNotebook), R `save.image()`, Julia
80	`Serialization`, JVM CRaC. Kishu's paper: incremental CRIU comparable on
81	checkpoint, up to 36× slower on checkout. For DAG fan-out, "clone kernel" is a
82	better primitive than save/restore (restore one image twice; replay emulates it).
83	Scopes give reactive-grade isolation cheaply; snapshots give REPL-grade isolation.
84	
85	## 4. Relationship to LSP
86	
87	jupyter-lsp spawns language servers server-side and proxies JSON-RPC; core has
88	`@jupyterlab/lsp` plumbing since 4.0, features live in jupyterlab-lsp; notebooks
89	are concatenated into a virtual document with position maps; magics handled by
90	regex overrides; LSP 3.17 notebook sync exists but jupyterlab-lsp hasn't adopted
91	it (most servers don't support it). LSP has no "free variables of this fragment"
92	request; its model is one linear program (references resolve textually), it runs
93	in jupyter_server's environment not the kernel's, and doesn't exist for remote or
94	WASM kernels. Reuse its infrastructure for the fallback provider only.
95	Precedent: Databricks' DBLS (JupyterCon 2025) embeds a language server in the
96	kernel and enriches `complete_request` with runtime context.
97	
98	## 5. Frontend: the DAG view
99	
100	Use React Flow (`@xyflow/react`, MIT, v12.x): nodes are React DOM components, so
101	a Lumino `CodeCell` (from `@jupyterlab/cells`) can be mounted in a custom node via
102	`Widget.attach` in a ref'd div. Open as a second `DocumentWidget` on the same
103	`INotebookModel`, building cell widgets from the shared cell models (verify two
104	CodeCell widgets on one model behave — first thing to prototype). Use
105	`nodrag`/`nowheel`/`nopan` on editors and outputs; `Handle` + `isValidConnection`
106	for typed ports; `NodeResizer`; parent nodes for grouping; dagre/ELK layout; clamp
107	zoom near 1 (ipywidgets/plotly under CSS scale). Persist positions/edges in cell
108	metadata. Runner-up: Rete.js v2. Not viable: the ComfyUI litegraph fork
109	(archived Aug 2025 into the ComfyUI_frontend monorepo as an internal module;
110	frontend repo is GPL-3.0; canvas-rendered nodes; ComfyUI itself is moving nodes to
111	Vue DOM). Prior art to read: marimo's dependency explorer (React Flow + ELK),
112	Elyra's pipeline editor (a node-graph editor inside JupyterLab), Hex Graph view.
113	
114	## 6. Process
115	
116	Prototype without touching the protocol: a comm target in ipykernel for the
117	messages above, the JupyterLab extension, optionally a CRIU provisioner. Validate
118	on ipykernel + one xeus kernel, then open a pre-proposal issue in
119	jupyter/enhancement-proposals. Subshells (JEP 91 → ipykernel 7 → other kernels)
120	is the model path.
121	
```

</details>

```
1	# jupyter-dag design conversation — verbatim transcript
2	
3	Chat with Claude, September 10–11, 2026. This is the design portion of the
4	conversation, reproduced verbatim (citation markup removed; web searches the
5	assistant ran between turns are not shown). It covers kernel state
6	save/restore, the DAG-view frontend library, the talk framing, the minimal
7	kernel-protocol features for reactivity plus DAGs, and the overlap with
8	language-server support.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## Turn 1
13	
14	**User (Thursday, September 10, 2026):**
15	
16	I want to design a DAG feature for jupyterlab that allows a user to string the input cells of a notebook into one or more DAGs, arranged however the user wants. For a DAG that has several output paths, it would be very useful to be able to save and restore the state of the notebook kernel right after the last unbranched step. For Python it's clear enough how to perform this kind of save and restore of state (`pickle(globals())` + some stuff). But the Jupyter project is all about language universalism; a cool feature that only works for python is not sufficient for inclusion into Jupyter/lab core.  What I would really want is to build save_state and restore_state functionality directly into the Jupyter kernel itself. How should I go about implementing these features into the Jupyter kernel? In particular, is there any universal way to represent the state of the interpreter underlying the kernel, independent of interpreter/kernel language? Maybe something along the lines of a way to serialize/deserialize vars + functions + classes?
17	
18	**Claude:**
19	
20	Short version: there is no language-independent representation of interpreter state, and "vars + functions + classes" can't be turned into one. What *can* be universal is the contract: an optional, protocol-level snapshot/restore feature that each kernel implements with whatever its language offers, that reports honestly what it couldn't capture, and that degrades to re-execution for kernels that can't do it at all. That's the shape a JEP for this would need, and it's how the debugger and subshells got in.
21	
22	**Why a serialization format can't be the universal layer**
23	
24	A running interpreter's state isn't a set of named values. It's an object graph with shared references and cycles, closures over mutable cells, class objects whose identity matters to already-created instances, mutated module state (monkey-patches, `sys.path`, RNG state), plus things that don't live in the heap at all: open files, sockets, DB connections, threads, subprocesses, GPU allocations, native-library internals. Any format expressive enough for the first group is by construction that language's own heap format (pickle, R's rds, Julia's `Serialization`), and nothing captures the second group. "Vars + functions + classes" is a source-level view; once you write it down, what you have is a script that *reconstructs* state, which is the replay approach rather than a snapshot. Even in Python, `pickle(globals())` is the weak version of this: modules, generators, C-backed objects without `__reduce__`, `__main__`-defined classes without dill all fail, and pickling variables one at a time silently breaks aliasing between them (dump the namespace as one object to preserve sharing).
25	
26	**What the universal layer should be: an optional feature in the messaging protocol**
27	
28	JEP 92 added a `supported_features` list to `kernel_info_reply` so a kernel can advertise which optional features it supports without coupling that to the protocol version, and subshells are specified as exactly such an optional feature. So the proposal is a feature like `"kernel state snapshots"` consisting of:
29	
30	- `snapshot_request`/`snapshot_reply` on the *shell* channel, not control, because you want it ordered relative to `execute_request`s ("after cell 7, before cell 8"). The reply carries `snapshot_id`, `fidelity: full | partial`, and `uncaptured: [{name, reason}]`.
31	- `restore_request`/`restore_reply`, plus list and delete.
32	- A language-neutral *manifest*: kernelspec, `language_info`, execution count at snapshot time, size, storage backend, captured names with type strings, uncaptured names. The payload is an opaque blob tagged with a format id (`python/dill`, `r/rds`, `criu`). Same pattern as `display_data`: universal envelope, typed opaque content. Blobs stay kernel-side and are referenced by id; they can be gigabytes and don't belong in a ZMQ message.
33	
34	The semantics are where reviewers will push, so nail them down: snapshot only when quiescent (with subshells, all of them idle); comms are invalidated on restore (widget state lives half in the frontend, so the kernel should close all comms before restoring); whether `In`/`Out`/execution count are restored or kept monotonic; restore never undoes side effects outside the process; partial fidelity is always reported, never silently degraded.
35	
36	**Three implementation tiers behind that contract**
37	
38	1. *Replay — every kernel, zero kernel changes.* The DAG extension knows the prefix path; "restore" is restart plus re-execute. Correct by construction modulo nondeterminism and side effects. This is the floor, and the fallback for partial snapshots.
39	
40	2. *Process-level — language-agnostic, Linux only.* CRIU (or DMTCP, which needs no root) images the whole kernel process: heap, threads, fds. The important architectural point is that this needs no cooperation from the kernel, so it belongs in a `KernelProvisioner` in `jupyter_client` plus a jupyter_server endpoint, and it then works for xeus-cling, IJulia, IRkernel, anything. Wrinkles: the kernel binds its ZMQ ports, so on restore it rebinds and the frontend's connect-side sockets reconnect on their own, but established TCP connections must be dropped at restore (CRIU's `--tcp-close`); GPU contexts need NVIDIA's `cuda-checkpoint` in concert with CRIU; images are machine-specific; macOS and Windows have nothing comparable. A cheap cousin is `fork()` at the branch point with the child kept stopped, but ZMQ isn't fork-safe and only the forking thread survives, so that variant does need kernel cooperation.
41	
42	3. *Language-native heap serialization — per kernel.* For Python, dill/cloudpickle over `user_ns` with per-object fallback is essentially what Kishu does: it checkpoints variable and code state of IPython sessions, supports branching states via Git-like commits and checkouts, and relies on cell replay to reconstruct unpicklable objects such as generators. ElasticNotebook goes further and computes a replication plan choosing store-vs-recompute per variable from dependencies, runtimes and sizes. That hybrid — serialize what you can, replay what you can't — is the right model for tier 3, and the `uncaptured` field in the reply is what lets the frontend drive the replay half. R's `save.image()` is unusually complete for this. Julia can serialize `Main`'s bindings but restoring type definitions into a live session is awkward enough that restore-into-fresh-process is the sane mode. JVM kernels have CRaC. C++ via cling has nothing but tier 2.
43	
44	Useful data point when arguing for tier 3 over tier 2: Kishu's evaluation found incremental CRIU comparable on checkpoint time but up to 36× slower on checkout, because a process image can't be restored selectively.
45	
46	**A DAG-specific reframing: clone, don't restore**
47	
48	For fan-out, save/restore is the sequential formulation of a parallel problem. Restoring one CRIU image twice on different ports gives you two kernels, one per branch, running concurrently. A `clone_kernel` provisioner operation is a more natural primitive for a DAG than snapshot/restore, and replay emulates it trivially (start a second kernel, replay the prefix). I'd design the extension against "clone" and treat snapshot/restore as one implementation of it.
49	
50	**How to proceed**
51	
52	Prototype without touching the protocol: a comm target in ipykernel (the same mechanism ipywidgets uses) for the messages above, your JupyterLab extension, and a CRIU provisioner for the language-agnostic tier. Once the semantics hold up on two kernels (ipykernel plus a xeus kernel is the usual bar), open a pre-proposal issue in the enhancement-proposals repo, which is the least formal stage and where feasibility and scope get discussed; the submission guidelines and JEP template are in the same repo. For the DAG semantics themselves, look at how marimo, Pluto.jl and dfnotebook/ipyflow define cell dependencies — all language-specific for the same reasons snapshots are, which is a useful argument to have ready when the JEP review asks why the core feature is a contract rather than a format.
53	
54	---
55	
56	## Turn 2
57	
58	**User (Friday, September 11, 2026):**
59	
60	For the UI component of jupyter-dag, I want to make an alternate view of a notebook in which each cell widget (input+output) is an arrangeable node that can be freely wired to any other cell, a la litegraph.js. litegraph.js is no longer maintained (aside from a "fork" maintained as a subdirectory in the comfyui-frontend project: https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI_frontend/tree/main/src/lib/litegraph), so what is the alternative that exists that has functionality that maps most closely to my vision for a notebook "DAG view"? In other words, what exists that I can use that would involve writing the least custom code myself? Would using the comfyui flavored "fork" of litegraph.js be viable?
61	
62	**Claude:**
63	
64	Use React Flow (`@xyflow/react`). It's the closest fit to "each cell is a draggable, wirable node" and the option with the least custom code, because the one non-negotiable property of your nodes — they must be real DOM, hosting a CodeMirror editor and an output area with arbitrary HTML and widgets — is React Flow's native model rather than something you bolt on.
65	
66	**Why the ComfyUI litegraph fork isn't viable as a dependency**
67	
68	Comfy-Org/litegraph.js was archived on August 5, 2025 and folded into the ComfyUI Frontend monorepo, with the stated reasoning that it was only ever used by ComfyUI and keeping it separate created unnecessary complexity; the merge was meant to enable faster development and bigger architectural refactoring. That is the maintainers telling you it's an internal module, not a library: no package boundary, no semver, and refactors driven by ComfyUI's needs. The import path changed from `@comfyorg/litegraph` to `@/lib/litegraph` inside ComfyUI, and the npm package is frozen at the last pre-merge release.
69	
70	The deeper problem is that litegraph draws nodes on a Canvas2D. A Jupyter cell can't be canvas-drawn, so you'd overlay DOM elements positioned and scaled over the canvas — ComfyUI's DOM-widget trick — and fight z-order, zoom scaling and event routing for every editor and output. ComfyUI itself has concluded that's a dead end: Nodes 2.0 moves their node framework from the litegraph canvas to Vue.js, because Canvas2D and litegraph now impose significant constraints on interface capabilities and custom node interoperability. There's also licensing: ComfyUI_frontend is GPL-3.0. The litegraph subtree was MIT as a standalone repo and may still carry its own license file (I couldn't fetch the directory to check), but pulling code out of a GPL repo into a BSD-ecosystem JupyterLab extension is a review conversation you don't want. Treat the fork as a reference for interaction details — slot rendering, link routing, reroutes, groups — not as a dependency.
71	
72	**Why React Flow specifically**
73	
74	It's MIT-licensed, and nodes are simply React components; the current release line is 12.x and it's still being published actively. JupyterLab ships React and `ReactWidget`, so the graph is an ordinary `ReactWidget` inside a `DocumentWidget` opened on the same `INotebookModel` as the notebook — the DAG view becomes a second view of the same document, the way Lab already opens a notebook as a plain editor. Things you don't write: pan/zoom, drag, multi-select, `Handle`s for ports with `isValidConnection` for typed slots, `NodeResizer`, parent nodes for grouping (your "one or more DAGs"), minimap and controls, ResizeObserver-based node measurement so edges track cells whose height changes when output arrives, and documented dagre/ELK auto-layout recipes.
75	
76	Custom code you will still write:
77	
78	- A node component that `Widget.attach`es a Lumino `CodeCell` from `@jupyterlab/cells` into a ref'd div and detaches on unmount, forwarding resize messages. Build those cell widgets from the notebook model's existing cell models so edits sync between views. This is small, but verifying that two `CodeCell` widgets bound to one cell model behave is the first thing to prototype.
79	- `nodrag`/`nowheel`/`nopan` classes on editor and output areas, so text selection and output scrolling don't move the canvas.
80	- Persisting positions and wiring into cell metadata.
81	- Zoom handling: React Flow scales the viewport with a CSS transform. CodeMirror 6 copes with scaled containers, but some outputs (ipywidgets, plotly) size themselves oddly under scale, so clamp `minZoom`/`maxZoom` near 1.
82	
83	**Runner-up and prior art**
84	
85	Rete.js v2 is litegraph's conceptual cousin — typed sockets, a dataflow engine — and renders nodes through React, so it also works; but it's more plugin assembly for fewer batteries, and its engine is dead weight when the kernel does the executing. jsPlumb Community and AntV X6 also host DOM nodes but leave you writing more of the editor. Skip anything canvas-only.
86	
87	Two things worth reading first: marimo's dependency explorer, which shows all cells as an interactive graph and is built on React Flow with ELK layout, and Elyra's pipeline editor, the existing example of a node-graph editor living inside JupyterLab (on IBM's `@elyra/canvas`), which shows the DocumentWidget and persistence plumbing you'll need regardless of graph library.
88	
89	---
90	
91	## Turn 3
92	
93	**User:**
94	
95	you mention a number of jupyter "successor" notebook projects (marimo, pluto.jl) and I know of some others (hex, databricks). If I wanted to make a 30 minute presentation for a Jupyter conference call "Children of Jupyter", what could I talk about? What interesting new features have popped up in the successor projects? What are the most interesting ways in which the original concept of "ipython notebook" has been reinterpreted?
96	
97	**Claude:**
98	
99	Here's a way to build it that gives you a thesis rather than a product tour: Jupyter's real invention wasn't the notebook UI, it was the 2010 split into kernel / wire protocol / document. Every "child" is a different choice about which of those three genes to keep and which to mutate. Some kept the kernel and replaced the document (Colab, VS Code, Deepnote, Datalore); some kept the document idea and replaced the kernel (Pluto, marimo, Livebook, Observable); some kept only the idea (Streamlit, Quadratic). That gives you a family tree slide, and every later section is one gene under mutation.
100	
101	**Opening (3 min): Jupyter had parents too**
102	
103	Mathematica notebooks (1988), Maple worksheets, the Sage notebook (2006), and the abandoned 2005 IPython notebook prototypes; then IPython 0.12 in December 2011. The point to land: the notebook idea is old, but the kernel protocol is what made forks cheap. A JupyterCon audience will enjoy Joel Grus's 2018 "I don't like notebooks" as the inciting incident for what follows — Hex's own reactivity announcement says it agrees with Grus that notebook state is broken.
104	
105	**Act I (6 min): fixing hidden state — the execution model mutates**
106	
107	This is the biggest reinterpretation: the cell stops being a REPL input and becomes a node in a dataflow graph. Observable (2017) made cells named expressions run in topological order. Pluto (2020) enforced one definition per variable and purges a cell's variables when you delete it. marimo builds a DAG on cells from definitions and references, runs descendants on change, and deliberately doesn't track mutations or attribute assignment; its dependency graph rejects multiple cells defining the same global name because the runtime needs an unambiguous graph. Hex models the project as a DAG behind a linear notebook UI and visualizes it in a Graph view. Show the price of admission too: the single-definition constraint, marimo's lazy mode as the compromise, Polynote's alternative rule that cells only see variables defined above them. Then the Jupyter-native responses: ipyflow and dfnotebook (reactive kernels), and Kishu, which checkpoints session state after each cell and offers Git-like commits and checkouts across branching states.
108	
109	One detail worth a slide: marimo's file format stores each cell as a function whose signature *is* its incoming edges. The DAG lives in the source, not in a sidecar.
110	
111	**Act II (4 min): the file is the program — the document mutates**
112	
113	Pluto notebooks are plain .jl with the package Manifest embedded at the bottom; marimo notebooks are plain .py you can run as a script, import, or test; Livebook is Markdown; Quarto is .qmd; Databricks stores .py with cell separators. Observable Notebooks 2.0 moved to a human-readable HTML-based format and to vanilla JavaScript — the `viewof` dialect that made Observable not-quite-JavaScript is gone, and the open-source Notebook Kit builds static sites from it. Deepnote's new `.deepnote` format goes further and describes the *project*: notebooks, integrations, environment, schedules, published apps, and endpoints in one YAML file. Themes: the environment moves inside the file (Pluto's Manifest, PEP 723 inline metadata plus uv sandboxing in marimo), and outputs move out of it into caches — marimo's WASM export now bundles a runtime cache so published notebooks hydrate outputs without recomputing, letting you share snapshots of runs that can't execute in a browser. Jupytext, MyST and nbformat's stability are Jupyter's side of this argument.
114	
115	**Act III (4 min): a cell isn't a code cell anymore**
116	
117	SQL cells everywhere (Hex, Deepnote, Databricks magics, marimo via DuckDB, Datalore, Observable) — the warehouse as a second kernel. Parameter cells as UI: Colab's `#@param` comments, Databricks widgets, Pluto's `@bind`, marimo's `mo.ui`, versus ipywidgets. No-code cells: Hex's explore cells, Deepnote blocks, and marimo's dataframe output with built-in paging, search, filtering and quick charts. Livebook's Smart Cells are the one to demo: a UI that generates real, editable code — code generation as interface, before LLMs. And the unifying counterexample: anywidget, the one widget standard that runs across Jupyter, marimo, VS Code, Colab, Panel and Solara — a child that reunified the family.
118	
119	**Act IV (4 min): beyond the scroll — space mutates**
120	
121	Hex's Graph view lets you drag cells anywhere and mirrors selection with the notebook view. Count puts cells on an infinite canvas. Datalore's report builder rearranges cells on a canvas into dashboard-style apps. marimo lets cells sit out of order or across columns, and as of its July 2026 launch week presents notebooks as live interactive slides with a dedicated slide editor. Livebook's branching sections fork evaluation from a point in the document. Quadratic and Python-in-Excel put code cells in a spreadsheet grid. This is your natural spot to demo jupyter-dag: a DAG view of a JupyterLab notebook plus kernel-state snapshots is Jupyter getting branching without giving up the REPL.
122	
123	**Act V (4 min): notebook → app → API → agent**
124	
125	Voilà, Streamlit (the rebellion: rerun from the top), marimo run, Hex apps, Deepnote apps and endpoints, Livebook apps. Then the 2025–26 turn: Hex's Notebook Agent traverses the project DAG to find upstream cells and isolate bugs; marimo pair puts coding agents inside a running kernel with access to in-memory data; Jupyter AI 3.0 made JupyterLab a host for external agents via ACP and MCP; Datalore ships an agent skill; Deepnote's CEO framed its open-sourcing as building a standard purpose-built for humans and agents co-authoring. And the twist that the kernel outlived the notebook: ChatGPT's python tool is a stateful Jupyter kernel with no notebook in front of it, and E2B's sandboxes are Jupyter kernels too.
126	
127	**The graveyard (2 min)**
128	
129	Beaker, Polynote (effectively dormant), Noteable (closed 2024), Hydrogen with Atom, and this June, Kotlin Notebook — JetBrains sunset it from IDEA 2026.2, saying AI tools changed how developers explore and prototype and many workflows that drove notebook adoption evolved with that shift. Pair that with Deepnote open-sourcing after seven years hosted. Lessons: polyglot-by-autotranslation didn't stick, proprietary dialects didn't stick, closed formats didn't stick; reactivity did, independently, in three ecosystems.
130	
131	**Close (2 min)**
132	
133	What Jupyter absorbed back: real-time collaboration, JupyterLite, Jupyter AI, subshells, Jupytext. What it hasn't: reactivity and the file format. Leave the audience with the protocol as the durable gene, `.ipynb` as the contested one, and the linear REPL as the one the children mutate most — then pitch the snapshot JEP from your first question as the way Jupyter gets branches without becoming marimo.
134	
135	Five one-minute demos would carry it: marimo reactivity on a slider, Pluto deleting a cell and its variables, Livebook a branching section, Hex the Graph view, and jupyter-dag. Verify dates before you present; several of these projects ship monthly.
136

138	
139	## Turn 4
140	
141	**User:**
142	
143	it seems like my idea for jupyter-dag and the concept of reactive notebooks have some overlap in how they might be implemented. In terms of features added to the jupyter kernel, what would be the minimal set of features required to support both in a jupyter appropriate (ie language agnostic) way?
144	
145	**Claude:**
146	
147	The overlap is bigger than it looks. Strip both ideas down to what they actually demand from the kernel and they're the same three primitives; the only difference is where the edges come from — inferred by the kernel (reactive) or drawn by the user (jupyter-dag). Everything else — topological scheduling, staleness marking, cycle detection, run modes, persistence of the graph — is frontend or server work and should stay there. The kernel is a REPL with a namespace; the minimal additions are all about making that namespace visible and controllable.
148	
149	**1. Code analysis: `analyze_request` → defines / references**
150	
151	Given one or more code strings, return the names each defines and references, plus flags like `confidence` and `has_unknown_references` for when the language can't be sure (Python `exec`/star-imports, R non-standard evaluation and `assign()`, macros in Julia). This is the one language-specific piece reactive notebooks need, and it belongs in the kernel for the same reason `complete_request` and `inspect_request` do: the kernel has the parser. Pluto, marimo, Hex and Observable all do exactly this analysis, each inside their own language-specific runtime.
152	
153	The nice symmetry with your project: jupyter-dag's manual wiring is the universal fallback for kernels that can't implement this (bash, SQL kernels, cling), and analysis is the optional enhancement that pre-populates or validates the edges. Even a SQL kernel can report `defines: [tables created]`, `references: [tables read]`, which is a good demonstration that the protocol is language-agnostic even when the "language" isn't a programming language.
154	
155	Worth pairing with a dynamic complement that's nearly free: an optional `namespace_delta: {added, rebound, removed}` field on `execute_reply`, computed by diffing the global names (and object identity where available) before and after execution. That's the ground truth static analysis approximates, it works for languages with no parser support, and it's what ipyflow does inside ipykernel already — so it's proven to be implementable there.
156	
157	**2. Namespace control: delete (and set)**
158	
159	"No hidden state" is implemented the same way everywhere: before re-running a cell, delete the names it previously defined, so a renamed variable or a removed cell doesn't leave a ghost binding. Pluto and marimo both do this. jupyter-dag needs it too, the moment a node is removed from a path. So: `namespace_request` with `delete: [names]`, and, because it costs nothing extra and makes ports meaningful, `set: {name: json_value}` — a language-agnostic way to bind a name to a JSON-ish value, which is what widget-bound variables (Pluto `@bind`, `mo.ui`), papermill-style parameters, and DAG input ports all reduce to. Don't add `get`: `user_expressions` on `execute_request` already evaluates expressions after the cell and returns MIME bundles, and a bare identifier is a valid expression in essentially every language.
160	
161	**3. Scopes: forkable namespaces**
162	
163	This is the primitive that unifies your branching problem with reactivity. `create_scope(parent) → scope_id`, `execute_request.scope`, `drop_scope`. A child scope starts as a shallow copy of (or a lookup chain onto) its parent. Run the shared prefix in S0, fork S1 and S2 from it, run branch A in S1 and branch B in S2. Branches are isolated as long as cells *rebind* rather than *mutate* — which is precisely the contract reactive notebooks already impose (marimo doesn't track mutations or attribute assignment). Pluto's implementation of variable deletion is literally this: Julia can't delete a binding from a module, so Pluto evaluates in fresh `workspace` modules and copies surviving bindings across. Scopes also compose with kernel subshells (JEP 91): independent branches can execute concurrently in separate subshells, each in its own scope.
164	
165	This also clarifies where the earlier snapshot/restore JEP sits. Scopes give you reactive-grade isolation (cheap, shallow, leaks mutation); snapshots give you REPL-grade isolation (expensive, deep, handles side-effecting code). Minimal is scopes; snapshots are the optional tier above for users who won't sign the reactive contract.
166	
167	**What's already there — use it, don't duplicate it**
168	
169	`stop_on_error` on `execute_request` aborts queued executions on failure, which is the partial-failure semantics a topological run needs. `silent`/`store_history` keep system-triggered reruns out of history. JupyterLab already sends `cellId` in execute_request metadata, so executions attribute to cells. Comms handle widget value sync. DAP `variables`/`inspectVariables` give introspection for debugger-capable kernels. `supported_features` (JEP 92) advertises each of the three new features independently, so a kernel can offer analysis without scopes or scopes without analysis.
170	
171	**Language-agnosticism, honestly**
172	
173	Analysis: good for Python, JS, Julia, R (with caveats), SQL; poor for bash and C++. Delete: Python, R, JS, SQL trivially; Julia only via the module trick; cling only via transaction unloading. Fork: Python dict copy, R `new.env(parent=)`, Julia modules, JS `vm` contexts; not C++, not SQL (copying schemas is not cheap). So all three are optional features with a defined degradation: no analysis → manual edges; no scopes → snapshot/restore or replay; no delete → warn that stale bindings persist. That's the same shape as the debugger: universal contract, per-kernel implementation, advertised capability.
174	
175	**The one thing to decide before writing any of it**
176	
177	Whether an edge means "B runs after A in the same namespace" or "B receives A's value". The former is what all of the above supports and keeps kernels as REPLs. The latter — cells as functions with explicit inputs bound from kernel-side value handles, marimo's model taken to its conclusion — makes typed ports and branch isolation trivial but abandons the shared namespace entirely, and that's a much bigger JEP. Start with the first; `set`/`user_expressions` let you emulate value-carrying edges on top of it without committing to the second.
178	
179	---
180	
181	## Turn 5
182	
183	**User:**
184	
185	Follow up on "1. Code analysis: `analyze_request`": how much does this overlap with the existing language server support/implementation in jupyter/lab? How is the language server stuff currently implemented?
186	
187	**Claude:**
188	
189	**How LSP is wired into Jupyter today**
190	
191	It's two pieces, neither of which touches the kernel. On the server side, `jupyter-lsp` is a jupyter_server extension that spawns language servers as subprocesses (pylsp, pyright, R's languageserver, LanguageServer.jl, texlab, and so on) and proxies their JSON-RPC over a WebSocket. On the frontend side, since JupyterLab 4.0 the plumbing lives in core as `@jupyterlab/lsp` — connection management, document adapters, and the feature registration mechanism — while the user-facing features (diagnostics, hover, jump-to-definition, rename, the LSP completion provider) still come from the separate `jupyterlab-lsp` extension. Core ships the components but no user-facing integration; the LSP service is off by default, and enabling it does nothing until a feature extension is installed, and no language servers come bundled.
192	
193	The interesting part is how a notebook is presented to a server that only understands files. jupyterlab-lsp builds a *virtual document* by concatenating every cell into one file, maps positions from cells into the concatenated file for requests and back again for responses, so the server only ever sees a single linear Python file. Magics are handled by regex "overrides" that rewrite `%timeit x` into something parseable, and foreign-language cells (`%%sql`, `%%R`) are "transcluded" into separate virtual documents for other servers. Because some servers insist on real files, the server extension mirrors those documents into a `.virtual_documents` directory; that's optional now, via a `requires_documents_on_disk` flag in the server spec.
194	
195	LSP 3.17 (2022) added native notebook synchronization — `notebookDocument/didOpen` sends each cell as a separate document with its own URI, and `didChange` carries cell additions and deletions — and servers like ruff-lsp have implemented it. jupyterlab-lsp hasn't adopted it: the maintainer's position is that it would simplify the client at the cost of not working with the majority of language servers, and that the cost/benefit ratio isn't clear yet. So today the concatenation model is what you'd be building on.
196	
197	**How much does that overlap with `analyze_request`?**
198	
199	Infrastructure: a lot. Semantics: almost none. What reactive/DAG semantics need is per-cell *definitions* and *free variables*, order-independent — exactly what Observable's Notebook Kit computes when it finds each cell's unbound references. LSP has no such request. You can approximate it: `documentSymbol` for top-level definitions, `semanticTokens` to classify identifiers (where the server implements it; support is uneven), `references`/`definition` per name to decide whether a reference is bound inside the cell or outside it. That's many round trips per cell, and the answer still comes out wrong in the ways that matter, because the language server's model is one linear program: a reference resolves to whichever definition precedes it textually, which is meaningless when the same name is defined on two branches of a DAG, or when your view arranges cells out of document order. Even 3.17 keeps the notebook as an ordered sequence forming one program; it makes cells first-class for synchronization, not for scoping.
200	
201	There are three further mismatches. The language server analyzes the *language*, not the kernel's *dialect* — IPython's transformations (magics, `!`, `?`, `df << %%sql`), Julia macros in the kernel's environment, R's non-standard evaluation — which is why jupyterlab-lsp needs its regex overrides in the first place. It runs in whatever environment jupyter_server lives in, not the kernel's, so its view of imports can differ from what will execute. And it doesn't exist at all where the kernel does: remote kernels behind a gateway, or JupyterLite/WASM. The kernel, by contrast, has the exact parser and pipeline the code will go through. In ipykernel the whole feature is roughly a hundred lines: `shell.transform_cell()` to expand magics, then `ast` or `symtable` to collect module-level assignments, imports, `global` declarations inside functions, and referenced-but-unassigned names; cell magics could additionally declare their own inputs and outputs (rpy2's `%%R -i x -o y` already says exactly that).
202	
203	The one thing LSP does better is being available while the kernel is busy; `complete_request` queuing behind a long execution is a known pain and part of jupyterlab-lsp's original motivation. Static analysis doesn't need the namespace, so `analyze_request` can go on the control channel, like `debug_request`, which ipykernel services in a separate thread. That neutralizes the advantage. The dynamic complement (`namespace_delta` on `execute_reply`) is inherently kernel-side anyway.
204	
205	**What I'd actually reuse**
206	
207	Follow the completer's pattern: JupyterLab 4's completer merges kernel, context, and LSP providers behind one provider manager, and your DAG extension can define an analogous `IAnalysisProvider` with three backends. The kernel provider (`analyze_request`) is primary and exact. An LSP provider, built on jupyterlab-lsp's existing connection manager and virtual-document position maps, is the approximate fallback for kernels that don't implement the feature. A zero-infrastructure heuristic provider can read the Lezer syntax trees CodeMirror 6 already builds for highlighting — assignment and name nodes are enough to *suggest* edges, which is all your manual-wiring fallback needs. That gives you something working on day one for every kernel, with the protocol addition as the upgrade path rather than a prerequisite.
208	
209	---
```

```
1	# The "genome" model of Jupyter descent (v3, simplified)
2	
3	Only significant changes count as a mutated gene; reimplementations of the same
4	idea do not. Four genes:
5	
6	**Execution model** — a persistent shared namespace where the user decides what
7	runs and in what order. Changed when the runtime decides (reactive dataflow),
8	when out-of-order execution is forbidden (Livebook, Polynote), when everything
9	reruns from the top (Streamlit), or when state forks (Livebook branching
10	sections, Kishu). Not changed by where the kernel runs, what language it speaks,
11	threads, or subshells.
12	
13	**File** — a list of typed blobs with optional outputs. JSON, Markdown, Python
14	with cell markers are all the same idea; dropping stored outputs is too. Changed
15	when the file carries something a cell list doesn't: dependency lock/environment
16	(Pluto's Manifest, marimo's PEP 723 block), an execution cache (marimo exports),
17	project-level config (Deepnote's manifest) — or when there is no cell list at all.
18	
19	**Cells** — the notebook model: an ordered list of code cells in the kernel's
20	language plus prose. Changed when cells can be something else (SQL executed
21	elsewhere, inputs, no-code spec cells, smart cells) or stop being a list
22	(canvas, graph). Not changed by magics, annotations on code cells (Colab forms),
23	or a language switch inside one runtime (Databricks, borderline).
24	
25	**Client** — a human editing and running cells one at a time; any notebook editor
26	qualifies, official or not. Changed when the notebook is consumed without an
27	editor: app, job/API, agent; or when the surface isn't a cell editor.
28	
29	## Classification
30	
31	| Project | Execution | File | Cells | Client |
32	|---|---|---|---|---|
33	| Colab · VS Code · nteract · Jupytext · JupyterLite | — | — | — | — |
34	| papermill / Jupyter Scheduler | — | — | — | job |
35	| Voilà | — | — | — | app |
36	| Jupyter AI | — | — | — | agent |
37	| Databricks | — | — | multi-language (borderline) | jobs |
38	| Quarto | — | freeze cache (borderline) | — | publishing |
39	| Datalore | — | — | SQL cells | report apps |
40	| Deepnote | — | project manifest | SQL, input, chart blocks | apps, endpoints |
41	| Observable | reactive | — | SQL cells, inputs | published, Framework |
42	| Pluto.jl | reactive | Manifest embedded | — | static export (borderline) |
43	| Hex | reactive DAG | project config | SQL, input, chart cells; graph | apps, agent |
44	| Livebook | enforced order, branching sections | — | smart cells, setup cell | apps |
45	| marimo | reactive | PEP 723 deps, cached export | SQL cells | app, script, ASGI, agent |
46	| ipyflow / Kishu (inside Jupyter) | reactive / checkpoints | — | — | — |
47	| jupyter-dag (proposed) | DAG, branches | — | graph | — |
48	| Count | reactive | — | canvas | canvas |
49	| Streamlit | rerun from top | script, no cells | none | app only |
50	| Quadratic / Python in Excel | recalculation | grid | grid | spreadsheet |
51	| ChatGPT tool / E2B | — | none | none | agent |
52	
53	## Consequences for the talk
54	
55	- Colab, VS Code, Datalore-as-editor etc. are distributions, not descendants.
56	- Jupyter has mutated its own client gene via subprojects since 2017 (papermill,
57	  Voilà, Jupyter AI) but has never mutated its execution gene in core; that has
58	  happened only in third-party kernels (ipyflow, akernel, Kishu). That is the gap
59	  the proposal targets.
60	- The file gene never defines a branch on its own; every project that changed
61	  the file also changed something else. Worth saying in the "file is the program"
62	  act: the file format is the gene the children treat as a consequence, not a cause.
63	- Judgment calls a reviewer may push on: Livebook in the execution column rests on
64	  enforced order + branching sections, not reactivity; Databricks sits in "new
65	  client" on the strength of jobs.
66	
67	## Figure
68	
69	`family-tree-v3.svg`: root (Jupyter, four genes), a strip of same-genome
70	distributions, five branches ordered by how much genome survives (new client;
71	new cells; new execution; kernel only; idea only), an extinct row (Beaker '14,
72	Polynote '19, Noteable '22–24, Kotlin Notebook '23–26). Filled dot = kept,
73	hollow dot + strikethrough = changed.
74	
75	## Corrected history to use on slides
76	
77	- Kernel/protocol designed 2010 (Granger, Pérez; pyzmq with Ragan-Kelley; GSoC Qt
78	  console), shipped IPython 0.11 July 2011; notebook + .ipynb shipped IPython 0.12
79	  December 21, 2011; Jupyter named 2014, "Big Split" IPython 4.0 in 2015.
80	- RTC: co-developed with Google as "CoLaboratory" in 2014 (repo under jupyter org;
81	  Chrome app ran code in-browser via PNaCl); Jupyter side became
82	  jupyterlab-google-drive on Google's Realtime API, which Google deprecated
83	  Nov 2017 / shut down Dec 2018; children had RTC (Colab, CoCalc, Deepnote, Hex)
84	  until JupyterLab 3.1 rebuilt it on Yjs in 2021; jupyter_collaboration in Lab 4.
85	- JupyterLite (2021) credits Jyve, Iodide (Mozilla; Pyodide began as its plugin),
86	  Basthon, p5 notebook.
87	- Subshells (JEP 91) are not reabsorbed from a child: internally motivated
88	  (widgets, variable inspectors, control-channel abuse); akernel was the in-family
89	  prototype. Jupytext is not in core.
90	- Better "taken back" examples: debugger (JEP 47, 2020) after PyCharm 2019;
91	  Jupyter Scheduler (2022) after papermill/Netflix, Databricks Jobs; Jupyter AI
92	  (2023) alongside Hex Magic, Noteable's ChatGPT plugin, Colab AI.
```

```
11	state after the last unbranched step. Python is easy (`pickle(globals())`), but

49	Datalore/Kotlin Notebook, Hex):** Proposed thesis: Jupyter's real invention was

52	Act I hidden state / reactive execution; Act II the file is the program; Act III a
53	cell isn't a code cell anymore; Act IV beyond the scroll; Act V notebook → app →

59	of kernel features that supports both, language-agnostically?
60	
61	**Assistant:** They need the same three primitives; they differ only in where
```
