28	## 2. analyze_request implementation in ipykernel: 'transform_cell then ast/symtable' as both designs state it
29	
30	OLD: ~100 lines: shell.transform_cell() then ast/symtable for module-level assignments, imports, `global` in functions, referenced-but-unassigned names; cell magics may declare their own I/O (rpy2 `%%R -i x -o y`); output defines/references/imports + confidence/has_unknown_references.
31	
32	NEW: Same mechanism (transform_cell followed by ast or symtable); imports folded into defines; a single `dynamic` flag; per-cell status with SyntaxError reported as an error entry.
33	
34	ASSESSMENT: Measured locally against IPython 9.17: a symtable-based analyzer over a 200-line cell averages 2.5 ms, so cost is a non-issue for batching whole notebooks. Correctness pitfalls that neither design mentions and that the naive recipe gets wrong: (1) transform_cell rewrites cell magics into a string argument — `%%time\nx = f(y)` becomes `get_ipython().run_cell_magic('time', '', 'x = f(y)\n')`, so the analyzer sees defines=[] refs=['get_ipython']; `%%time`, `%%capture`, `%%prun`, `%%debug` bodies must be re-analyzed from the string, and `%%R -i x -o y` needs magic-specific argument parsing (there is no registry API declaring a magic's I/O; the notes' idea requires inventing one). (2) `!ls $d` and `%timeit g(z)` likewise hide `d` and `z` (var_expand happens at run time, interactiveshell.py:2571-2575). (3) `symtable` has no ALLOW_TOP_LEVEL_AWAIT flag: `await coro(); r = 1` raises SyntaxError from symtable even though IPython runs it (run_ast_nodes compiles with PyCF_ALLOW_TOP_LEVEL_AWAIT, interactiveshell.py:3755-3760); the analyzer must wrap the cell in an async function scope and read that scope's table. (4) `del x` shows as assigned in symtable — it is a removal, not a define; neither design's schema has a 'removes' slot, so `del` must be folded into `dynamic` or handled by namespace_delta. (5) `x += 1` is both a reference and a define; `obj.attr = q` is a mutation that the reactive contract treats as a reference. (6) `global G` inside a function correctly yields G as a define only if child tables are walked. (7) star import and exec/eval/globals()/vars() are the `dynamic` cases; single-line cells pass through the prefilter, so automagic (`timeit x` without %) depends on the live registry and on whether `timeit` is shadowed in user_ns (prefilter.py:455, 463) — this is the one real sense in which prior executions change parsing. The new design's error entry per cell (status/ename/evalue) is the right shape because SyntaxError must be surfaced per cell, not fail the batch. Confidence grades (old) vs single flag (new): the concrete Python sources of uncertainty are all binary per cell, so the flag loses nothing in Python; R's NSE produces graded uncertainty (column names look like free variables) where a per-reference flag would be more useful than either.

65	## 4. namespace delete: does a new execute_request field force a do_execute signature change, or is a hook cleaner?
66	
67	OLD: Standalone `namespace_request {delete: [...]}` on shell — a new handler, no change to do_execute.
68	
69	NEW: `execute_request.namespace_delete: [...]` applied before the code; ipykernel reads execute fields with defaults, so an unsupported list is silently ignored — flagged as the one failure that breaks the no-hidden-state promise.
70	
71	ASSESSMENT: No forced signature change either way. kernelbase.execute_request already builds `do_execute_args` from what the subclass's do_execute accepts, using `inspect.signature` at __init__ (`_accepts_parameters`, kernelbase.py:76-87, 320-322, 823-826); `**kwargs` also counts as accepting. Adding `namespace_delete` to that probe list means bash_kernel's five-argument do_execute keeps working untouched and IPythonKernel opts in by adding a keyword-only parameter — identical to how cell_meta/cell_id landed. The 'silently ignored' failure is real (verified live: an execute_request with `namespace_delete: ['x']` returned ok and x survived) but is not intrinsic to the field: kernel_info can append the feature string only when `_do_exec_accepted_params['namespace_delete']` is true, computed in the base class, so a non-supporting kernel never advertises it. The cleaner shape for both designs is a base-class hook, e.g. `async def do_namespace_delete(self, names) -> not_deleted`, called by kernelbase before do_execute (new) or by the namespace_request handler (old), advertised when overridden — the pattern of do_is_complete/do_debug_request (kernelbase.py:1133-1135, 1206-1207). The hook is transport-independent; the two designs differ only in the wire path. For xeus the field route means extending `execute_request_config` (a struct; source-compatible, ABI-breaking → rebuild) while the message route means a new xinterpreter virtual; both are xeus-core changes. What the ipykernel hook does: `shell.user_ns.pop(name, None)` plus `shell.user_ns_hidden.pop(name, None)` (marimo does exactly `if name in self.globals: del self.globals[name]`); `shell.del_var(name, by_name=True)` additionally scrubs the main-mod cache but refuses `__builtin__`/`__builtins__` (interactiveshell.py:1562-1597). Names that must be refused or the shell breaks: `__builtins__`, `__builtin__`, `__name__` (reset itself skips them, 1524-1528), `get_ipython`, `exit`, `quit`, `open`, `In`, `Out`, `_ih`, `_oh`, `_dh` (init_user_ns, 1457-1486). Deleting a binding does not free the object if `Out[n]`/`_n`/displayhook `_` still reference it (del_var's by-object branch handles that, 1586-1606) — 'no hidden state' at the binding level, not the memory level. A zero-protocol prototype exists for the new design's field: Lab already spreads arbitrary keys into execute_request *metadata* (`deletedCells` and `cellId`, widget.ts:1776-1781, cellexecutor.ts:80-93), kernelbase forwards metadata as `cell_meta` (kernelbase.py:797, 823-824), IPython puts it on ExecutionInfo (interactiveshell.py:3418-3426) and fires `pre_run_cell(info)` — but only when not silent (3455-3456), so an IPython-extension implementation cannot serve the silent purge path; the ipykernel do_execute implementation can.

83	## 5. namespace delete per language: what can and cannot be deleted
84	
85	OLD: Delete trivial for Python, R, JS, SQL; Julia only via Pluto's fresh-module trick; cling via transaction unloading; kernels without delete warn that stale bindings persist.
86	
87	NEW: Same operation, folded into execute_request; Julia may advertise analysis without delete; Pluto's module trick 'only existed to emulate delete in Julia'.
88	
89	ASSESSMENT: Python: dict deletion; limits listed above. R: `rm(list=names, envir=.GlobalEnv)`; locked bindings (`lockBinding`) refuse; S4 classes/methods live in hidden `.__C__`/method tables and need removeClass/removeMethod, so a `setClass` cell is not fully undone by rm. Julia: pre-1.12 a module binding cannot be removed, hence Pluto's `move_vars(..., to_delete, methods_to_delete)` into a fresh `workspace#N` module; Julia 1.12 has `Base.delete_binding(mod, sym)` (found only in issue/discourse snippets, not in NEWS.md; treat as internal/unexported), and methods added to existing generic functions are not bindings at all — Pluto tracks `methods_to_delete` separately. So 'Julia can't delete' is outdated for 1.12 bindings but still true for methods; IJulia would need both. JavaScript (Deno kernel): top-level `let`/`const`/`class` live in the script scope, are not properties of globalThis, and cannot be deleted; only `var`/implicit globals can be removed via `delete globalThis.x`. Deno's REPL and kernel evaluate with CDP `replMode: true` (session.rs), which V8 introduced so `let` can be re-declared (PR #7784 'enable await and let re-declarations'), so *rebinding* works where *deletion* does not — the reactive re-run path is fine, the purge-a-deleted-cell path is not. bash: `unset -v name`, `unset -f fn`; `readonly` variables cannot be unset; exported env of already-spawned children is untouched. SQL: DROP TABLE/VIEW destroys data rather than unbinding a name; 'delete before re-run' maps to CREATE OR REPLACE, and DROP of a shared warehouse table is not something a notebook plugin should do implicitly (marimo drops only its own DuckDB tables, with IF EXISTS and warning on failure). C++ (xeus-cpp): clang-repl's Undo unloads the most recent partial translation unit(s) — LIFO only — and xeus-cpp does not expose it; there is no per-declaration delete. Both designs agree these are feature-gated; the new design's three separate strings (analysis, delete, delta) is what lets IJulia/Deno advertise analysis+delta without delete, which the old design's single-feature-per-primitive scheme also allowed — no substantive difference.

100	## 6. 'Purge without running': standalone namespace_request (old) vs execute_request with empty code + silent (new) — measured against ipykernel 7.3
101	
102	OLD: A separate shell message deletes names; no execution involved.
103	
104	NEW: Send execute_request with code '' and silent=true carrying namespace_delete; nothing else changes.
105	
106	ASSESSMENT: Verified live against ipykernel 7.3.0 / IPython 9.17.1. Empty code + silent=true: no execute_input on iopub, execution_count unchanged (reply execution_count 1 before and after), no history entry, status ok, user_expressions still evaluated (a purge can double as a 'get'), busy/idle status still published. Internally: kernelbase skips the counter bump and execute_input when silent (kernelbase.py:810-812); IPython's run_cell_async returns before touching history, counter, or the `pre_execute`/`pre_run_cell` events for empty/whitespace cells (interactiveshell.py:3429-3432, 3454-3456); ipykernel still fires `post_execute` in its finally (ipkernel.py:452-455), so matplotlib-inline's flush hook runs (harmless). Empty code WITHOUT silent is broken: kernelbase publishes execute_input with count 2, IPython does not increment, the reply says 1 and the next real cell re-publishes count 2 — the frontend would show a duplicated prompt number; so the new design's 'silent set' is a hard requirement, not a nicety. Lab's own `CodeCell.execute` refuses empty code (widget.ts:1770), so the plugin must call `kernel.requestExecute` directly; fine. The old design's namespace_request goes through the same dispatch_shell and also publishes busy/idle (kernelbase.py:429, 494), so there is no status-flicker advantage either way. Two real semantic differences: (1) Abort: dispatch_shell aborts only `execute_request` (kernelbase.py:441-450); after a stop_on_error failure, a queued silent purge execute is answered `status: aborted` (frontend must handle that reply shape for purges), whereas a queued namespace_request would still run — deleting names for a re-run that then never happens. The field design fails safe for 're-run' purges and arguably wrong for 'cell removed' purges; the message design is the reverse. (2) Message count: a reactive re-run of N cells is N messages with the field, 2N with the separate message; on a busy shell the extra message also doubles queue positions. Unknown-type failure mode favours the field: an old kernel ignores the field (verified) but never answers namespace_request (verified: no reply, future hangs) — both need the feature gate, only one hangs without it.

116	## 7. execute_reply.namespace_delta: {added, rebound, removed} (old) vs {added, removed} (new) — cost and correctness in ipykernel
117	
118	OLD: Diff global names and object identity before/after; 'ipyflow proves it works inside ipykernel'.
119	
120	NEW: Exact set differences of names only; rebinding detection dropped because identity comparison either keeps old values alive or compares recycled ids; static analysis already says which names a cell assigns; the field gives bash 'defines' for free.
121	
122	ASSESSMENT: Cost is not the discriminator: on a synthetic 20,000-name namespace `set(user_ns)` before/after plus two differences averaged 0.8 ms and an `{name: id(v)}` snapshot 0.9 ms; real user namespaces are hundreds of names. The correctness points are: (1) Filtering — a raw key diff of a non-silent execution reports IPython's own injections: displayhook pushes `_`, `__`, `___`, `_N` (displayhook.py:231-241) and history pushes `_i`, `_ii`, `_iii`, `_iN` (history.py:1139-1143), both via `push(..., interactive=False)` which also records them in `user_ns_hidden` (interactiveshell.py:1675-1676); the `%who` rule — drop names whose object is identical to the `user_ns_hidden` entry (magics/namespace.py:272-276) — is the correct filter, and neither design mentions it. (2) Concurrency — subshells share one user_ns by design; `set(dict)` while another subshell thread mutates it can raise 'dictionary changed size during iteration' (use `dict.copy()`, which is atomic under the GIL), and the diff attributes the other subshell's assignments to this cell; the field should be omitted or flagged when another subshell was busy during the run. Neither design addresses it. (3) Rebound — the new design's memory/id-reuse objection is accurate: holding the pre-run dict copy keeps every old object alive until the reply, so `del big; big = load()` doubles peak memory; comparing bare ids gives false negatives when the allocator reuses an address. What is lost by dropping it: for `dynamic`-flagged cells (exec, star import, `globals()[k] = v`) static analysis cannot say which pre-existing names were reassigned, and `added` cannot either; that is the one case where `rebound` carried information the frontend cannot get elsewhere. IPython's own precedent uses identity (`drop_by_id`, interactiveshell.py:1678-1694) but for a different problem. (4) Ambiguity in the new design: it does not say whether `removed` includes names removed by the pre-run `namespace_delete` of the same request — if the 'before' snapshot is taken before the delete they appear, otherwise they don't; the frontend needs one answer. Other kernels: R `ls(.GlobalEnv, all.names=TRUE)` cheap; IJulia `names(Main, all=true)` cheap but `ans` appears; bash needs an extra `compgen -v` / `declare -p` round-trip through pexpect per cell (exact for shell variables; functions via `compgen -A function`); SQL needs an information_schema query before and after, seconds on warehouses — should be off by default there; Deno: `Object.keys(globalThis)` misses `let`/`const`, which live in the script scope; the CDP `Runtime.globalLexicalScopeNames` call is what a correct implementation would use (existence of that CDP method not verified here); C++: no.

133	## 8. Scopes (create_scope/drop_scope + execute_request.scope): how they would actually be implemented in ipykernel and what breaks
134	
135	OLD: Child scope = shallow copy of, or lookup chain onto, the parent (Python dict copy, R new.env(parent=), Julia modules, JS vm contexts); reactive-grade isolation as long as cells rebind rather than mutate; composes with subshells for concurrent branches.
136	
137	NEW: Drop scopes entirely; single-definition-per-name plus disjoint definitions make branches non-interfering; mutation isolation comes from the server tier.
138	
139	ASSESSMENT: Concrete ipykernel implementation constraints, verified: `run_code` does `exec(code_obj, self.user_global_ns, self.user_ns)` with `user_global_ns = user_module.__dict__` (interactiveshell.py:1362-1364, 3821-3823). Two consequences kill the notes' phrasing: (a) 'lookup chain' is impossible — `exec()` requires a real dict for globals (`TypeError: exec() globals must be a dict, not ChainMap`, reproduced); (b) a bare dict copy assigned to `user_ns` is also wrong, because if globals and locals differ, module-level code behaves like a class body — `y = 1; def f(): return y; f()` raises NameError (reproduced). A scope therefore has to be a fresh module object whose `__dict__` is the copy, swapped into `shell.user_module`/`shell.user_ns` around each execute (the setter asserts a dict, 715-719; `init_create_namespaces` also rebuilds `ns_table`, 1357-1360). What then breaks or changes: functions defined in scope S1 carry `f.__globals__` = S1's dict forever, so 'merge back' or calling them from another scope reads stale bindings; classes get `__module__` = the scope module's name and pickling by reference fails unless each scope module is registered in `sys.modules` (IPython registers only `__main__`, 1425-1426); `globals()` identity differs per scope, which some libraries (e.g. `%run` machinery, `__main__` guards, `from __main__ import`) observe; `In`/`Out`/`_` are shared list objects after a shallow copy, so history is global (acceptable); `%who` works because it reads whatever `shell.user_ns` is current; comm/widget message handlers run in the shell thread with whatever user_ns is current and comm_msg carries no scope field, so a widget callback fires in the last-used scope (comm manager is process-global, ipkernel.py:52-64); the displayhook `_N` pushes go to the current scope. Composition with subshells does NOT come for free: InteractiveShell has a single `user_ns` attribute, and subshell threads already share it by JEP 91 design; per-branch concurrent scopes would need a context-local `user_ns` inside IPython (a contextvar-backed property, like ipykernel's `_shell_parent`, kernelbase.py:327-331), i.e. an IPython change, not an ipykernel one. `del` inside a child leaves the parent intact (good); mutation of shared objects leaks (the stated contract). R is the language where the notes' model is literal: `evaluate(code, envir = new.env(parent = globalenv()))` and closures capture the right env; IRkernel hard-codes `.GlobalEnv` so it is a one-argument change. Julia: Pluto's module-per-workspace plus `move_vars` is the existing implementation. C++/SQL: none. Net: the new design removes the primitive with by far the largest semantic surface; what is lost is isolation for two DAG branches that legitimately rebind the same name (forces a rename or serial prefix re-run), which the single-definition rule the new design leans on already forbids in marimo/Pluto/Hex.

2	## 11. Feature advertising: JEP 92 conformance of 'optional fields gated by a feature string' and the debug_request transport idea
3	
4	OLD: Each primitive advertised as its own supported_features string.
5	
6	NEW: Three strings (analysis, delete, delta); frontend gates on them; a prototype could ride inside debug_request because ipykernel answers some DAP commands without a session, rejected as a category slip.
7	
8	ASSESSMENT: JEP 92 explicitly allows an optional feature to be 'a list of additional messages and/or a list of additional fields in different existing messages', so gating `namespace_delete`/`namespace_delta` fields on strings is conformant, and Lab already parses the list (default.ts:688-691). Neither JEP 92 nor the spec defines a naming convention or registry; the strings are free text until a JEP names them. 17	## Corrections
18	  - OLD (kernel-design-notes.md §2a; transcript turn 4): 'namespace_delta … diff global names/identity before and after … it's what ipyflow does inside ipykernel already'. ipyflow does not diff namespaces; it instruments execution with pyccolo/sys.settrace handlers (before_call, after_argument, before_attribute_load …) and tracks object ids per statement (ipyflow_tracer.py). It proves kernel-side dataflow tracking is possible in ipykernel, not that before/after diffing is.
19	  - OLD (§2b, §2c; transcript turn 4): 'Julia can't delete a binding'. True through Julia 1.11; Julia 1.12 added binding partitions and `Base.delete_binding(mod, sym)` (seen in JuliaLang issues/discourse; not listed in the 1.12 NEWS.md, so treat as internal). Methods added to generic functions still cannot be removed that way — Pluto's `methods_to_delete` path remains necessary.
20	  - OLD (§2c): child scope as 'shallow copy of / lookup chain onto parent (Python dict copy …)'. A lookup chain cannot be Python's globals (`exec() globals must be a dict, not ChainMap`, reproduced), and a bare dict copy assigned as user_ns with the original module as globals breaks closures over cell-level names (NameError reproduced). The Python implementation must be a fresh module per scope swapped into shell.user_module/user_ns.
21	  - OLD (§2c): scopes 'compose with subshells for concurrent branches'. Not in ipykernel as it stands: InteractiveShell has one `user_ns` attribute shared by all subshell threads; concurrent per-branch scopes need a context-local namespace inside IPython.
22	  - OLD (§2a): 'serve it on the control channel … to avoid queuing behind a busy shell'. Holds for ipykernel (ControlThread always present) and xeus split servers (xeus-python's xaserver); does not hold for xeus's default xserver_zmq (main thread polls both channels), IRkernel (single-threaded R), or the Deno kernel (one tokio select loop). The responsiveness benefit is kernel-specific, not a protocol property.
23	  - OLD (§2a): '~100 lines in ipykernel' via transform_cell + ast/symtable. The naive recipe mis-analyzes cell magics (`%%time` body becomes a string literal), line magics/`!` with `$var`, top-level await (symtable has no ALLOW_TOP_LEVEL_AWAIT flag), and `del`; a correct analyzer is materially larger.
24	  - OLD and NEW: 'user_expressions already covers get'. IRkernel returns an empty namedlist for user_expressions, bash_kernel and metakernel return {}, xeus-cpp ignores the argument. Get exists today only on ipykernel, xeus-python and IJulia.
25	  - NEW: 'ipykernel reads execute fields with defaults, so an unsupported delete list would be silently ignored, and that is the one failure that breaks the no-hidden-state promise'. Confirmed live (extra field ignored, name survived), but it is avoidable inside kernelbase: advertise the feature string only when do_execute accepts the parameter / the hook is overridden, exactly as `_supports_kernel_subshells` and debugpy availability gate the existing strings (kernelbase.py:991-1009).
26	  - NEW: analysis on shell 'stays ordered with executions, which matters when an earlier cell registers a magic that changes how a later cell parses'. Registering a cell or line magic does not change transform_cell's output — `%%foo`/`%foo`/`!` are rewritten textually without consulting the registry (inputtransformer2.py:223, 715-720). Ordering matters only for single-line cells through the prefilter (automagic and user_ns shadowing, prefilter.py:455, 463) and for extensions that register `input_transformers_post`/`ast_transformers`. And the ordering is lost precisely when the design's own responsiveness route (send on a subshell) is used, since subshells are not ordered with the main shell.
27	  - NEW: shell placement 'imposes no threading requirement on kernel authors'. True for the shell channel on kernels without subshells; on ipykernel the recommended subshell route runs transform_cell in a subshell thread concurrently with main-shell execution — the same cross-thread access as the control route (ipykernel already does this for complete_request on subshells, ipkernel.py:552).
28	  - NEW: 'Pluto's fresh-module trick only existed to emulate delete in Julia'. move_vars also carries `methods_to_delete` and macro/JS-link invalidation, and fresh modules were also how Pluto redefined structs before Julia 1.12 allowed type redefinition; 'only' overstates it.
29	  - NEW summary table: 'new optional fields 2' for the old design. The old design has three fields on existing messages (execute_reply.namespace_delta, execute_request.scope, and the optional namespace_delta rebound sub-field aside); minor but the table undercounts by one.
30	  - BOTH: 'purge = execute with empty code' works only with silent=true. Verified: empty code without silent publishes execute_input with a count that IPython never consumes, so the next real cell reuses the same prompt number.

32	## Open questions
33	  - Does `namespace_delta.removed` in the new design include names removed by the same request's pre-run `namespace_delete`? Depends on whether the 'before' snapshot is taken before or after the delete; neither design says.
34	  - Where do 'could not delete' results go in the new design? execute_reply has no slot for refused/missing names (e.g. __builtins__, In, Out, JS let/const, R locked bindings); the old design's namespace_reply could carry per-name status. A `not_deleted` list on the reply, or an error status, needs deciding.
35	  - Should a queued silent purge be aborted with the rest of the queue after stop_on_error? With the new design it is (dispatch_shell aborts every execute_request); with the old design it is not. Correct behaviour differs for 're-run' purges (abort is right) vs 'cell deleted' purges (abort is wrong).
36	  - Should namespace_delta be suppressed or flagged when another subshell executed concurrently? Subshells share user_ns, so the diff is contaminated; also `set(user_ns)` can raise if another thread mutates it mid-iteration (use dict.copy()).
37	  - How does an analyzer learn a cell magic's declared inputs/outputs (`%%R -i x -o y`, `%%sql result <<`)? No registry API exists; either a new magic attribute convention or a per-magic table inside the analyzer is required. Neither design specifies it.
38	  - Top-level `await` in analysis: the analyzer must wrap the cell in an async function scope for symtable; the design should state that the reported defines are the would-be module globals of that scope.
39	  - IJulia: whether control-channel messages are serviced concurrently with a running cell was not verified (Julia tasks are cooperative; IJulia's socket loops are tasks).
40	  - xeus ≥ 5/6 subshell support: no mention in release notes through 6.0.2 or in xinterpreter.hpp / xkernel_core.cpp on main; treated as unsupported but this is an unverified negative.
41	  - `Base.delete_binding` public status and exact semantics (constants, typed globals) in Julia 1.12 — verified only via issue/discourse snippets, not documentation.
42	  - V8 replMode: `let` re-declaration is verified (Deno PR #7784); whether `const`/`class` re-declaration is also permitted in the Deno kernel was not verified.
43	  - CDP `Runtime.globalLexicalScopeNames` as the way for a JS kernel to include let/const in namespace_delta — existence assumed from memory, not verified here.
44	  - Cost policy for namespace_delta on SQL/warehouse kernels (information_schema before/after each cell can take seconds) — should the feature string be advertised per connection rather than per kernel?
45	  - Whether the kernelbase should offer a `do_namespace_delete` hook (transport-independent) rather than a do_execute parameter — the choice affects xeus (config-struct field vs new virtual) and metakernel/bash_kernel equally under both designs.

68	## 2. (1) Build the dependency graph of a cold notebook before anything runs
69	
70	OLD: analyze_request batch on the control channel; frontend `IAnalysisProvider` with kernel/LSP/Lezer backends so something works before or without the kernel.
71	
72	NEW: analyze_request batch on the shell channel; positional list out; `dynamic` flag; imports folded into defines; no frontend fallback mentioned.
73	
74	ASSESSMENT: Both give the same graph input: per-cell defines/references, one batch message, at notebook open. Both need a *running* kernel; neither answers while the kernel is starting, and neither answers on bash/cling. On a cold kernel shell and control are both idle, so the channel choice makes no difference here. The frontend owns everything else under both: name matching (defines→references), topological sort, cycle detection, multi-definition detection, and persistence. Difference: the old design names the fallback providers (mirroring `ICompletionProvider`'s identifier/rank/isApplicable pattern, completer/src/tokens.ts:56-88) so the reactive plugin can show an approximate graph before kernel_info arrives; the new design is compatible with that but silent, so the reactive plugin author must add it anyway. Folding imports into defines is right for edge-building (a `references` to `pd` resolves to the import cell); the old design's separate `imports` list only mattered for display. The new design's positional per-cell `status: error` with ename/evalue for a syntax error is more useful to the plugin than a graded confidence: a syntax error means 'keep the last good analysis for this cell and mark it', which is the marimo behavior.

81	## 3. (2) Rewire when a cell is edited but not run; (14) analysis responsiveness while a long cell runs, with and without subshells
82	
83	OLD: analyze_request on control so it never queues behind a busy shell ('like debug_request, which ipykernel services in a separate thread').
84	
85	NEW: analyze_request on shell; 'responsiveness during a long run comes from sending it on a subshell where the kernel has them. ipykernel 7 routes any shell message by its subshell id, so that works today'; on kernels without subshells it queues behind the running cell.
86	
87	ASSESSMENT: Both designs' frontend does: debounce edits, analyze only the changed cell (batch of 1), diff defines/references against the cached analysis, re-run cycle/conflict checks, and (for renames) record that the old name is now defined by nobody so it goes on the next delete list. The difference is latency during a long-running cell. Verified facts: ipykernel's control channel runs in its own ControlThread (kernelapp.py:414) under `_control_lock` (kernelbase.py:344-348), and control already accepts every shell message type (kernelbase.py:289-298), so the old design's placement is idiomatic for ipykernel. Verified: ipykernel 7 deserializes only the header and routes any shell message to the subshell named by `header.subshell_id` (kernelbase.py:582-592); complete/inspect are ordinary shell handlers (kernelbase.py:276-287); subshells exist iff a shell_channel_thread exists (kernelbase.py:1545-1547). Lab exposes `kernel.supportsSubshells` (default.ts:280-282, gated on the 'kernel subshells' feature string at 688-691), `requestCreateSubshell` (throws if unsupported, 862-880), and a `subshellId` setter on any KernelConnection (default.ts:221-229), so a plugin can hold one connection whose subshellId is set to an 'analysis subshell'. Caveats for both: (i) GIL — a CPU-bound cell on the main shell only yields every 5 ms (`sys.getswitchinterval()` = 0.005 locally), so control- or subshell-hosted analysis is slowed, not blocked; (ii) thread safety — `shell.transform_cell` for single-line cells enters `self.builtin_trap` and runs prefilter (interactiveshell.py:3614-3619), which mutates interpreter-global state; calling it from the control thread or a subshell thread while user code runs is a race under *both* designs (the new design's default main-shell placement avoids it; its subshell escape hatch reintroduces it, as does today's complete_request on a subshell); (iii) JEP 91 calls using control for this kind of interaction 'considered bad practice', which a reviewer will raise against the old design; (iv) the control lane is single-file (`_control_lock`), so a long debug_request delays analysis. On kernels without subshells (IRkernel, IJulia, bash_kernel; xeus subshell status unverified) the new design gives no live rewiring during a long run — the plugin must fall back to a heuristic provider or accept a stale graph until idle; the old design stays live on any kernel with a control thread. The new design's ordering argument (a cell that registers a magic changes how later cells parse) is only partly true in IPython: `%%foo` is rewritten to `run_cell_magic('foo', ...)` regardless of whether `foo` exists (inputtransformer2.py:223-233; verified output), but automagic/prefilter (3614-3619) and `input_transformers_post` (3622) do depend on live state.

98	## 4. (3) Stale markers
99	
100	OLD: Frontend work ('staleness marking ... stay out of the kernel'); namespace_delta with `rebound` could refine it.
101	
102	NEW: Frontend work; namespace_delta {added, removed} only.
103	
104	ASSESSMENT: Identical ownership: the scheduler marks a cell stale when its source changes without a run, when an ancestor runs, or when an ancestor's defined-name set changes; this is marimo's lazy mode ('marking cells as stale instead of running them'). Neither design reports 'value changed', so a rerun that produces an identical value still stales descendants — same as marimo. The only kernel contribution is namespace_delta as a consistency check: if a run's `added` contains a name the analysis did not predict, descendants that read it are stale and the graph needs an edge. Dropping `rebound` costs nothing here because staleness is driven by 'ran', not 'changed'. Delta must be defined over user names only: a naive key-diff of `user_ns` after one history-storing run returns `['_1','_i','_i1','_ii','_iii','x']`; filtering by `user_ns_hidden` leaves `['x']` (verified locally). Neither design says this; the ipykernel implementer must.

111	## 5. (4) Rerun descendants on change with partial-failure semantics
112	
113	OLD: Reuse `stop_on_error`: 'aborts queued executions on failure, which is the partial-failure semantics a topological run needs'.
114	
115	NEW: Inherits the same reuse; adds nothing; delete-before-run means a failed cell's previous names are already gone when it fails.
116	
117	ASSESSMENT: Both designs leave the policy to the scheduler, and the marimo target policy is: descendants of an errored cell do not run ('marimo now always prevents cells from running if any of its ancestors raised an exception'), independent siblings do. `stop_on_error` is coarser than that under both designs. Verified mechanics: on an error ipykernel sets an aborting flag for *that subshell* (kernelbase.py:868-870, 1301-1308), aborts only execute_requests (443-449, so analyze/complete still run), and — with `stop_on_error_timeout` defaulting to 0.0 (242-243) — aborts only requests already sitting in the ZMQ queue when the dummy 'stop aborting' message is processed (1310-1315, 398-409). Consequences: if the scheduler pre-queues the whole topological order on one shell, an error aborts every queued cell including independent siblings (over-abort); if it sends one cell at a time (the only way to get per-branch policy), stop_on_error is inert and the scheduler skips descendants itself; if branches run on separate subshells, an error on A's subshell does not touch B's queue (good) but also does not abort A's descendants queued elsewhere (scheduler must). So the old design's 2d claim overstates what stop_on_error provides. Specific to the new design: because `namespace_delete` is applied before the code runs, a failed rerun leaves the cell's names undefined; the scheduler must record that (otherwise a later manual run of a descendant NameErrors, exactly the case marimo 0.20 fixed with 'ancestor raised'). Under the old design the delete is a separate namespace_request, so the frontend could choose to delete only after a successful run — an option the new design removes (a cell that fails keeps neither old nor new bindings; marimo behaves the same way, so this is defensible for the reactive plugin, less obviously so for the DAG plugin).

124	## 6. (5) 'No hidden state' on cell deletion or variable rename
125	
126	OLD: `namespace_request {delete: [names]}` as its own shell message; Julia via fresh-module trick.
127	
128	NEW: `execute_request.namespace_delete` applied before the code; purge-without-run = execute with empty code and `silent`; warns that an unsupported list is silently ignored, so gate on the feature string.
129	
130	ASSESSMENT: Same frontend bookkeeping under both: a per-cell ledger of names-defined-at-last-run (from analysis at run time, corrected by delta.added), so that on rerun the delete list = old names − new names, on rename = the old name, on cell deletion = all its names; then descendants of the deleted cell are rerun/invalidated (marimo: 'Cells that previously referenced these variables are automatically re-run and invalidated'). The new design's piggyback is a real simplification: delete+run is one shell message, atomic w.r.t. other clients' executes on the same subshell, and the common case needs no extra round trip; the purge-only case works (verified: `run_cell('')` succeeds and `silent` leaves execution_count unchanged) but must bypass CodeCell.execute. Failure modes differ: the new field is read with `.get` defaults so an older kernel ignores it silently (kernelbase.py:791-796 pattern) — the no-hidden-state promise breaks quietly; the old design's unknown `namespace_request` gets only a log warning and *no reply* (kernelbase.py:466-468), so the Lab future never resolves — loud, but a hang. Either way the plugin must gate on the feature string before offering the reactive mode. Neither design specifies what 'delete' scrubs: a plain `del user_ns[name]` leaves the object alive through `Out` and `_` (verified: after `del`, the instance is still in `Out` and `_`), whereas IPython's `del_var` by object also clears output history and displayhook refs (interactiveshell.py:1562-1608). For a reactive plugin promising no hidden state, the spec should say which; otherwise `_`/`Out[n]` remain reachable and a cell reading `_` sees stale data. Julia: see finding (15).

139	## 7. (6) Two DAG branches that both define the same name (e.g. `model`)
140	
141	OLD: Scopes: fork S1, S2 from the prefix scope; run each branch in its own scope; isolation holds if cells rebind rather than mutate; composes with subshells.
142	
143	NEW: Scopes removed: 'the DAG plugin can enforce the same rule [one definition per name], or at least flag a violation before running'; users needing isolation use the server-level clone-kernel tier.
144	
145	ASSESSMENT: This is the largest UX divergence for the DAG plugin. Old: the plugin creates a scope at every fork point, maps branch→scope, tags each execute_request with `scope`, and — because a child is a shallow copy at fork time — must drop and re-fork children whenever the shared prefix reruns, and must name the scope when reading a port value. That scope-lifecycle state machine is scheduler-owned and is not small, but same-name branches Just Work, including running both concurrently on two subshells. Kernel-side feasibility in ipykernel is weaker than the notes imply: IPython has one `InteractiveShell` with one `user_ns`/`user_global_ns` shared by every subshell thread (ipkernel.py:386 `shell = self.shell`; ipkernel.py:694 `exec(code, shell.user_global_ns, shell.user_ns)`); running two scopes concurrently means swapping the namespace per request under concurrency, which is a change to IPython's run_cell path, not a dict copy. New: the plugin must (a) detect the conflict from analysis defines (impossible on kernels without analysis until delta.added shows `model` from two nodes after the fact), (b) refuse to run, or (c) serialize: run branch A, run A's readers, `namespace_delete: ['model']`, run branch B, run B's readers — correct but sequential and the readers of A's `model` become stale/unrunnable once B ran, which is what the DAG user wanted to avoid, or (d) clone the kernel per branch (REST endpoint that does not exist yet; Linux/CRIU or replay). Hex and marimo do ship (b) ('marimo requires that every global variable be defined by only one cell'), so the reactive plugin loses nothing; the DAG plugin loses its headline branching feature unless (d) lands. The new design's 'Pluto's fresh-module trick only existed to emulate delete' is accurate about Pluto (WorkspaceManager `move_vars`/`bump_workspace_module` exist because 'Julia cannot delete bindings') but does not address that the old design used scopes for *branch isolation*, which is a different job.

155	## 8. (7) Parameter sweep: run the same subgraph with several inputs
156	
157	OLD: Fork N scopes from the prefix, `set` the parameter in each, run the subgraph in each (optionally N subshells), read results with `user_expressions` + `scope`.
158	
159	NEW: No set, no scopes: sequential loop in one namespace (generated assignment cell per value, then the subgraph, then user_expressions), or N cloned kernels for parallelism.
160	
161	ASSESSMENT: Old: the sweep is N×(create_scope, namespace set, k executes, drop_scope) with no language-specific code generation; results are isolated per scope so they can be collected after all runs. New: the plugin must emit a language-specific assignment cell per value (this is papermill's translator problem, which papermill solves with per-language PythonTranslator/RTranslator/JuliaTranslator/ScalaTranslator classes and an injected-parameters cell), run sequentially because each iteration overwrites the last (results must be read out via user_expressions on the last execute of each iteration before the next starts), and parallelism requires clone-kernel. The new design's objection that JSON→binding is ambiguous in R/JS/Julia is true, but it does not go away — it moves from the kernel (which knows its language, and already does the reverse mapping in `user_expressions` via `display_formatter.format`, interactiveshell.py:2936-2948) into every frontend plugin, which then needs a translator table and is no longer language-agnostic. Net: the sweep is the case where dropping set+scopes costs the DAG plugin the most code.

The new design's 'nothing is lost' is defensible in one sense the old notes did not spell out: `namespace_delete` is a protocol op whose *implementation* in IJulia can be Pluto's trick (move surviving bindings to a fresh module, evaluate future cells there — `move_vars`/`bump_workspace_module`), so Julia can advertise delete under either design; what it cannot do under either is redefine structs cleanly or drop methods on old types. What the new design does lose for Julia is only the branch-isolation use of scopes (finding 6). Gating matrix the plugin must implement under the new design: analysis ∧ delete → full reactive; analysis ∧ ¬delete → reactive with ghost warning; ¬analysis ∧ delta → DAG with suggested output ports; none → manual DAG only. The old design's matrix is the same plus a scopes axis (branching on/off). Which kernels land where is unverified beyond ipykernel; IRkernel/IJulia/xeus subshell and control-thread behavior were not confirmed by any source I found.

83	## 16. Scheduler ownership summary and where old-design scopes/set help or hurt the frontend
84	
85	OLD: Kernel: analyze (control), namespace delete+set, scopes (create/execute-in/drop), optional delta with rebound, optional snapshot tier. Frontend: graph, topo order, cycles, staleness, conflicts, scope lifecycle.
86	
87	NEW: Kernel: analyze (shell), execute_request.namespace_delete, execute_reply.namespace_delta{added,removed}. Frontend: everything else, plus per-language parameter code-gen and conflict refusal; isolation deferred to a server clone-kernel REST op.
88	
89	ASSESSMENT: Common to both (scheduler-owned): topological order; cycle detection (marimo: hard error); staleness; multi-definition conflict detection from analysis defines; per-cell ledger of names defined at last run and computation of delete lists; failure propagation (block descendants of an errored ancestor, keep siblings), sending cells one at a time or per-branch subshells because stop_on_error is queue-scoped; heuristic/LSP analysis providers for cold start, busy non-subshell kernels, and kernels without analysis; persistence of manual edges and positions in cell metadata; feature-string gating. Old-only frontend work: scope lifecycle (create at fork, branch→scope map, drop/re-fork children when the prefix reruns, scope on every execute and every user_expressions read, scope×subshell mapping, undefined comm/widget behavior inside child scopes). New-only frontend work: language-specific assignment code generation for parameters and sweeps (papermill's translators, in the plugin); refusing or serializing same-name branches; clone-kernel orchestration against a REST endpoint that does not exist yet. Where scopes+set made the frontend simpler: (6), (7), (8), (10) — each collapses to one message per branch/parameter. Where they made it harder: invalidation of child scopes on prefix rerun is a second dependency graph the scheduler must maintain, and the ipykernel implementation risk (shared InteractiveShell namespace) could have stalled the prototype. For the *reactive* plugin alone, the new design is sufficient and simpler; for the *DAG* plugin, the new design covers linear-with-fan-out DAGs under disjoint definitions and defers genuine branching to a tier outside the kernel protocol.

98	  - OLD design (kernel-design-notes.md:52-55; transcript turn 4): `stop_on_error` is described as 'the partial-failure semantics a topological run needs'. It is coarser: ipykernel aborts every execute_request already queued on the same subshell (kernelbase.py:868-870, 1301-1315, timeout default 0.0 at 242-243), so it over-aborts independent siblings if the scheduler pre-queues, and does nothing if the scheduler sends one cell at a time. The scheduler must implement 'block descendants of an errored ancestor' itself.
99	  - OLD design (kernel-design-notes.md:45-50): 'Scopes ... composes with subshells' and 'Python dict copy' understate the ipykernel cost. IPython has one InteractiveShell with one user_ns shared by all subshell threads (ipkernel.py:386, 694); per-request namespace switching under concurrency is a change to IPython's run_cell path, not a dict copy.
100	  - OLD design (transcript turn 5): placing analyze_request on the control channel 'neutralizes' the busy-kernel problem, but `shell.transform_cell` for single-line input enters `builtin_trap` and prefilter (interactiveshell.py:3614-3619), which is not safe to run from another thread while user code executes; and JEP 91 calls using control for this 'considered bad practice'. The old notes do not mention either.
101	  - NEW design (new-design.md:36-41): namespace_delta 'gives parser-less kernels such as bash the defines half of an edge for free'. Not free: bash_kernel is a pexpect REPL wrapper with no parsing and would need before/after variable enumeration inside each command turn; and a set-difference misses reassignment of existing names, the common case in shell scripts (verified analog: rebind invisible to key diff).
102	  - NEW design (new-design.md:14-19): 'Pluto's fresh-module trick only existed to emulate delete in Julia, so nothing is lost there' is true of Pluto but answers the wrong question — the old design's scopes were for branch isolation (two branches defining `model`), which the new design gives up for the DAG plugin unless the server-level clone-kernel tier exists. Julia delete itself can still be implemented under either design by module swapping.
103	  - NEW design (new-design.md:27-32): 'comms already carry widget-bound values' as the replacement for `set` is Python/ipywidgets-specific; a comm target requires kernel-side code in each language, so it is not a language-agnostic path for a Lab plugin. 104	  - NEW design (new-design.md:43-51): 'stays ordered with executions, which matters when an earlier cell registers a magic that changes how a later cell parses' is only partly true for IPython: `%%foo` is rewritten to run_cell_magic regardless of registration (inputtransformer2.py:223-233); only automagic/prefilter and input_transformers_post depend on live state (interactiveshell.py:3614-3623).

122	## 1. Protocol footprint (message types, fields, feature strings, channels)
123	
124	OLD: Section 2 adds four request/reply pairs (analyze_request, namespace_request, create_scope, drop_scope), two optional fields (execute_request.scope, execute_reply.namespace_delta), and section 3 adds four more pairs (snapshot, restore, list, delete). Uses two channels: control for analyze_request, shell for everything else. Feature strings are never enumerated; transcript turn 4 says the three new features are advertised independently, snapshots would be a fourth.
125	
126	NEW: One new pair (analyze_request/reply on shell), two optional fields (execute_request.namespace_delete: [str], execute_reply.namespace_delta: {added, removed}), three feature strings (not named in the text; by implication: analysis, delete, delta). Shell channel only, with subshells as the responsiveness escape hatch. Snapshot/clone moved to jupyter_client provisioner + Jupyter Server REST.
127	
128	ASSESSMENT: The new design's table (1 pair / 2 fields / 3 strings vs 4+4 / 2 / 4) is arithmetically fair to the old design as written. Two things the table hides: (a) the old design's feature-string count of 4 is an inference, since kernel-design-notes.md never lists strings; (b) the new design has three feature strings for a surface of one message and two fields, a worse ratio than JEP 91 (one string for three control messages plus a header field) or the debugger (one string for two message types plus DAP additions). JEP 92 explicitly allows one feature to be 'a list of additional messages and/or a list of additional fields', so bundling was available; the new design's justification (bash advertises delta without analysis; Julia advertises analysis without delete) is a real language-coverage argument and a reviewer would probably accept it if each string maps to a crisp, separately testable contract. On channels, the new design is strictly smaller: it never asks a kernel to put non-control work on the control socket. The ipykernel precedent that most matters for footprint: ipykernel 7.3.0 declares kernel_protocol_version 5.3 while shipping 5.5 features advertised through supported_features, which shows the community already accepts small feature-gated deltas without version bumps; the smaller delta is the one that lands the way subshells did.

Optional request fields: the spec lists allow_stdin and stop_on_error as plain fields with no versionadded annotation (the only annotated execute_request change is 'user_variables removed' in 5.0), and jupyter_client's adapter.py shows how field-level changes are bridged across versions with setdefault/pop. That is exactly the hazard the new design admits for namespace_delete (see failure-mode finding). Optional reply fields: spec style already includes conditionally present reply keys (is_complete_reply.indent 'For other statuses, this field does not exist'; kernel_info_reply.supported_features 'Optional'). So namespace_delta as a reply field is ordinary spec style in both designs. The new design's deletedCells precedent is weaker than stated: Lab pushes deleted cell ids into notebook.model.deletedCells (actions.tsx:3344, 3358), passes them through CodeCell.execute (cellexecutor.ts:80-93) into the execute_request *metadata* dict (cells/src/widget.ts:1776-1781, outputarea/src/widget.ts:1047), the spec never mentions deletedCells or cellId (grep of messaging.rst finds neither), and ipykernel/IPython contain no reference to deletedCells at all (kernelbase.py:797-798 extracts only cellId). It is Lab-private context metadata that no kernel acts on. A spec reviewer would say: information a kernel must act on goes in content, so namespace_delete in content is correct, but the deletedCells citation is precedent for the frontend bookkeeping only, not for a kernel-visible field. One real precedent the new design could have used and did not: ipykernel already probes do_execute's signature to pass cell_meta/cell_id only to kernels that accept them (kernelbase.py:319-322, 823-826); a namespace_delete parameter would slot into that same opt-in mechanism, which is how a wrapper kernel (bash_kernel, IRkernel are not wrappers, but the many kernelbase subclasses are) would signal support.

The debugger precedent the old design leans on is different in kind: JEP 47 put debug_request on control because DAP commands must work while the shell is stopped at a breakpoint, and JEP 80 later put kernel_info on control for the same reason ('the shell channel may be stopped'). Neither is 'this is cheap so it should not wait'. The new design's read of the precedent is the correct one. The new design is also right that the DAP route is a category slip: ipykernel does answer five commands with no session (debugger.py:320-326: debugInfo, inspectVariables, richInspectVariables, modules, copyToGlobals) and dumpCell carries source (debugger.py:464-478), but dumpCell is a started-session handler (309-317) and the whole path requires debugpy; the new design already confines this to a prototype transport.

170	## 4. What the spec and JEP 91 say the control channel is for; does a static-analysis request belong there
171	
172	OLD: analyze_request on control, justified by 'static analysis needs no namespace' and 'avoid queuing behind a busy shell'.
173	
174	NEW: analyze_request on shell; responsiveness during a long run comes from a subshell where available.
175	
176	ASSESSMENT: The spec's definition: 'This channel is identical to Shell, but operates on a separate socket to avoid queueing behind execution requests. The control channel is used for shutdown and restart messages, as well as for debugging messages.' Running it in a separate thread is a recommendation, not a requirement. JEP 91's motivation is the decisive text against the old design: it lists completion, introspection and inspecting state while busy as the things users wanted, then says 'Since the control channel has had its own thread it has been possible to use the control channel for such interactions, but this is considered bad practice as it should only be used for control purposes, and the processing of those messages should be almost immediate.' Subshells are the sanctioned answer to precisely the problem the old design solves by using control. A spec maintainer would cite that sentence and ask the old design to move analysis to shell. Two further problems with the old design's premise: (1) 'needs no namespace' is not true of the ipykernel implementation it proposes, because shell.transform_cell (interactiveshell.py:3598-3612) consults the registered magics/input transformers, which are mutable interpreter state that an earlier execute can change; the new design names this (a cell registering a magic changes how a later cell parses). (2) The benefit only materializes on kernels with a control thread: ipykernel has one (kernelapp.py:414, 613-616) and xeus's split server does, but xeus-zmq's default server polls shell and control in one loop (xserver_zmq_default.cpp:28-42), IRkernel polls hb/shell/control in one synchronous loop (kernel.r:393-397), and IJulia runs control as a cooperative @async task (eventloop.jl:69-71); on all of those a control-channel analyze_request queues behind execution anyway. The new design's phrase 'imposes no threading requirement on kernel authors' is slightly loose (the control route does not formally require a thread either) but the substance holds: shell placement asks nothing new of any kernel, and control placement only pays off where a thread exists. Analysis batches are also not 'almost immediate' by JEP 91's standard when a frontend sends a whole notebook.

6	## 5. Ordering guarantees: shell vs control vs subshell, and the analysis-ordering claim
7	
8	OLD: analyze_request on control (unordered relative to shell executions); snapshot_request deliberately on shell 'ordered with executions'. No statement about ordering of analysis vs execution.
9	
10	NEW: analyze_request on shell so it 'stays ordered with executions, which matters when an earlier cell registers a magic that changes how a later cell parses'; and 'responsiveness during a long run comes from sending it on a subshell'.
11	
12	ASSESSMENT: JEP 91 is the only text that states the ordering model explicitly: 'A subshell request may be processed concurrently with other subshells. Within an individual subshell, requests are processed sequentially.' Control has no ordering relation to shell; ipykernel serializes control messages among themselves with _control_lock (kernelbase.py:273, 344-348) but nothing orders them against shell. The old design therefore gets no ordering for analysis at all, which is consistent with its claim that analysis is namespace-free, but that claim is wrong for magics (previous finding). The new design's two claims are individually true and jointly a trade-off it does not spell out: a request sent to a child subshell is ordered only within that subshell, so the moment the frontend uses the subshell escape hatch it gives up the ordering argument it just made. In practice the frontend picks per call (main shell when it needs the post-execution parse state; a subshell when it needs an answer during a long run) and the design should say so. The subshell route also runs transform_cell concurrently with an executing main shell, which is the same thread-safety question as the control route; ipykernel's own subshells do run arbitrary code concurrently so this is no worse than what JEP 91 already allows, but it is not the 'no concurrency' story the new design's wording implies. Note the messaging spec source references an execution_semantics label (messaging.rst:558) whose definition I could not find in messaging.rst; the explicit 'shell is sequential' guarantee is in JEP 91, not the spec body.

34	## 7. Failure mode on a kernel that ignores unknown fields / unknown message types
35	
36	OLD: delete is a separate namespace_request; scopes are separate messages plus an execute_request.scope field.
37	
38	NEW: delete is an execute_request field; admits 'an unsupported delete list would be silently ignored, and that is the one failure that breaks the no-hidden-state promise'; relies on feature-string gating.
39	
40	ASSESSMENT: The two designs fail differently, and the difference is the strongest argument a reviewer has against the new design's field placement. Unknown message type on shell: ipykernel logs 'Unknown message type' and sends no reply but still publishes idle (kernelbase.py:466-468, 494); JEP 91 codifies this ('Unrecognised shell request messages ... will be ignored as normal'); on control it logs an error and sends no reply (kernelbase.py:370-372); IRkernel logs 'Unhandled control message' (kernel.r:338). So the old design's namespace_request on an unsupporting kernel hangs the frontend future, which is loud and detectable by timeout, and no code runs. Unknown field on execute_request: every kernel checked reads with defaults, so the new design's namespace_delete is dropped and the cell executes against stale bindings with an ok reply. That is a silent correctness failure, and the new design says so. Both designs require gating on the feature string, so under correct gating neither fails; under a gating bug the old design fails safe and the new design fails unsafe. The old design's execute_request.scope has the same silent-ignore hazard (a kernel without scopes would run branch code in the main namespace), so the old design is not free of it either; it just does not admit it. Mitigations available to the new design within its own shape: make a kernel that advertises delete echo what it removed in the reply (namespace_delta.removed already exists, so the frontend can verify the purge happened), which turns the silent failure into a detectable one without a new message.

A flat namespace_delete is consistent; if set returns later it becomes a sibling namespace_set, which is accretive, not breaking, so the flat choice does not foreclose anything. On the message name: every existing stateless code request is named for the question it answers (is_complete, complete, inspect); 'analyze' names an activity and overlaps in the reader's mind with inspect_request, which already returns information about code. Expect the review to push for a name that says what comes back. A concrete schema problem in the new design: every other request's `code` field is a string (execute, complete, inspect, is_complete), and the new design makes `code` a list of strings; reusing a conventional field name with a different type is the sort of thing a spec maintainer rejects on sight, and jupyter_client/Lab typings assume code: string. The old design gives no schema, which is a bigger gap for a JEP but means it has not yet made this mistake. On 'dynamic': the old design's has_unknown_references distinguishes 'may reference names I can't see' from 'may define names I can't see'; those break upstream and downstream edges respectively, and a single flag forces the frontend to treat both as 'run after everything and invalidate everything after'. Folding imports into defines loses a distinction the old design kept; it can be re-added as an optional key, so it is additive, but a frontend that wants to exclude module names from edges has no way to tell.

75	## 10. Is the new design a forward-compatible prefix of the old one; where do they fork irreversibly
76	
77	OLD: analyze on control; delete+set as namespace_request; scopes as three additions; snapshots as four shell messages; delta with rebound; analyze_reply with imports and graded confidence.
78	
79	NEW: analyze on shell; delete as execute_request field; set, scopes, snapshots removed from the kernel protocol; delta without rebound; imports folded into defines; single dynamic flag.
80	
81	ASSESSMENT: Additive later: set (as namespace_set field or message), scopes (create/drop messages plus execute_request.scope), snapshots (new messages), namespace_delta.rebound, analyze_reply.imports. Nothing in the new design blocks any of these, so on those axes it is a prefix. Two forks are real. (1) Channel for analysis. Once specified on one channel, moving it costs a deprecation cycle (shutdown_request's move from shell to control took the 5.4 deprecation and is still listed on both). JEP 80 shows a message can later be allowed on both channels, so shell-first is not a dead end, but 'on both' is a special case the spec has used exactly once and JEP 91's language makes control-later unlikely to be accepted. Choosing shell first is the reversible direction. (2) Delete as field vs message. A field cannot later be retired in favor of a message without leaving two ways to do one thing, which reviewers dislike; conversely a message can always be complemented by a convenience field. The new design's field also changes semantics: delete is a pre-step bound to an execution, and standalone purge becomes 'execute empty code, silent' (the spec sanctions empty code + silent for the counter, messaging.rst:547-549, so this works, but it publishes busy/idle and execute-path side effects for a purge). This is the fork where the designs commit differently, and the new design's own admission about silent ignore is the cost of its choice. A third, softer fork: analyze_reply's shape (code as list, single dynamic flag) would be a breaking change to revise once kernels ship it, so the schema must be settled before ipykernel implements it.

115	  - Neither design specifies what a kernel that advertises delete does when a name cannot be removed (Julia bindings, cling): reply status, partial-failure reporting, whether the code still runs.
116	  - Neither design specifies where the pre-run delete sits relative to transform_cell, the execute_input broadcast, silent, and store_history.
117	  - Neither design names its supported_features strings or says whether they carry a version; JEP 91 itself says a version specifier is probably needed (kernel-subshells.md:90-92).
118	  - Thread-safety of running IPython's transform_cell off the main thread (on the control thread in the old design, on a subshell thread in the new design's escape hatch) is not established; ipykernel's DAP handlers read user_ns from the control thread and subshells run code concurrently, so there is precedent for both, but no verification here.
119	  - The exact protocol versions in which allow_stdin and stop_on_error were added could not be verified: the spec lists them without versionadded annotations (messaging.rst:500-520) and the 5.0/5.1 changelog entries do not mention them.
120	  - The explicit 'shell requests are processed sequentially' guarantee appears in JEP 91 (kernel-subshells.md:172-173); messaging.rst references an execution_semantics label (line 558) whose definition I did not find in that file, so I could not quote the spec body on shell ordering.
121	  - Whether dropping scopes is acceptable for the user-drawn DAG plugin depends on a product decision neither design makes explicit: two branches that legitimately define the same name (x = f(a) on one, x = g(a) on the other) are forbidden under the new design's one-definition rule and were the case scopes existed for.
122	  - How the new design's 'analysis on a subshell' interacts with JupyterLab's default of running comms on one subshell per comm target (default.ts:94-104) was not examined.
123	  - Spec text at messaging.rst:1198 reads 'Kernels supporting subshells must include debugger in supported_features', which looks like a copy error in the spec itself; irrelevant to either design but worth knowing when quoting that section.

128	## 1. Static analysis (analyze_request): per-language parser availability and undecidability
129	
130	OLD: analyze_request returns defines/references/imports + confidence/has_unknown_references; kernel-side because the kernel has the parser; served on the CONTROL channel because 'static analysis needs no namespace'; claims 'good for Python, JS, Julia, R (with caveats), SQL; poor for bash and C++'; ipykernel impl = transform_cell + ast/symtable, '~100 lines'.
131	
132	NEW: Same message, on the SHELL channel (shares complete/inspect dispatch, stays ordered with executions 'when an earlier cell registers a magic that changes how a later cell parses'); imports folded into defines; single boolean 'dynamic' flag; responsiveness via subshells.
133	
134	ASSESSMENT: Per-language matrix. PYTHON (ipykernel): parser in-kernel; tested transform_cell+symtable in the local venv. It works for plain code (`df += 1` -> defines [df]; `def f(): global q; q=1` -> defines f and q-via-global), but every magic body is hidden: `%%time\nx = 1` transforms to `get_ipython().run_cell_magic('time', '', 'x = 1\n')` and symtable reports defines=[] references=['get_ipython']; same for `%timeit z = ...` and `%%capture out` (which actually defines `out`). So the ipykernel analyzer must special-case run_cell_magic/run_line_magic string arguments and per-magic I/O declarations; the old design's '~100 lines' undercounts this. Undecidable: exec/eval (`exec('w = 3')` -> defines []), `from os.path import *` (defines []), globals()[k]=, setattr on __main__, %run/%store. R (IRkernel): evaluates in .GlobalEnv (IRkernel R/execution.r: `evaluate(request$content$code, envir = .GlobalEnv, ...)`); R has parse()/getParseData() and codetools::findGlobals in-process, so the primitive is implementable, but findGlobals' own doc says the result 'is an approximation' and 'assumes no use of assign and rm'; NSE (with/subset/dplyr column names) yields false-positive free references; library()/attach()/source()/load()/data() are defines the analyzer cannot enumerate. JULIA (IJulia): Meta.parse in-kernel and Pluto's ExpressionExplorer is a working reference; but Pluto expands macros INSIDE the live workspace module before resolving the topology (src/evaluation/MacroAnalysis.jl:1-3 `import .WorkspaceManager: macroexpand_in_workspace`, and Run.jl:157 cells_to_macro_invalidate), because a macro's expansion depends on macro definitions that exist only after earlier cells ran. This falsifies the old design's premise that analysis 'needs no namespace' for Julia and supports the new design's ordered-shell-channel placement. JS: Deno parses every input with deno_ast/swc before evaluation (cli/tools/repl/session.rs, parse_module + ImportCollector) so an analyzer is in-kernel; ijavascript/nel runs code with `vm.runInThisContext(code)` (nel lib/server/main.js:296) and has no analysis step, though node bundles acorn. Undecidable in both: globalThis[k], eval, dynamic import, `with`. BASH (bash_kernel): pexpect REPLWrapper around a bash subprocess; no parser is reachable, `bash -n` is syntax-only (`bash -n -c 'x=$(cat f); eval "$y"'` passes), eval/source/read/declare -n make it hopeless; would not advertise. C++ (xeus-cpp): the full clang parser is in-process, so declared and referenced names are exact, but a cell cannot be parsed without the accumulated TU state (types, templates from earlier PTUs) — again not namespace-free; the old design's 'poor for C++' is too pessimistic, the real constraint is order-dependence. SQL: for SQLite the authorizer callback runs at prepare time and reports SQLITE_READ per table/column and CREATE/INSERT/DROP per table (sqlite.org/c3ref/set_authorizer.html: 'invoked only during sqlite3_prepare()'), so exact per-statement table reads/writes are available without executing; xeus-sql (SOCI over DB2/Firebird/MySQL/ODBC/Oracle/PostgreSQL/SQLite3) has no common parser, so it is backend-specific. JVM (IJava = JShell): `SourceCodeAnalysis.sourceToSnippets(String)` converts source to Snippet objects without installing or executing them (javadoc), so declared names (VarSnippet/MethodSnippet/TypeDeclSnippet names) are exact; referenced names are not exposed (dependents() is a snippet graph 'designed to be inclusive and may include many false positives'), so JVM advertises defines-only or a heuristic references list. Net: analysis is implementable with a dynamic flag in Python, R, Julia, JS(Deno), C++, SQLite, and defines-only in JVM; not in bash or generic SQL. Both designs are right that it is optional; the new design's channel choice is the one that is correct for Julia and for IPython cell magics, and the old design's channel-responsiveness argument is kernel-specific (see channel finding).

149	## 2. Delete of a top-level binding: per language, with what Pluto's workspace modules actually do
150	
151	OLD: `namespace_request {delete:[names]}`; 'Delete: Python, R, JS, SQL trivially; Julia only via the module trick; cling only via transaction unloading'; Pluto's fresh workspace modules cited as 'the Julia version' of scopes.
152	
153	NEW: `execute_request.namespace_delete: [names]` applied before the code; 'Pluto's fresh-module trick only existed to emulate delete in Julia, so nothing is lost there' (justifying dropping scopes); 'Julia can advertise analysis without delete'; notes that ipykernel would silently ignore an unknown field, so the frontend must gate on the feature string.
154	
155	ASSESSMENT: PYTHON: exact. `InteractiveShell.del_var` (interactiveshell.py:1562-1606) deletes by name across user_ns/user_global_ns/user_ns_hidden and also scrubs Out history and `_`/`__`/`___`; a `namespace_delete` pre-step slots naturally before run_cell in ipkernel.do_execute (ipkernel.py:405-462). R: exact, `rm(list=names, envir=globalenv())`; attached packages are on the search path, not in globalenv, so 'delete' of a library() cell has no rm equivalent (would need detach()). JULIA: pre-1.12 there is no binding removal; Julia 1.12 adds `Base.delete_binding(mod, sym)` but its docstring says 'The implementation of this functionality is currently incomplete. Do not use this method on versions that contain this disclaimer except for testing' (release-1.12 base/runtime_internals.jl:260-273). What Pluto does (verified in source): (1) each reactive run evaluates in a brand-new `Main.workspace#N` module (PlutoRunner/src/evaluation/workspace.jl:11-22, `Core.eval(Main, :(module $(new_workspace_name) ... end))`); (2) `move_vars` re-imports every surviving name from the old module into the new one and simply omits names in `vars_to_delete` — the docstring is explicit: 'This is how Pluto "deletes" globals - it doesn't, it just executes your new code in a new module where those globals are not defined' (deleting globals.jl:15-23); (3) for deleted non-const names it additionally sets `old_module.sym = nothing` to free memory, but this is skipped when `isconst` — 'sometimes impossible, eg. when $symbol was constant' (lines 64-77) — which is exactly why the module trick is needed for structs and `const`: pre-1.12 they cannot be redefined or cleared in place, and the new module has no binding for them; (4) method invalidation is a SEPARATE mechanism, not the module trick: `delete_toplevel_methods` walks the function's method table and calls `Base.delete_method` on methods whose `file` ends in the cell id, then (pre-1.12) re-inserts shadowed external methods via `jl_method_table_insert` (lines 130-185); the docstring gives the motivating case: after deleting a cell containing `Base.sqrt(s::String) = ...`, `sqrt("one")` must error again (line 22). So the new design's sentence is half right: the fresh module exists for deletion (incl. const/struct 'deletion'), but 'delete' in Julia is two mechanisms (module bump + method-table surgery), and dropping scopes does not make it go away — the new design keeps delete, and IJulia's only viable implementation of it is the module bump, which is implementable because IJulia already evaluates in a `kernel.current_module` field (execute_request.jl:130-131, 147) rather than a hard-coded Main. Saying 'Julia can advertise analysis without delete' is therefore a choice, not a limitation, and it gives up no-hidden-state for the one language whose flagship reactive notebook is built on exactly this. JS: NOT trivial, contradicting the old design. Tested in node 26: after `vm.runInThisContext('var a=1; let b=2; const c=3')`, `delete globalThis.a` returns false and `a` remains (var globals are non-configurable), `b`/`c` are not properties of globalThis at all (declarative record), and re-running `let b = 5` or `var b = 5` throws 'Identifier 'b' has already been declared'. ijavascript's maintainer confirms this is inherited from node's REPL and recommends var (n-riesco/ijavascript#117). Deno evaluates with CDP `Runtime.evaluate` `repl_mode: Some(true)` (session.rs:982), which permits re-declaring let/const across cells but still provides no removal. So JS kernels cannot advertise delete; the only route is a fresh realm/context — i.e. the scope primitive the new design removed. BASH: exact, `unset -v name` / `unset -f fn` (tested: `foo` unset after `unset foo`). C++: clang-repl's `Interpreter::Undo(N)` 'can only go N incremental inputs back' (LIFO, no dependency tracking; D126682), so deleting an arbitrary earlier binding is impossible; xeus-cpp registers only `file` and `xassist` magics (src/xinterpreter.cpp:531-533), no undo; would not advertise. SQL: DROP TABLE/VIEW is exact but destroys data (a 'delete before re-run' of a CREATE TABLE AS cell re-computes the table — acceptable for reactive semantics, surprising for DAG users); DuckDB has RESET VARIABLE for its session variables. JVM: `JShell.drop(snippet)` removes a variable/method/type and 'update[s] the JShell evaluation state accordingly', returning events for dependents (javadoc) — exact, and dependents are re-marked, which is closer to reactive invalidation than any other language offers natively. Conclusion: delete is exact in Python, R, bash, SQL, JVM; module-bump-only in Julia; unavailable in JS and C++. The new design's fold into execute_request is fine for all of these (it is a pre-step in every kernel), and its gating warning is correct: kernelbase.py:791-804 reads only known keys with `.get` defaults and the spec says extra fields must be tolerated, so an ungated `namespace_delete` is silently dropped.

2	ASSESSMENT: Enumeration per language. PYTHON: `user_ns` keys minus `user_ns_hidden` (IPython maintains user_ns_hidden precisely so that its own injected names are excluded from %who-style listings, interactiveshell.py:1327, 1441-1479); cheap and exact; it catches star imports and exec-created names that analysis cannot. R: `ls(globalenv(), all.names=TRUE)` diff — exact for globalenv, but `library()` changes `search()` not globalenv, so a delta that only diffs globalenv reports a library cell as defining nothing; a faithful R delta must also diff `search()`/`loadedNamespaces()`. JULIA: `names(Main, all=true, imported=true)` diff — this is literally what Pluto does to enumerate a workspace (deleting globals.jl:45) — but `names` excludes `using`-imported names unless `usings=true`, a keyword that 'requires Julia 1.12 or later'; Pluto tracks `using` statements separately from names and re-executes them in the new module (Run.jl:161-169 module_imports_to_move; deleting globals.jl:7-13 do_reimports). `removed` is always empty in Julia (no deletion). JS: `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(globalThis)` misses every let/const/class (tested: `b` absent); the correct enumeration is CDP `Runtime.globalLexicalScopeNames` ('Returns all let, const and class variables from global scope'), which Deno can issue through the inspector session it already drives; ijavascript would need node's `inspector` module. BASH: `compgen -v` / `declare -F` diff works (tested: added {arr, foo}, function bar) but is noisy — PIPESTATUS, `_`, RANDOM, SECONDS, LINENO change on their own — and bash_kernel must inject the enumeration around the user's code through the pexpect pipe, so 'for free' is generous but it is implementable. C++: each input is a partial translation unit; enumerating the new PTU's top-level Decls from the clang AST is exact and cheap; removed only via undo. SQL: catalog diff (`sqlite_master`, information_schema) is exact for DDL (tested: `select name,type from sqlite_master` lists t,u) and free; DML changes are invisible, which is correct for table-level edges. JVM: `JShell.eval` already returns the list of SnippetEvents (added/OVERWRITTEN/DROPPED) and `variables()/methods()/types()` enumerate active snippets — the delta is exact and free. Is it more universal than analysis? Yes: all eight have a top-level enumeration; only bash and generic SOCI-SQL lack a parser. But it is strictly weaker: (a) it never yields references, so it can pre-populate only the 'defines' side and cannot schedule ahead of a run; (b) it is post-hoc, so the first run of a cell is unscheduled; (c) without `rebound`, a cell that re-assigns an existing name (the common reactive case: `df = clean(df)`) produces an empty delta — the new design says static analysis already reports assignments, which is true only where analysis exists, so for bash the delta detects new names but not re-assignments; (d) 'exact set difference' is exact relative to each language's chosen enumeration, and the R library()/Julia using/JS let-const cases show the enumeration itself has to be defined per language in the spec. The old design's `rebound` via identity is indeed unsound in Python (ids recycle; keeping references defeats GC), so dropping it is right; a value-hash or version counter is the alternative neither design mentions. The old design's ipyflow claim is unverified here (ipyflow instruments execution with tracing rather than diffing names; I did not confirm either way).
