15	## 4. Forkable scopes: per-language substrate and what mutation leaks look like
16	
17	OLD: `create_scope(parent)`, `execute_request.scope`, `drop_scope`; child = shallow copy or lookup chain (Python dict copy, R new.env(parent=), Julia modules, JS vm contexts; not C++/SQL); 'correct as long as cells rebind rather than mutate'; composes with subshells.
18	
19	NEW: Removed entirely: reactive plugin enforces one definition per name; DAG plugin can enforce or flag it with analysis; under rebind-not-mutate, disjoint definitions in one namespace cannot interfere; mutation isolation belongs to the server clone tier.
20	
21	ASSESSMENT: Substrate per language. PYTHON: `dict(user_ns)` copy; ipykernel already supports swapping `user_ns` at runtime (ipkernel.py:98-109 observes `user_ns` and re-runs `shell.init_user_ns()`), so the mechanism exists; leaks: any in-place mutation (`lst.append`, `df['x']=...`, `model.fit()`), class/module state, `sys.modules`. R: `new.env(parent = globalenv())` + `eval(expr, envir = child)`; `<-` in the child stays in the child, `<<-` walks up into the parent; because R values are copy-on-modify, ordinary mutation of vectors/lists/data.frames does NOT leak — only reference objects (environments, R6, RefClass, data.table `:=`, external pointers) do; R is the best-behaved language for this primitive. JULIA: module bump is exactly Pluto's workspace design; consts and structs can be redefined in the child; leaks: mutation of shared Arrays/Dicts, method definitions on shared functions (which is why Pluto needs delete_toplevel_methods). JS: node `vm.createContext(Object.assign({}, parent))` — tested: child rebinding `x = 10` did not touch the parent (`x` stayed 2) while `arr.push(99)` leaked (parent arr became [1,2,99]); nel currently runs in the main context (runInThisContext), so adopting scopes changes ijavascript's execution model; Deno has one V8 context per ReplSession and I did not verify `node:vm` createContext support in Deno. BASH: a `( ... )` subshell cannot persist state back (tested: `foo` unset after `( foo=99 )`); no scope primitive. C++: none (a PTU cannot be forked); SQL: none short of copying the database; JVM: none — JShell has no namespace fork and its default execution engine is out-of-process, so a new JShell is a new JVM. Assessment of the removal: the new design is right that scopes give no protection against mutation in any language (the leak set above is identical to what disjoint-definitions-in-one-namespace leaks), so for isolation the primitive buys little beyond what the single-definition rule already gives. What is lost is not isolation but deletion: for JS (no delete possible in-place) and Julia (delete = module bump), 'fresh scope without these names' IS the delete implementation. Under the old design a JS kernel could advertise scopes and the frontend could emulate delete by re-forking; under the new design JS has no path to no-hidden-state at all and Julia must implement the module bump behind the `delete` string anyway. The old design's 'composes with subshells for concurrent branches' is true only for ipykernel today (see channel finding).

31	## 5. Set from JSON: exact ambiguities per language and what papermill's translators do
32	
33	OLD: `namespace_request {set: {name: json}}`: 'a language-agnostic way to bind a name to a JSON-ish value' for widget-bound variables, papermill-style parameters, DAG input ports.
34	
35	NEW: Removed: 'Mapping JSON onto a language binding is ambiguous in R, JavaScript, and Julia, which is why papermill keeps per-language translators, and comms already carry widget-bound values'; returns only if value-carrying edges are adopted.
36	
37	ASSESSMENT: PYTHON: unambiguous (int/float/str/bool/None/dict/list); papermill PythonTranslator only special-cases nan/inf. R: genuinely ambiguous, and the kernel's own JSON layer shows how: jsonlite's parser maps a JSON integer to R `integer` if it fits int32, to `double` above that, and to a character string above 2^53 when bigint_as_char (src/parse.c:55-68); `1.0` becomes double; R has no scalars so `1` and `[1]` are both a length-1 vector; with default simplification an array of objects becomes a data.frame and an array of arrays a matrix (jsonlite quickstart table); JSON null inside an array becomes NA, alone becomes NULL. papermill sidesteps all of this by emitting `list(...)` for BOTH JSON arrays and objects (translators.py:289-296) — never atomic vectors, never data frames — and rewrites names by stripping leading underscores (303-307). So a `set` for R would have to pick one convention (papermill's most-generic one is defensible), and the receiving cell must coerce. JS: JSON numbers are doubles; `JSON.parse("9007199254740993")` yields 9007199254740992 (tested) and BigInt cannot be serialized ('Do not know how to serialize a BigInt'), so 64-bit ids are lossy in both directions; `1.0` arrives as integer-valued 1. JULIA: JSON.jl maps number to Int64 or Float64 by presence of a decimal point, object to Dict{String,Any}, array to Vector{Any}; papermill emits `Dict("k" => v)` and `[...]` (translators.py:343-350); the ambiguity is Dict vs NamedTuple vs a user struct and Vector{Any} vs a typed vector, which matters for dispatch — a set-provided `Vector{Any}` hits different methods than the `Vector{Float64}` a cell would have produced. BASH: strings only; papermill's BashTranslator quotes with shlex, emits `(a b c)` for lists, and inherits the base `translate_dict`, which raises NotImplementedError (translators.py:76-78, 521-545) — so even papermill cannot set a dict in bash. C++, SQL, JVM: statically typed; papermill has no C++/SQL/Java translator at all (registered: python, R, scala, julia, matlab, .net-csharp, .net-fsharp, .net-powershell, bash and spark variants, translators.py:548-561); the Scala/C#/F# translators guess `L` suffix for out-of-int32 integers (313-314, 414-416, 450-452). Verdict: the new design's factual claim is correct and the papermill evidence supports it; the old design's 'costs nothing extra' undersells that a spec would need a per-language coercion table. Two things the new design should weigh, since they are not wrong but unaddressed: (1) the sole language where set is trivially exact is Python, which is also the only language with a widget stack that already uses comms, so 'comms already carry widget-bound values' is again Python-shaped; (2) the old design's fallback ('a bare identifier is a valid expression' for get via user_expressions) is fine in all eight languages, so the asymmetry (get universal, set not) is real and argues for the new design's choice.

47	## 6. Channel placement and responsiveness: control vs shell vs subshell is kernel-specific, not language-agnostic
48	
49	OLD: analyze_request on the control channel 'like debug_request, which ipykernel services in a separate thread', to 'avoid queuing behind a busy shell' and neutralize LSP's availability advantage.
50	
51	NEW: analyze_request on the shell channel; 'imposes no threading requirement on kernel authors'; ordering with executions matters for magics; 'Responsiveness during a long run comes from sending it on a subshell where the kernel has them. ipykernel 7 routes any shell message by its subshell id, so that works today.'
52	
53	ASSESSMENT: Who actually has a control thread: ipykernel yes (control.py ControlThread; debugger.py:320-326 lists the session-free DAP handlers the new design cites); xeus only when the kernel uses the `xserver_zmq_split` family ('the shell and the control channels have dedicated threads'), while the default `xserver_zmq` server has 'a single thread [that] polls both the shell and the control channels' (xeus-zmq docs/source/server.rst:12-18); IRkernel's main loop is one `zmq.poll` over hb/shell/control with no threading (R/kernel.r), so control gains nothing there and IRkernel does not even emit `supported_features`; IJulia services control and shell as two `@async` tasks (eventloop.jl), which are cooperative — a compute-bound cell that never yields blocks the control task (Julia task semantics; not separately cited); Deno's jupyter server drives one ReplSession on one event loop (jupyter/mod.rs:154) and I did not verify control handling. So the old design's responsiveness benefit is real on ipykernel and split-server xeus kernels only. Who has subshells: ipykernel 7 advertises 'kernel subshells' (kernelbase.py:995-997) and routes any shell message by `header.subshell_id` (kernelbase.py:582-591, 597-621), and the JEP says 'All shell and stdin messages will allow the optional subshell_id field'; I found no subshell implementation in xeus core (grep of xkernel_core.cpp/xinterpreter.hpp found only debugger references), and none in IRkernel/IJulia/Deno. So the new design's responsiveness story is ipykernel-only today, but it degrades gracefully (a kernel without subshells just answers after the current execution) and it imposes nothing on kernel authors, whereas the old design's control placement would be semantically wrong for Julia (macro expansion needs the live module) and for IPython cells that depend on magics registered by earlier cells (transform_cell consults `input_transformer_manager` and `input_transformers_post`, which %load_ext can extend, interactiveshell.py:3598-3625). On language agnosticism the new design is the safer default; the old design's argument only holds where the kernel already has the debugger's threading.

66	## 7. Feature advertisement and degradation: which languages advertise what under each design, and whether 'three independent feature strings' holds
67	
68	OLD: Four optional features (analysis, namespace ops = delete+set bundled, scopes, snapshots), each advertised independently via JEP 92 supported_features; degradation: no analysis -> manual edges; no scopes -> snapshot/replay; no delete -> warn stale bindings persist.
69	
70	NEW: Three strings: analysis, delete, delta; 'bash can advertise the delta without analysis and Julia can advertise analysis without delete. The frontend has to gate on them.'
71	
72	ASSESSMENT: Matrix under the NEW design (advertise = implementable with honest semantics). Python/ipykernel: analysis (with magic-body handling and dynamic flag), delete, delta — all three. R/IRkernel: all three, with analysis flagged dynamic often (NSE) and delta defined over globalenv+search(). Julia/IJulia: analysis (must expand macros in current_module, so shell-ordered), delta (added only; `using` invisible before 1.12 `usings=true`), delete only if IJulia adopts a Pluto-style module bump behind the string — feasible via `kernel.current_module` but a real engineering item; otherwise none, and `removed` is then always empty. JS/Deno: analysis yes (deno_ast in-kernel), delta yes if via Runtime.globalLexicalScopeNames, delete no (replMode gives redefinition but not removal). JS/ijavascript: analysis possible (not present today), delta partial (globalThis props miss let/const), delete no. bash: delta only. C++/xeus-cpp: analysis yes but state-dependent (shell-ordered, which the new design permits), delta yes (new PTU decls), delete no (LIFO undo, and not exposed). SQL/xeus-sqlite: analysis yes (authorizer), delta yes (catalog), delete yes (DROP) but destructive; SQL/xeus-sql generic: delta only. JVM/IJava: analysis defines-only (sourceToSnippets), delta yes (eval events), delete yes (drop). Under the OLD design the same languages split as: analysis same set; namespace-ops string must cover set too, which is exact only in Python and would force R/Julia/JS kernels to pick a coercion convention and bash/C++/SQL/JVM to advertise a half-feature or nothing (bash can delete but cannot set a dict; JVM can drop but cannot set untyped) — the bundling is the old design's real weakness for language agnosticism; scopes: Python, R, Julia, JS(node) could advertise, bash/C++/SQL/JVM not; snapshots: process-level tier needs no kernel string at all (both designs agree). Does the new design's degradation story hold? Mostly yes: the three strings are genuinely independent (bash: delta only; C++: analysis+delta; JVM: delete+delta+partial analysis; Deno: analysis+delta), and factoring delete out of the old namespace-ops bundle is the single biggest agnosticism gain, because delete is exact in five of eight languages while set is exact in one. Two gaps: (1) the story quietly concedes no-hidden-state for Julia, JS and C++ — for JS and C++ that concession is forced, for Julia it is a choice the old design's scope primitive would have expressed more naturally (fork-without-names); the new design should say 'Julia implements delete by module bump' rather than 'Julia can advertise analysis without delete'. (2) delta's meaning must be normative per language (R search path, Julia using, JS lexical scope), or two kernels advertising the same string will disagree; the new design's 'both are exact set differences' hides that. Also a practical note for the new design's 'purge = execute with empty code and silent': Lab's `CodeCell.execute` returns early on `!code.trim()` (cells/src/widget.ts:1775-1781), so the plugin must call `kernel.requestExecute` directly; ipykernel with silent=True does not bump execution_count (kernelbase.py:810-812), so the mechanism is otherwise sound.

84	## 8. 'Imports are defines' across languages (new design's folding of the imports list)
85	
86	OLD: analyze_reply carries a separate `imports` list alongside defines/references.
87	
88	NEW: 'Imports are defines, so there is no separate list.'
89	
90	ASSESSMENT: True for Python (`import numpy as np` binds `np` in user_ns; `from m import a, b` binds a, b), for JS (import bindings), for JVM (JShell imports are snippets, though they bind no variable), and for C++ (#include/using declare names). False in the two languages whose import statements bind nothing enumerable in the top-level namespace: R `library(dplyr)` attaches a package environment to the search path (globalenv unchanged), and Julia `using Foo` makes exported names resolvable in Main without adding them to `names(Main)` (the `usings` keyword to include them exists only from 1.12). In both, a reactive graph needs the import cell to be an ancestor of every cell that references an exported name, which a defines list cannot express without enumerating the package's exports (hundreds of names, and in R the analyzer would have to load the package to know them). Pluto handles this by keeping `using` statements as a separate class (Run.jl:161-169 module_imports_to_move; MacroAnalysis.jl `can_help_resolve_cells` treats cells with usings as able to 'unlock' other cells' resolution). A separate `imports` entry (module names, not bound names) is therefore load-bearing for R and Julia and is one place the old design's shape was more language-agnostic; the new design could recover it by letting a kernel report a wildcard define such as `"dplyr::*"`, but as written the folding loses information. Star imports in Python (`from x import *`) are the same problem in reverse: analysis cannot list the defines, delta can.

98	## Corrections
99	  - OLD design: 'Delete: Python, R, JS, SQL trivially' is wrong for JS. In node (ijavascript/nel runs code via vm.runInThisContext, nel lib/server/main.js:296) top-level `let`/`const`/`class` live in the global declarative record and cannot be deleted or redeclared ('Identifier 'b' has already been declared', reproduced in node 26; n-riesco/ijavascript#117), and even `var`-declared globals are non-configurable (`delete globalThis.a` returned false). Deno's `repl_mode: Some(true)` (cli/tools/repl/session.rs:982) allows redeclaration but not removal. No JS kernel can advertise delete without a fresh context.
100	  - OLD design: 'Static analysis needs no namespace, so serve it on the control channel' is false for Julia (Pluto expands macros in the live workspace module before topology resolution: src/evaluation/MacroAnalysis.jl:1-3 `macroexpand_in_workspace`) and for IPython when earlier cells register input transformers/magics (transform_cell consults `input_transformer_manager` and `input_transformers_post`, interactiveshell.py:3598-3625), and for C++ where a cell cannot be parsed without the accumulated TU state.
101	  - OLD design: 'like debug_request, which ipykernel services in a separate thread' generalizes only to ipykernel (control.py ControlThread) and xeus kernels built on `xserver_zmq_split` (xeus-zmq docs/source/server.rst:12-18); IRkernel polls hb/shell/control in one loop (R/kernel.r) and IJulia uses cooperative `@async` tasks (eventloop.jl), so the queuing benefit is not language-agnostic.
102	  - OLD design: 'Analysis: ... poor for ... C++' is too pessimistic: xeus-cpp has the full clang parser in-process, so declared/referenced names are exact; the real limitation is order-dependence, not parser quality. 'cling only via transaction unloading' is right in spirit but clang-repl's Undo is LIFO-only (D126682: 'can only go N incremental inputs back') and xeus-cpp does not expose it (registered magics are `file` and `xassist`, src/xinterpreter.cpp:531-533).
103	  - OLD design: '~100 lines in ipykernel' for analysis omits that transform_cell turns every cell/line magic body into a string argument (tested: `%%time\nx = 1` -> `run_cell_magic('time', '', 'x = 1\n')`, symtable defines=[]), so magic bodies need separate parsing and per-magic I/O rules (`%%capture out` defines `out`).
104	  - OLD design: 'it's what ipyflow does inside ipykernel already' (for name-diff namespace_delta) — unverified in this review; ipyflow instruments execution rather than diffing names as far as I know, but I did not read its source, so treat the sentence as unsupported rather than wrong.
105	  - OLD design: 'Julia can't delete a binding from a module' is now dated: Julia 1.12 has `Base.delete_binding(mod, sym)`, though its docstring says the implementation 'is currently incomplete. Do not use this method on versions that contain this disclaimer except for testing' (release-1.12 base/runtime_internals.jl:260-273). Practically still true.
106	  - NEW design: 'Pluto's fresh-module trick only existed to emulate delete in Julia, so nothing is lost there' — the first half is confirmed by Pluto's own docstring ('This is how Pluto "deletes" globals - it doesn't, it just executes your new code in a new module', deleting globals.jl:16), but the conclusion is wrong in two ways: (a) the new design keeps delete, and the module bump is Julia's only implementation of it (const/struct bindings cannot even be nulled: lines 64-77 skip `isconst`), so Julia still needs the machinery; (b) Pluto's 'delete' also includes method-table surgery (`Base.delete_method` on cell-defined methods plus re-insertion of shadowed external methods, lines 130-185), which no scope or delete primitive in either design specifies. Dropping scopes also removes the only route to delete for JS.
107	  - NEW design: 'Julia can advertise analysis without delete' frames a choice as a constraint: IJulia evaluates in a settable `kernel.current_module` (execute_request.jl:130-131, 147), so a Pluto-style module bump behind the delete string is implementable.
108	  - NEW design: 'Both are exact set differences' for namespace_delta — exact only relative to a per-language enumeration the spec would have to define: R `ls(globalenv())` misses `library()` (search path), Julia `names(Main, all=true, imported=true)` misses `using` unless `usings=true` (1.12+; Pluto tracks usings separately, Run.jl:161-169), JS `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(globalThis)` misses let/const (needs CDP Runtime.globalLexicalScopeNames), bash `compgen -v` includes PIPESTATUS/`_`/RANDOM noise.
109	  - NEW design: 'Imports are defines, so there is no separate list' is false for R `library()` and Julia `using`, which bind nothing enumerable at top level yet must be graph ancestors of every cell using an exported name; the old design's `imports` list carried information the new design loses.
110	  - NEW design: 'gives parser-less kernels such as bash the defines half of an edge for free' — implementable, but bash_kernel is a pexpect wrapper (takluyver/bash_kernel kernel.py) that must inject `compgen -v`/`declare -F` before and after each cell through the tty and filter shell-internal variables; and without `rebound`, re-assignments (the common reactive case) produce an empty delta wherever analysis is absent.

116	  - Whether IJulia's `kernel.current_module` is intended to be mutable per execution (it is read in execute_request.jl; I did not find its declaration or any setter), i.e. whether a Pluto-style module bump can be done without forking IJulia.
117	  - Whether Deno's jupyter server handles control-channel messages concurrently with a running cell, and whether Deno's `node:vm` compatibility layer supports `createContext` well enough for a scope primitive.
118	  - ipyflow's actual mechanism for namespace tracking (tracing vs name diffing) — not read; the old design's 'ipyflow proves it works' is unverified either way.
119	  - Whether any xeus-based kernel (xeus-zmq 3.x era) implements JEP 91 subshells; grep of xeus core found nothing, but I did not exhaustively check xeus-zmq or xeus-python release notes.
120	  - Pre-1.12 Julia: whether names brought in by `using` appear in `names(Main; imported=true)` after first resolution (the 1.12 docstring implies they do not without `usings=true`; older behavior unverified).
121	  - Whether DuckDB (the SQL engine marimo/Hex users are most likely to hit) exposes a prepare-time table-access API equivalent to SQLite's authorizer for exact analysis; I verified only SQLite's authorizer and DuckDB's SET VARIABLE.
122	  - Whether CppInterOp/xeus-cpp plan to surface clang-repl Undo (a CppInterOp PR was referenced in search results but not read), which would give C++ a LIFO-only delete.
123	  - For R, the practical false-positive rate of free references under NSE (dplyr/data.table column names) — determines whether an R analyzer should default the `dynamic` flag on for any cell calling a data-masking verb.
124	  - Neither design specifies what `namespace_delta.removed` means in a language where delete is impossible (Julia, JS, C++): always empty, or 'names that became undefined' via other means (e.g. Deno redeclaration to undefined).
125	  - Neither design specifies whether delete of a name that a `library()`/`using` cell provided means detach/unload (R detach() is possible; Julia cannot unload a module), i.e. the semantics of deleting an import-defined edge source.

130	## 1. Same-name branches in a DAG (two variants both called `model`)
131	
132	OLD: Scopes: `create_scope(parent)`, `execute_request.scope`, `drop_scope`. Run the shared prefix in S0, fork S1/S2, run branch A in S1 and branch B in S2; both branches may bind `model` without interfering (kernel-design-notes.md §2c; transcript turn 4 §3).
133	
134	NEW: Scopes removed. The DAG plugin enforces one definition per global name (or flags a violation before running), on the grounds that this is 'the model Hex and marimo already ship' (new-design.md lines 14-19). Users who need isolation for mutating code get a server-level clone-kernel operation.
135	
136	ASSESSMENT: Steelman for OLD: the user-drawn DAG is the case the one-definition rule fits worst. The whole point of fan-out is 'same recipe, different variant', and the natural code for that is two cells both ending in `model = fit(...)`. Under NEW, the user must rename (`model_a`, `model_b`) and every downstream cell in each branch must be edited to match, which destroys the copy-a-branch workflow; or the plugin must clone a kernel per branch, which costs a process, a fresh import of every library, and a re-run or CRIU restore of the prefix. Scopes give a dict copy at fork time. Steelman for NEW: the rename cost is exactly the cost marimo, Pluto and Observable users already pay (marimo: 'marimo requires that every global variable be defined by only one cell'; Observable: same-named cells 'are temporarily overridden to throw a ReferenceError'; Pluto: same rule), so the reactive plugin needs no scopes at all, and the DAG plugin's fallback (kernel clone) already had to exist for mutating code. The two disagree only about whether the DAG plugin deserves a cheaper middle tier. Verdict: depends on whether the DAG plugin is expected to be used with copy-pasted branches (then OLD's scopes are the feature) or with reactive-style disjoint names (then scopes are dead weight). Correction of a NEW-design premise: Hex's duplicate-definition behaviour could not be verified; Hex docs only say the graph is 'built automatically based on variable references in Python and SQL code' and warn against `globals()`. 'Hex and marimo already ship' this rule is verified for marimo only.

145	## 2. Parameter sweeps / fan-out over inputs and typed input ports
146

Two consequences. (1) Module migration is a kernel-internal implementation of `delete`, not a scope: it needs no protocol-visible scope id, so NEW's `namespace_delete` list is implementable by IJulia exactly as Pluto does it. NEW's phrasing 'Julia can advertise analysis without delete' undersells this — Julia CAN implement delete; what it cannot do is the naive `del`. (2) The Pluto docstring also shows the cost Pluto accepts: a whole-notebook module bump on every run, with `import` re-execution (`do_reimports`), and a known caveat that delete_method cannot restore a shadowed original method. So OLD's claim that 'Pluto's module trick is the Julia version' of scopes is a category slip in the other direction: Pluto has one module per notebook at a time, never one per branch (workspace.module_name is a single Symbol; bump_workspace_module replaces it). Neither design has evidence that a per-branch Julia module chain works at Pluto-scale. Verdict: dropping scopes does not remove Julia's path to no-hidden-state; NEW is right on substance, wrong in wording; OLD's Julia-scopes analogy is unsupported by Pluto.

176	NEW: On the shell channel, sharing the dispatch path of complete/inspect, ordered with executions (matters when an earlier cell registers a magic); responsiveness during a long run via a subshell where the kernel has them; 'ipykernel 7 routes any shell message by its subshell id, so that works today' (new-design.md lines 47-51).

Routing by header subshell_id is at kernelbase.py:578-595. xeus-zmq's default server has the MAIN thread poll both shell and control ('Main thread: polls both shell and control channels; executes interpreter code'); xeus-r (main.cpp: make_xserver_default) and xeus-cpp (main.cpp: make_xserver_zmq) use it, so on those kernels a control-channel analyze_request queues behind execution exactly as a shell one would. xeus-python uses the split server (xaserver.cpp: make_xserver_shell…), so control is concurrent there. IRkernel is a single `zmq.poll(c(hb, shell, control))` loop handling messages 'one by one'. IJulia runs control and shell in separate `@async` tasks on one thread, so control is serviced only when the executing task yields. As of the gh code search (which can be incomplete) neither xeus nor xeus-zmq contains the string 'subshell'; xeus-zmq 4.0.0 (released 2026-03-04) release notes are absent. So the set 'concurrent control, no subshells' = xeus-python (split server) and ipykernel 6.x; the set 'no concurrent control at all' = xeus-r, xeus-cpp/cling, IRkernel, effectively IJulia. Steelman OLD: on xeus-python today, control is the only place analysis would return during a long run. Steelman NEW: (a) JEP 91's own text: using control for non-control interactions 'is considered bad practice as it should only be used for control purposes'; a reviewer will quote it. (b) Ordering: `transform_cell` is dialect-dependent (`%%R -i x -o y`, user-registered magics), and only the shell channel is ordered with the execute that registers the magic; control analysis can be wrong for the cell right after `%load_ext`. (c) Thread-safety: `transform_cell` for one-line cells runs `with self.builtin_trap:` (interactiveshell.py:3612-3615), which swaps builtins process-wide; running it on the control thread concurrently with user code on the main thread is a latent race that OLD incurs on every analyze and NEW only when the frontend opts into a subshell. (d) Latency under NEW when the shell is busy is bounded by the same JEP-91 mechanism Lab already uses for comms (kernel.ts:115-125 sends comm messages on subshells). 12	## 5. REPL-grade isolation for mutating code: does CRIU-via-provisioner really need no kernel-protocol change?
13	
14	OLD: Tier 2 'needs no kernel cooperation', lives in a jupyter_client KernelProvisioner + server endpoint; 'kernel rebinds ZMQ ports, --tcp-close'; comms invalidated on restore; clone preferred over restore (notes §3; transcript turn 1).
15	
16	NEW: Snapshot/restore/clone leave the kernel protocol entirely; process-level checkpointing is a provisioner plus a REST endpoint, 'a REST change that touches no kernel message'; DAG plugin codes against server-level 'clone kernel' (new-design.md lines 21-25).
17	
18	ASSESSMENT: Both designs make the same claim; checking it component by component. ZMQ ports: the kernel binds ROUTER/XPUB sockets once at startup (kernelapp.py:352-392, `_bind_socket` 269-287); there is no message to rebind, and CRIU restores listening TCP sockets itself ('TCP in Listen and Established states' supported), so in-place restore of the SAME kernel needs no kernel action but requires the port to be free — CRIU fails with 'Can't bind inet socket: Address already in use' otherwise (issues #516, #167). Clone (two live copies) therefore needs a distinct network namespace per copy plus port mapping, or a kernel that re-binds on request; the former is provisioner/container work (Enterprise-Gateway-style remote provisioners already map ports), the latter would be a protocol change. OLD's 'kernel rebinds ZMQ ports' is therefore inaccurate as written: either CRIU restores the same ports or someone must supply new ones; nothing in ipykernel rebinds. Established connections: the server's DEALER/SUB sockets reconnect after `--tcp-close`; ZMQ handles that. Heartbeat: a plain thread + REP socket (heartbeat.py:27-79), restored like any thread. Connection file: unchanged for in-place restore; for clone the provisioner writes a new one (local_provisioner.py:212-244 is where that happens today). Frontend session state: Lab discards messages whose `header.session` differs from the kernel session it learned from kernel_info_reply (default.ts:686, 1340-1344); CRIU preserves process memory, so the restored kernel keeps the same session id and Lab notices nothing — good for in-place restore, but it also means execution_count silently regresses and IPython's In/Out history contains post-snapshot entries the process has forgotten. Auto-restart hazard: jupyter_client's KernelRestarter polls `provisioner.poll()` every 3 s and calls `restart_kernel(now=True)` if the process is gone (restarter.py:115-145; manager.py:783-793); a CRIU dump that kills the original, followed by restore, must keep `poll()` reporting alive across the gap or jupyter_server will replace the kernel — provisioner-level, but a real design constraint. Comm state: the kernel-side comm registry is restored to snapshot time while the frontend's `_comms` map reflects now; the reconciliation primitive already exists in the protocol (`comm_info_request`, kernelbase.py:1020-1037) and Lab's `_clearKernelState` (default.ts:1305-1322) is what an autorestart runs. So the OLD design's 'comms invalidated on restore' can be done by the frontend after restore (comm_info + close/reopen) rather than by the kernel. Verdict: the shared claim survives for in-place restore; for clone it survives only if isolation comes from network namespaces, not from kernel cooperation. NEW is right that no kernel MESSAGE is required; OLD's own wording ('kernel rebinds ZMQ ports') contradicts its 'no cooperation' claim and should be fixed. Neither design addresses the restarter race or the counter/history regression. GPU (cuda-checkpoint), Linux-only, and macOS-dev-machine constraints stand.

34	
35	OLD: A dedicated shell message `namespace_request {delete: [...], set: {...}}` (notes §2b).

37	NEW: `namespace_delete` is an optional list on execute_request applied before the code; purge-only is 'an execute with empty code and silent set' (new-design.md lines 27-34).
38	
39	ASSESSMENT: Measured against ipykernel 7.3.0 + IPython 9.17.1. A silent, empty execute: publishes status busy then idle on iopub (kernelbase.py:427 and the idle after the handler) — so does ANY shell message including OLD's namespace_request (same dispatch_shell path), so churn is identical. Does not bump the kernel execution counter or publish execute_input when silent (kernelbase.py:810-812); IPython forces store_history=False when silent and bumps its own counter only if store_history (interactiveshell.py:3434-3440); IPython returns early on empty cells before pre_execute/pre_run_cell (3428-3431), so autoreload's pre_run_cell hook (autoreload.py:914) does not fire; ipykernel still fires post_execute/post_run_cell in its finally (ipkernel.py:453-456), so matplotlib-inline's flush_figures (backend_inline.py:180) and autoreload's post_execute_hook do run — harmless but nonzero. Attached consoles inject a foreign cell only on execute_input (foreign.ts:98-105), so a silent purge is invisible to them. user_expressions still evaluate (ipkernel.py:498-499). One frontend snag: Lab's `CodeCell.execute` refuses to send empty code (widget.ts:1770-1775), so the plugin must call `kernel.requestExecute` directly for a purge. One protocol snag: the delete must be applied by the kernel BEFORE its interpreter's empty-cell short-circuit, which is an implementation note for every kernel. Failure mode comparison: a kernel that lacks the feature ignores `namespace_delete` silently (kernelbase.py:793-804 reads content with .get defaults) — NEW admits this and gates on feature strings; OLD's unknown `namespace_request` gets `log.warning('Unknown message type')` and NO reply at all (kernelbase.py:466-468), so the frontend future hangs — worse than silent ignore unless the frontend also gates. Advantages OLD keeps: a distinct message is easier to grep in logs and to specify (no 'empty code' special case), and delete+set in one message is atomic relative to other clients' executes; under NEW, atomicity comes from the same request carrying delete and code, which is actually the tighter guarantee for the common case (delete-then-rerun cannot be interleaved by another client). Verdict: on observable behaviour the two are nearly indistinguishable; NEW's fold is cheaper and gives delete-before-run atomicity for free; the only real cost is the frontend must bypass CodeCell.execute for purges.

52	
53	OLD: `namespace_delta: {added, rebound, removed}` computed by diffing names and object identity before and after execution; 'ipyflow proves it works inside ipykernel' (notes §2a; transcript turn 4).

55	NEW: `{added, removed}` only; identity comparison 'either keeps old values alive during the run or compares ids that get recycled'; static analysis already reports assignments (new-design.md lines 36-41).

57	ASSESSMENT: Steelman OLD: `rebound` is the one dynamic signal that catches what static analysis cannot: `exec(...)`, `globals()['x'] = ...`, `%store -r`, `%run`, `from m import *` overwriting an existing name, and bash/SQL kernels with no parser (where 'rebound' is the only way to learn a cell overwrote a table/variable rather than created it). Without it, the reactive plugin cannot invalidate dependants of `x` when a dynamic cell rebinds `x`. IPython itself already does identity-based bookkeeping: `drop_by_id` (interactiveshell.py:1678-1695) holds object references to decide whether the user rebound a name, so 'hold a reference during the run' is an accepted pattern in the codebase. Steelman NEW: holding a reference to every global for the duration of a run defeats `del big; big = load()` memory patterns and changes refcount-visible behaviour (weakref callbacks, `__del__`), which a REPL user will notice; comparing raw ids is unsound because CPython reuses addresses. Also correction to OLD: ipyflow does not derive its information from a before/after identity diff — it uses pyccolo's AST instrumentation and sys.settrace-level tracing, and is documented to miss mutations through function boundaries; so ipyflow proves dataflow tracking can live inside ipykernel, not that this specific mechanism works. Verdict: `rebound` is genuinely useful for the dynamic/parser-less cases and the memory objection can be bounded (hold ids plus a weakref or type/size fingerprint rather than a strong ref; still imperfect), but NEW is right that it is the least well-defined field and the one reviewers will pick at; making it an optional third key rather than deleting it is the obvious middle, though that is a third design and out of scope here.

83	## 9. Semantic debt of scopes in Python: mutation leaks, closures/classes, globals() identity, pickling, %who, debugger, copy-vs-chain
84	
85	OLD: Child scope = 'shallow copy of / lookup chain onto parent (Python dict copy ...)'; correct 'as long as cells rebind rather than mutate' (notes §2c).
86	
87	NEW: Drops scopes; cites the same rebind contract as the reason a single namespace suffices.
88	
89	ASSESSMENT: Concrete Python facts that a scopes JEP would have to answer. (1) IPython executes with `exec(code_obj, self.user_global_ns, self.user_ns)` where `user_global_ns` is `user_module.__dict__` (interactiveshell.py:1363-1364, 3823), a single attribute on the shell; every function defined in a cell captures that exact dict as `__globals__`. A function defined in S0 and called from S1 reads S0's dict, so `x = 2` in S1 is invisible to `f()` defined before the fork — shallow copy semantics break the most basic 'redefine a parameter, rerun the model function' case unless the child is a chained mapping, and `exec` requires a real dict for globals, so a chain must be a dict subclass whose `__missing__` walks parents (works for LOAD_GLOBAL via `__getitem__`? no: LOAD_GLOBAL bypasses `__getitem__` on dict subclasses; only `__missing__` is honoured, which is fine, but `globals()` returns the subclass and pickling/`copy` of it may surprise). (2) `%who`/`%who_ls` read `shell.user_ns` (namespace.py:270-276), the debugger's VariableExplorer reads `get_ipython().user_ns` (debugger.py:91-93), `copyToGlobals` writes via `globals()[name]` (debugger.py:674-692), `user_expressions` evaluates in `user_global_ns/user_ns` (interactiveshell.py:2950-2975): all of these would need a scope parameter or would silently show only the parent scope. (3) Subshells share the one namespace (JEP: 'within the same process namespace'; ipkernel do_execute uses the single `self.shell`, ipkernel.py:386), so OLD's 'composes with subshells' means swapping `shell.user_ns` per request across threads, which is a race; a real implementation must thread a namespace argument through run_cell/run_code. (4) Classes: instances created in S0 keep their class object; redefining the class in S1 breaks isinstance across branches — same as today, not new debt, but scopes make it easier to hit. (5) Comms/widgets: a widget model created in S0 lives in the comm manager, not in any scope; observers attached in S1 mutate shared model state — mutation leak by construction. (6) Copy vs chain after a parent change: with copy, later S0 executes are invisible to S1 (users will call it 'stale'); with chain, they leak in (users will call it 'spooky'); the design has to pick and document. NEW avoids all six by not having scopes; the price is the branch-isolation loss above. Verdict: OLD's '~100 lines' estimate covers analysis only; scopes in ipykernel require changes in IPython proper (run_cell signature, magics, debugger), which is the single strongest argument for NEW.

98	## 10. How marimo, Hex, Observable and Pluto got by without kernel-side scopes or set
99	
100	OLD: Cites Pluto's module trick as the Julia scope implementation and marimo's no-mutation contract as the isolation contract (transcript turn 4 §3).
101	
102	NEW: Claims one-namespace + one-definition 'is the model Hex and marimo already ship' and that Pluto's modules only emulate delete (new-design.md lines 14-19).
103	
104	ASSESSMENT: marimo: one shared globals dict per kernel — `Runner` holds a single `glbls: MutableGlobals` passed to every `evaluate(cell, self.glbls)`; isolation exists only for underscore-prefixed names ('local to a cell: they can't be read by other cells', implemented by name mangling, not a namespace) and by the rule of one definer per global; mutations 'don't trigger reactive re-runs'; deleting a cell 'deletes its global variables from program memory'. No per-branch isolation. Set: `mo.ui` values arrive through the frontend-kernel channel and are assigned in-kernel, i.e. marimo's own 'comm'. Pluto: one workspace module per notebook at a time, migrated wholesale on delete; `@bind` values are assigned by the runner; no per-branch modules. Observable: runtime variables in one module; duplicates error; `viewof` inputs are ordinary variables. Hex: verified only that the graph derives from variable references and that `globals()` breaks it; whether two cells may define the same variable, and what Hex does then, could not be verified from the docs fetched (open question). So NEW's claim is fully verified for marimo, Observable and Pluto, and unverified for Hex. The common pattern across all four: single namespace, unique definer, deletion on re-run/removal, inputs injected by the runtime through the same channel that carries widget state. That is exactly analysis + delete + comms, i.e. NEW's surface. None of them needed scopes because none of them offers user-drawn branches over the same names — which is precisely the feature the DAG plugin adds, so the precedent argues for NEW only for the reactive plugin.

113	## 11. Semantic debt of `set` (JSON → binding)
114	
115	OLD: `set: {name: json}` as language-agnostic binding for widget values, parameters, ports (notes §2b).
116	
117	NEW: Dropped; ambiguity in R/JS/Julia; papermill's translators as evidence; comms already carry widget values (new-design.md lines 29-32).
118	
119	ASSESSMENT: Verified: papermill maintains per-language translators with divergent choices (R None→NULL and dict→list(); Julia None→nothing and dict→Dict(); MATLAB None→NaN; C# None raises; Bash None→'' and list→parenthesised). A protocol `set` would have to legislate these mappings for every language or leave them kernel-defined, in which case `set` is no more portable than generated code and reviewers will ask why it is not an `execute_request` with kernel-generated source. Steelman OLD: a kernel-side `set` avoids injection/quoting bugs in frontend-generated source (papermill's translators exist partly to get quoting right), can accept binary buffers (the message envelope already supports buffers, which source text cannot carry), and gives typed ports a home. But in-protocol precedent for pushing values into the kernel is comms (spec: comm_msg with buffers), which is what ipywidgets uses today, so OLD's own 'reuse what exists' rule (notes §2d) argues against a new `set`. Verdict: NEW is right on substance and has the stronger precedent; the one case OLD's `set` handles better (large binary inputs to a port) is served by comms.

164	## 15. Part C — scenarios where the two designs produce visibly different end-user behaviour
165	
166	OLD: Scopes + set + standalone namespace ops + control-channel analysis + rebound.
167	
168	NEW: Single namespace + delete-on-execute + shell/subshell analysis + added/removed only.
169	
170	ASSESSMENT: (1) Duplicate names across DAG branches: OLD runs both; NEW refuses or warns and asks for a rename or a kernel clone. (2) Parameter sweep node with three inputs: OLD runs three forks (concurrently with subshells) in one process; NEW runs sequentially in one namespace (last value wins, dependants of the shared name are ambiguous) or spawns three kernels. (3) Redefining a helper after a fork: OLD (copy semantics) leaves child branches running the old helper until re-forked; NEW re-runs dependants in the one namespace exactly like marimo. (4) `%who`, variable inspector, debugger panel: OLD shows the parent scope unless every tool is taught about scopes; NEW shows everything, always. (5) A cell that mutates `df` in place: identical hidden-state behaviour in both (neither tracks mutation); OLD additionally leaks the mutation across branches sharing the object. (6) Analysis while a long cell runs: OLD returns on ipykernel and xeus-python, queues on xeus-r/xeus-cpp/IRkernel/IJulia; NEW returns on ipykernel 7 via a subshell (and on any future subshell kernel), queues elsewhere; NEW is always ordered after magic-registering cells, OLD may analyse with the wrong transformer state. (7) Dynamic rebinding (`exec`, `%run`, star import overwrites `x`): OLD's `rebound` lets the reactive plugin invalidate `x`'s dependants; NEW misses it unless static analysis flagged the cell as dynamic and the plugin treats 'dynamic' as 'invalidate everything'. (8) Bash/SQL kernels: identical (delta gives defines; manual wiring) except OLD can report overwrites via rebound. (9) Removing a cell: OLD sends namespace_request delete; NEW sends a silent empty execute with namespace_delete — the user sees busy/idle flicker in both and no counter change in either; an attached console sees nothing in either. (10) Julia: same in both once IJulia implements delete by module migration; OLD's scope-as-module offers nothing IJulia can build on beyond that. (11) Widget-bound variables and DAG input ports: OLD `set` vs NEW comms/generated assignment — same visible result; differs only in how quoting/type errors surface (kernel-side vs frontend-side). (12) Isolation for mutating code: both end at kernel clone/CRIU; users see multiple kernels in the running-kernels panel in both.

175	## Corrections
176	  - OLD (kernel-design-notes.md:75-78; transcript turn 1): 'needs no kernel cooperation ... kernel rebinds ZMQ ports' is self-contradictory and inaccurate. ipykernel binds ports only at startup (kernelapp.py:352-392) and has no rebind path; CRIU itself restores listening sockets to the same ports and fails if they are taken (criu.org/Sockets; criu issues #516, #167). In-place restore needs no kernel action; clone needs a network namespace per copy (provisioner-level) or a new kernel mechanism, not 'the kernel rebinds'.
177	  - OLD (kernel-design-notes.md:29-31; transcript turn 4 §1): 'ipyflow proves it works' for an identity-diff namespace_delta overstates the precedent. ipyflow tracks dataflow through pyccolo AST instrumentation and tracing, not a before/after identity diff of globals, and is documented to miss mutations through function boundaries (arxiv 2511.21994). It proves in-kernel dataflow tracking is feasible, not this mechanism.
178	  - OLD (kernel-design-notes.md:45-50; transcript turn 4 §3): 'Pluto's implementation of variable deletion is literally this [scopes]' and 'Julia modules' as the scope backend. Pluto keeps one workspace module per notebook and migrates the whole notebook on delete (deleting globals.jl:16-21; WorkspaceManager.jl bump_workspace_module); it never forks per-branch modules. Pluto is precedent for delete-by-migration, not for scopes.
179	  - OLD (kernel-design-notes.md:49): 'Composes with subshells' is unsupported as stated. Subshells share one namespace ('within the same process namespace', JEP 91) and ipykernel executes every subshell request through the single `self.shell` whose `user_ns`/`user_global_ns` are shell attributes (ipkernel.py:98-109, 386; interactiveshell.py:1363-1364, 3823). Per-request scope selection across threads requires threading a namespace argument through IPython's run_cell/run_code, a change the notes do not account for.
180	  - OLD (kernel-design-notes.md:26-28; transcript turn 5): placing analyze_request on control 'like debug_request' collides with the JEP 91 text, which calls using control for non-control interactions 'bad practice as it should only be used for control purposes'. It also only buys responsiveness on kernels with a separate control thread: ipykernel and xeus-python (split server), not xeus-r/xeus-cpp (default single-thread server), IRkernel (single poll loop) or, in practice, IJulia (cooperative tasks).
181	  - NEW (new-design.md:17-18): 'the model Hex and marimo already ship' — verified for marimo (single glbls dict; one definer per global), Pluto and Observable; NOT verified for Hex. Hex docs fetched state only that the graph is built from variable references and that globals() breaks reactivity; nothing found on duplicate definitions.
182	  - NEW (new-design.md:69-70): 'Julia can advertise analysis without delete' implies Julia cannot do delete. Pluto shows a Julia kernel can implement delete by module migration (deleting globals.jl:16-21, 75, 86, 143); IJulia simply has not. The feature split is still right, the reasoning is not.
183	  - NEW (new-design.md:49-51): 'Responsiveness during a long run comes from sending it on a subshell where the kernel has them ... that works today' is true for ipykernel 7 (kernelbase.py:578-595) but as of a gh code search no 'subshell' code exists in xeus or xeus-zmq (xeus-zmq 4.0.0, 2026-03-04, no release notes), so today it works for one kernel implementation. Also, IPython's `transform_cell` runs `with self.builtin_trap:` for single-line cells (interactiveshell.py:3612-3615), which is process-global; running analysis on any non-main thread (control in OLD, subshell in NEW) shares this hazard.
184	  - NEW (new-design.md:29-30): 'Purging without running ... is an execute with empty code and silent set' omits that JupyterLab's CodeCell.execute refuses to send empty code (cells/src/widget.ts:1770-1775), so the plugin must call kernel.requestExecute directly, and that IPython short-circuits empty cells before any transform (interactiveshell.py:3428-3431), so the kernel must apply namespace_delete before handing code to the interpreter. Neither is a flaw in the design, both are unstated implementation requirements.
185	  - NEW (new-design.md:63-67 table): counting 'new message pairs' as the cost metric understates the case. JEP 92 (one optional field) went proposal-to-merge in 5 months; JEP 91 (new threading semantics) took 21 months to merge and 34 months to a shipped ipykernel, with no xeus implementation yet. The saving in NEW is removing the one JEP-91-class item (scopes), not the message count.

Based on the search results, I found information about how Hex and other reactive notebook systems handle variable definitions across cells.

Hex projects are backed by a graph which links cells together and defines how they re-execute. The reactive execution model is designed to handle variable dependencies automatically.

While the search results don't specifically mention an error message about variables "defined in multiple cells," they do highlight how reactive notebook systems address this issue. Hex maps the relationships between cells into a graph that helps power its reactive execution model, with linkages automatically inferred from variable or dataframe references.

For comparison, the marimo notebook system takes a stricter approach: Variables are bound in exactly one cell: defining the same name in two cells is a hard error rather than a race.

If you're encountering a specific error message in a Hex notebook about variables being defined in multiple cells, it would likely occur when the reactive execution engine detects conflicting definitions that create ambiguity in the dependency graph. To resolve this, you would need to ensure each variable is defined in only one cell and then referenced (not redefined) in other cells.

Based on the search results, here's what I found:

JEP 91 introduces kernel sub-shells to allow for concurrent code execution. Subshells open their own shell socket, and appear as a separate kernel in the UI on which you can connect any client.

Regarding xeus-zmq specifically, xeus-zmq provides various implementations of the xserver API from xeus, based on the ZeroMQ library. These implementations all conform to the Jupyter Kernel Protocol specification.

The search results show that xeus-zmq version 4.0.0 was accepted on March 17, 2026, but the specific release notes discussing subshells implementation in xeus-zmq for 2026 were not included in the search results. For detailed information about subshells support in xeus-zmq 4.0.0 or other 2026 releases, you may want to check the official xeus-zmq GitHub repository releases page or changelog directly.

# Variables in Hex: Multi-Cell Definition and Execution

Based on the documentation provided, here's what Hex covers regarding variables across cells:

## Variable Definition Across Cells

Variables can be defined in multiple cell types: "Variables result from defining an input in an **Input cell**, or executing a function in a **Code cell**."

Once created, these variables have broad reference capabilities: "variables can be referenced in other **Code**, **Input Parameter,** and **Text cells**, and in filter fields in **Chart** and **Transform cells**."

## Reactive Execution Model

Hex employs a reactive approach rather than strictly linear execution. The system "maps the relationships between your cells into a graph that helps power its **reactive execution model**." These connections are "automatically inferred from variable or dataframe references, without any need for user definition."

## Limitations in Documentation

The provided documentation does **not** explicitly address:
- How Hex handles duplicate variable names across cells
- Specific rules for which cells execute when a variable is redefined
- Detailed comparison between reactive versus linear execution ordering

The material emphasizes that cell relationships drive execution but doesn't detail the prioritization logic when variables are reassigned multiple times.

42	# decisions_for_max
43	- Is the user-drawn DAG allowed to have two branches that define the same name? Yes means the OLD design's scopes (or a server-level clone that does not exist on a plain install), a scope-lifecycle state machine in the scheduler, and an IPython change to make per-request namespaces work under subshells; it preserves copy-a-branch and in-process parameter sweeps. No means the NEW design's one-definition rule, renames on fan-out, sequential sweeps in one namespace or N kernels via replay, and a DAG plugin that covers fan-out over disjoint names only. This is the product decision the whole scopes debate reduces to, and it is a decision about the DAG plugin, not the reactive one.
44	- Which plugin is first. The reactive plugin needs analysis, delete, and delta and nothing else; every shipped reactive system (marimo, Pluto, Observable) runs on that surface, so the NEW design is sufficient for it. The DAG plugin as originally motivated (branching, sweeps, input ports) needs scopes and set or a clone tier. Choosing reactive-first makes the NEW design the proposal and the DAG plugin a fan-out-over-disjoint-names tool; choosing DAG-first keeps the OLD design's items 2b/2c on the table and accepts a JEP-91-class review.
45	- Channel for analyze_request. Control: responsive today on ipykernel and xeus-python (the two validation kernels), against JEP 91's explicit 'bad practice' guidance, unordered with executions (wrong for Julia macros and C++ TU state, and for IPython single-line automagic), and a deprecation cycle to move later. Shell: conformant, ordered on the main shell, responsive only via subshells (ipykernel only today) and unordered again when subshelled, and the reversible direction if the choice later needs revisiting. The thread-safety question does not discriminate; the norms-versus-present-capability trade does.
46	- Delete as an execute_request field or a standalone message. Field: delete-then-rerun is atomic and one message; a stale-kernel failure is silent (mitigable by advertising the string only when do_execute accepts the parameter and verifying via delta.removed); purges need a silent empty execute that bypasses CodeCell.execute; a queued purge is aborted with the rest of the queue after stop_on_error (right for re-run purges, wrong for cell-removed purges); delete happens even if the code then fails. Message: fails loud (no reply, future hangs), keeps the option of delete-only-after-success, doubles message count, is not aborted by stop_on_error (deletes names for a rerun that never happens), and adds a message pair to the proposal.
47	- Delete-before-run or delete-on-success. marimo deletes before running and a failing cell leaves its names undefined ('ancestor raised' blocks descendants). For the DAG plugin a failed rerun that has already destroyed the previous binding may surprise users. The NEW design fixes delete-before-run by construction; the OLD design leaves the choice to the frontend. Either is defensible; it must be chosen and documented, and the scheduler must record 'names undefined because run failed' under delete-before-run.
48	- Keep `rebound` (as an optional key) or drop it. Drop: no held references, no id recycling, smaller schema, additive later. Keep: the only signal for dynamic writes to names owned by other cells (exec, %store -r, %%R -o onto an existing name, `global` inside a function called from another cell) and for reassignment in parser-less kernels (`count=$((count+1))` yields an empty delta), with a weakref-where-possible hybrid bounding the memory cost. The choice depends on the `dynamic`-cell policy decision.
49	- Keep `set` or drop it. Keep: language-agnostic input ports and parameters in one message; the kernel owns the JSON-to-binding mapping; a spec must legislate the mapping per language (papermill-style table) with an escape hatch like Pluto's transform_value. Drop: parameters become generated assignment source (per-language templates in the plugin; papermill covers twelve kernel names and no JS/C++/SQL) or ipywidgets comms (Python and xeus only), so the language-agnostic input cell disappears from the first version.
50	- Keep a separate `imports` list or fold imports into defines. Fold: matches marimo, one less key. Keep: R `library()` and Julia `using` bind nothing enumerable yet must be graph ancestors of every cell using an exported name; a drawn-DAG UI wants to hide import edges and not flag two branches that both `import numpy as np` as a conflict. Additive later, but folding loses information for two of the target languages.
51	- One flag or two for uncertainty. A single `dynamic` flag forces the frontend to treat 'may define names I cannot see' and 'may reference names I cannot see' identically (run after everything and invalidate everything after). Two flags let a star-import cell be scheduled differently from an NSE-heavy R cell. Per-reference confidence (OLD's graded form) is only useful for R's NSE.
52	- Three feature strings or fewer. Three (analysis, delete, delta) lets bash advertise delta only, Deno analysis plus delta, JVM delete plus delta, at the cost of a worse string-to-surface ratio than JEP 91 or the debugger and three contracts to write. One or two strings simplify the JEP and force kernels to implement all-or-nothing. Either way the strings must be named and each contract made testable before ipykernel ships them.
53	- What to build before October 19 versus what to propose. A comm-target prototype in ipykernel carries either design unchanged, so the prototype can implement the NEW surface (analysis, delete-on-execute, delta) and still leave scopes and set open in the pre-proposal. The decision is whether the talk's proposal slide shows the small surface (matches the 'opt-in reactive execution first' thesis and the JEP 92 precedent) or the full surface (matches the DAG motivation and invites the JEP 91 comparison).
54	- Which second kernel validates the design. xeus-python shares IPython and proves little; Deno (parser in-kernel, no delete for let/const, no comms), IRkernel (single poll loop, no user_expressions, library() invisible to delta) or IJulia (module-bump delete, macro ordering) each exercise a divergence the lenses found. Choosing one costs implementation time in an unfamiliar codebase; choosing xeus-python costs the credibility of the language-agnostic claim.
55	
56	# strongest_case_for_old
57	The OLD design is the only one of the two that serves the feature this project was started for. A user-drawn DAG exists to fan out: run a shared prefix, then several variants that naturally reuse the same names, or the same subgraph over several inputs. Scopes plus set make each branch or parameter one message each inside one process, with the loaded data shared and concurrent execution on subshells available, and they let the frontend read a losing branch's value afterward. The NEW design gives that up and points at a clone-kernel tier that, on a plain install without per-kernel network namespaces, is replay: a full prefix re-run per branch. Its analysis placement on control is responsive today on both kernels the notes plan to validate on (ipykernel and xeus-python), which the NEW design's subshell route matches only on ipykernel; its standalone namespace_request fails loud where the NEW field fails silent, and it keeps the option of deleting only after a successful run, which DAG users will expect. Its richer reply shapes carry information the NEW design discards and would need to add back: a separate imports list is load-bearing for R library() and Julia using and for a drawn-graph UI, and rebound is the only signal for dynamic writes to existing names and for reassignment in parser-less kernels. Its errors are correctable by narrowing rather than redesign: drop 'composes with subshells', say 'fresh module per scope' instead of 'dict copy', fix the Pluto and ipyflow citations, and move analysis to shell if the JEP 91 sentence proves decisive. Everything the NEW design keeps is a subset of it, so it is the design to write down in full and then cut from, not the one to reconstruct later.
58	
59	# strongest_case_for_new
60	The NEW design is the surface every shipped reactive notebook actually runs on: marimo, Pluto and Observable each use one namespace, one definer per name, deletion of a cell's names before rerun or on removal, and static analysis of defines and references, with widget values arriving through the runtime's own channel. That is analysis plus delete plus delta plus comms, and nothing more; the talk's thesis is 'opt-in reactive execution first', and this is what that thesis needs. What it cuts is the one JEP-91-class item: scopes touch how every kernel executes code, their semantics as written are unsound in Python (functions keep __globals__ bound to the parent dict so a child's rebind is invisible to pre-fork code; exec rejects a chain; one user_ns is shared by all subshell threads, so concurrent scopes need an IPython change), Pluto never forked workspaces, and shallow copies leak the same mutations a single namespace does. JEP 92 (one optional field) went from proposal to merge in five months; JEP 91 took twenty-one months to merge, thirty-four to a shipped ipykernel, and has no xeus implementation yet. Delete as a request field makes delete-then-rerun atomic and halves the message count, and its silent-ignore hazard is closable inside kernelbase by advertising the string only when do_execute accepts the parameter and verifying through delta.removed. Shell placement follows JEP 91's explicit guidance, is the direction that can be revisited, and is the correct choice for Julia macros and C++ translation-unit state even though the IPython magic example was weak. Every cut is additive later (set, scopes, rebound, imports, snapshots), while the two forks it commits to (shell channel, delete as field) are the ones with the cheaper reversal path. For a proposal that has to survive review and land in ipykernel the way subshells did, the smaller surface with the sounder semantics is the one that ships.
61	
```

54	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: The claim is accurate and directly demonstrated; the OLD design says the same thing. (b) In R's environment-chain version, `<<-` writes through to parent environments (rebinding leak). (c) For Python the lookup-chain variant rests on passing a dict subclass as exec globals, which the language docs say is not allowed. So the OLD design's 'correct as long as cells rebind rather than mutate' was itself overstated, and the NEW design's argument against scopes is stronger than it states.

209	## [holds_with_caveats] Binding a JSON value to a name is semantically ambiguous in R (numeric vs integer, vector vs list vs data frame), JavaScript (number vs BigInt, integer precision), and Julia (Int64 vs Float64, Dict vs NamedTuple), and papermill maintains per-language parameter translators precisely because of this.
210	
211	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: The ambiguity half holds (R and Julia documented; JS BigInt/precision documented; Pluto and marimo both ship conversion hooks for exactly this reason). The papermill half is a misattribution: papermill's translators exist because papermill injects a *source-code* cell and each language has its own literal syntax and assignment form (`NULL` vs `nothing`, `list()` vs `Dict()`, `name=val` with shlex quoting for bash). They do not resolve the semantic ambiguity; they hard-code one choice per language (JSON array -> R `list(...)` never a vector; JSON int -> bare `1`, which is a double in R; Julia object -> `Dict`). Also, papermill has no JavaScript translator at all, so citing papermill as evidence about JavaScript is unsupported. Unverified: the specific R integer-vs-numeric point.
212	
213	MATTERS: The NEW design uses this as the reason to drop `set`. The correct lesson from papermill is narrower: a JSON->binding operation needs a per-kernel default mapping (which a kernel-side `set` could supply, the way each papermill translator does, but inside the kernel where the parser and types live). So the ambiguity is an argument that `set` needs a specified per-kernel mapping plus an escape hatch (Pluto's transform_value / marimo's _convert_value), not proof that `set` is unworkable. It equally undercuts the OLD design's claim (transcript-design-verbatim.md line 159) that `set` "costs nothing extra".

NOTE: I could not verify the integer-vs-numeric sub-claim from a primary source (no R installed locally; the vignette "contains no discussion of JSON numbers being parsed as integers versus doubles"); the scalar/vector/list/data-frame ambiguity is documented, integer-vs-double is plausible but unverified.

250	## [holds_with_caveats] Computing 'added' and 'removed' names per execution as set differences of the top-level namespace keys is cheap and exact in Python, R, Julia, bash, and SQL, and is more universally implementable than static analysis.
251	
252	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: Holds cleanly for Python and R globalenv (with IPython's hidden-name filter applied). For Julia 'removed' is always empty. For bash it is implementable via hidden REPL commands but is neither free nor a complete picture of what a cell defines. For SQL the claim is unsupported: no single namespace exists, catalog queries are not cheap on remote warehouses, and they are not exact under concurrency. 'More universally implementable than static analysis' is true for bash (no AST available) but not obviously for SQL (sqlglot-style parsers exist and are dialect-aware).
253	
254	MATTERS: The new design drops `rebound` and `set`/scopes partly on the strength of `namespace_delta` being a near-universal ground truth. If the delta is only clean for Python/R, the 'gives parser-less kernels the defines half of an edge for free' benefit shrinks to bash-with-caveats, and the argument that the new design loses nothing relative to the old one on non-Python kernels weakens.
255	
256	EVIDENCE:
257	  - Reproduced in venv (python 3.14.6, IPython 9.17.1): set(sh.user_ns) before/after run_cell on a 100k-name namespace costs 2.82 ms; dict(user_ns) shallow copy 0.85 ms. Cheap in Python.
258	  - Reproduced: raw set difference is NOT exact without filtering. 'x = [1,2,3]' → raw added ['_i','_i1','_ii','_iii','x']; 'x' (expression) → raw added ['_2','_i2']. Filtering by shell.user_ns_hidden gives ['x'] and [] respectively. IPython/core/history.py:1139-1143 pushes _i, _ii, _iii, _iN via shell.push(to_main, interactive=False); IPython/core/interactiveshell.py:1671-1676 marks non-interactive pushes hidden. So an ipykernel implementation must diff against user_ns_hidden (identity check as in IPython/core/magics/namespace.py:272-276), not raw keys.
259	  - Reproduced: set difference is blind to rebinding: 'x = [4]' after 'x = [1,2,3]' → added [], removed []. 'del x' → removed ['x']. from math import * → 56 names added (exact, as claimed).
260	  - R: IRkernel evaluates with evaluate(..., envir = .GlobalEnv) (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IRkernel/IRkernel/master/R/execution.r), so ls(.GlobalEnv, all.names=TRUE) diff is well-defined and cheap. Not verified: attach()'d frames and package loads (library()) alter what is *visible* without changing .GlobalEnv, so 'references satisfied' is not the same as 'names in globalenv'.
261	  - Julia: 'Julia does not have an analog of MATLAB's clear function; once a name is defined in a Julia session (technically, in module Main), it is always present' (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/variables-and-scoping/ via search; also github.com/JuliaLang/julia/issues/24205). So 'removed' is structurally always empty for a Julia kernel; v1.12.1 NEWS.md mentions world-age redefinition of constants but no binding deletion API (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JuliaLang/julia/v1.12.1/NEWS.md). A Base.delete_binding was referenced in search results but I could not verify it in the release notes.
262	  - bash: bash_kernel drives one persistent bash via pexpect (pexpect.spawn("bash", ['--rcfile', bashrc], ...)) and already sends hidden commands (PS1/PS2/PROMPT_COMMAND, 'export PAGER=cat') (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/takluyver/bash_kernel/master/bash_kernel/kernel.py). 263	  - SQL: no primary source found for a SQL kernel that has a 'top-level namespace'. 'Cheap and exact' for SQL is unsupported.

265	## [holds_with_caveats] Detecting 'rebound' names by object identity is either unreliable (id() values are recycled after garbage collection so a rebinding to a new object can be missed) or costly (holding strong references to every prior value during execution defers freeing replaced objects; weak references are unavailable for int, str, tuple, list, dict).
266	
267	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: The two failure modes named are real and reproducible. But the claim is framed as an exhaustive dichotomy and it is not: (1) a weakref-where-possible / id-elsewhere hybrid removes the memory cost for most heavy objects and confines the recycling hazard to list/dict/immutables; (2) instrumentation (what ipyflow actually does, via pyccolo) detects rebinding and mutation exactly, at implementation and runtime cost. 'Costly' should be stated as a memory-lifetime cost, not a time cost; the time cost is under a millisecond even for 100k names.
268	
269	MATTERS: If the synthesis accepts the dichotomy at face value, `rebound` is dropped as infeasible; if the hybrid or tracing routes are acknowledged, dropping `rebound` becomes a scope/simplicity choice rather than a necessity, and the comparison table's 'nothing lost' framing needs qualification. It also flags that the OLD design's ipyflow citation for identity diffing is inaccurate.
270	
271	EVIDENCE:
272	  - Reproduced (python 3.14.6): weakref.ref() raises TypeError for int, str, tuple, list, dict, float, bytes, and bare object(); succeeds for set, frozenset, functions, user-class instances. The listed five are correct (and the list is if anything incomplete).
273	  - Reproduced id recycling miss: setup 'x = [1,2,3]', then cell 'x = None\nx = [9,9,9]' → id(x) before == id(x) after, so an id-only comparison reports NO rebind although x was rebound to a new object. Same for 'del x; x = [4,5,6]'. In a 200-iteration del/realloc loop the id was reused 200/200 times. Plain 'x = [9,9,9]' and 'x = list(x)' (RHS allocates while old value alive) are detected correctly.
274	  - Cost side: the time cost of holding a shallow copy is negligible (dict(user_ns) 0.85 ms for 100k names); the real cost is memory/lifetime — the pre-run copy keeps every replaced object alive until the run ends (e.g. the previous DataFrame during a re-run of a read_csv cell). The claim's wording ('defers freeing replaced objects') is accurate on that point.
275	  - Omitted third option: ipyflow does rebinding/mutation detection by instrumentation, not by identity diffing — ipyflow-core install_requires includes 'pyccolo>=0.0.95' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipyflow/ipyflow/master/core/setup.cfg). The old design's transcript (transcript-design-verbatim.md:155) cites ipyflow as proof that identity diffing 'works inside ipykernel', which misattributes ipyflow's mechanism; the new design's either/or omits tracing as an option altogether.
276	  - Hybrid not considered: weakrefs where supported (functions, classes, user instances, sets; numpy/pandas objects are commonly weakref-able but I could not verify here — numpy/pandas are not installed in the venv) plus id+type for the non-weakref-able builtins would remove the memory cost for the heavy objects that matter and confine the recycling hazard to small immutables and list/dict.
277	  - Identity also under-reports for cached immutables: 'x = "ab"' re-executed yields the same interned object (reproduced), so identity cannot distinguish 'rebound to an equal cached value' from 'untouched'; the old design already hedged with 'object identity where available' (transcript-design-verbatim.md:155).

279	## [holds_with_caveats] Static analysis already reports which names a cell assigns, so rebinding information from the kernel adds nothing the reactive scheduler needs.
280	
281	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: For a marimo/Pluto-style scheduler that enforces one static definition per name and re-runs on definition events, kernel rebinding info is indeed not required. It does add something for the two uses the new design itself assigns to `namespace_delta`: (a) checking static analysis against runtime behavior in the `dynamic` cases (exec, globals()[...], `global` inside a function called from another cell), where a rebind of an existing name is invisible to both static analysis and added/removed; (b) parser-less kernels, where without `rebound` a cell that re-assigns an existing name yields an empty delta, so the one-definition rule cannot be enforced there. The `namespace_delete` pre-step partially compensates for the cell's own names but not for cross-cell violations.
282	
283	MATTERS: Determines whether dropping `rebound` is free. For the reactive plugin proper it is; for the 'verify static analysis' and 'bash gets defines for free' benefits the new design advertises, dropping `rebound` narrows both, and the synthesis should not credit the new design with those two benefits at full strength.

285	EVIDENCE:
286	  - marimo docs (https://docs.marimo.io/guides/reactivity/): 'When a cell is run, marimo automatically runs all other cells that reference any of the global variables it defines'; 'marimo statically analyzes each cell ... to determine its references ... definitions'; 'marimo does not track mutations to variables, nor assignments to attributes'; 'marimo requires that every global variable be defined by only one cell'. Pluto docs (https://plutojl.org/en/docs/reactivity/): 'Pluto tracks the dependencies between cells by looking at the syntax tree'; 'Two cells cannot both define x'. So the marimo/Pluto scheduler triggers on definition events from static analysis, not on runtime rebinding or value change — the core of the claim holds for that scheduler.
287	  - Counter-evidence 1 (dynamic definitions): reproduced in IPython 9.17.1 — 'def f(): global g; g = 1' then 'f()' in a later cell: the *calling* cell's delta shows added ['g']; "exec('h = 5')" → added ['h']; "globals()['k'] = 1" → added ['k']. Static analysis of the calling cell sees none of these. They were visible only because the names were new; had g/h/k already existed, neither static analysis nor added/removed would report the rebind. This is exactly the case the new design's own `dynamic` flag admits static analysis cannot cover, so 'adds nothing' is false there.
288	  - Counter-evidence 2 (the design's own stated purpose): new-design.md:39-41 says the field 'checks static analysis against what actually happened' and gives parser-less kernels 'the defines half of an edge for free'. Without `rebound`, a bash cell that assigns an already-existing name produces an empty delta (set difference is blind to rebinding — reproduced above with 'x = [4]'), so a second-definition conflict on a parser-less kernel is undetectable, and the static-vs-runtime check misses any runtime rebinding of names the cell did not statically define.
289	  - Mitigating factor the design does not state: under its own `namespace_delete` pre-step (new-design.md:26-29), a cell's previously-defined names are deleted before the re-run, so the cell's own re-definitions reappear in `added`. Rebinding information is therefore recoverable for the cell's *own* names without `rebound`; what remains invisible is rebinding of names owned by other cells (the violation case) and dynamic rebinding.
290	  - Neither identity-based `rebound` nor static assignment analysis detects mutation (lst.append, df['c'] = ...); only tracing does (ipyflow/pyccolo). So on mutation the two approaches are equally blind and the claim is neutral there.

293	# BUNDLE delta-rebound / verifier: ecosystem
294	
295	## [holds_with_caveats] Computing 'added' and 'removed' names per execution as set differences of the top-level namespace keys is cheap and exact in Python, R, Julia, bash, and SQL, and is more universally implementable than static analysis.
296	
297	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: Cheap: yes in all five. Exact: only after per-language filtering (IPython's `_N`/`_iN`/`_exit_code` via user_ns_hidden; bash's `_`, `PIPESTATUS`, `REPLY`; Julia's compiler-generated names and duplicates), and not under concurrency: with subshells (or user threads) sharing one namespace, a before/after diff misattributes concurrent writes. In Julia `removed` is always empty; in R `library()` imports are invisible to a globalenv key diff, so 'imports are defines' cannot be recovered from the delta there; in Julia it needs `usings=true` (1.12+). For SQL the 'top-level namespace' is a design decision the claim skips (tables in a shared, backend-specific catalog vs Hex-style named result variables), and a catalog diff is neither exclusive to the session nor uniformly cheap. 'More universally implementable than static analysis' holds for bash and is a wash for Python/R/Julia; for SQL both routes are dialect-specific.
298	
299	MATTERS: If the delta is not exact, the NEW design's stated use of it, 'checks static analysis against what actually happened' and 'gives parser-less kernels ... the defines half of an edge for free', produces false edges (concurrent writes, shell noise) or missing defines (R imports, Julia deletes), which weakens the argument that the delta can replace the OLD design's richer analysis fields.
