301	EVIDENCE:
302	  - Python/ipykernel: IPython itself writes names into user_ns on every execution, so a raw key diff is not 'exact' without filtering: displayhook pushes `_`, `__`, `___` and `_<N>` (IPython/core/displayhook.py:208-246), HistoryManager pushes `_i`, `_ii`, `_iii`, `_i<N>` (IPython/core/history.py:1133-1140), `!cmd` sets `_exit_code` (interactiveshell.py:2723). These go through `push(..., interactive=False)` into `user_ns_hidden` (interactiveshell.py:1327, 1671-1676), so a filter exists, but the kernel must apply it.
303	  - Python concurrency: ipykernel 7 subshells run against one shell/user_ns (ipkernel.py do_execute uses the single `self.shell`); the per-subshell asyncio lock only serializes within a subshell (kernelbase.py:614-621: 'do not accept any other shell messages on the same subshell'). JEP 91: 'A subshell request may be processed concurrently with other subshells' and other threads act 'within the same process namespace' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jupyter/enhancement-proposals/master/91-kernel-subshells/kernel-subshells.md). A before/after diff on one subshell therefore attributes another subshell's (or a user thread's) additions to this cell.
304	  - R: ls() 'If FALSE, names which begin with a '.' are omitted' and sorting dominates its cost, so `ls(globalenv(), all.names=TRUE, sorted=FALSE)` is the cheap form (https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/ls.html). `library()` attaches to the search path, not globalenv, so an R key-diff of globalenv reports no 'define' for a cell whose only effect is an import, unlike Python where `import x` adds a key.
305	  - Julia: `names(x::Module; all, imported, usings)` docstring: with all=true it 'also includes non-public names ... deprecated names, and compiler-generated names'; 'names may return duplicate names'; 'sym ∈ names(SomeModule) does not imply isdefined'; `usings` requires Julia 1.12+ (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JuliaLang/julia/master/base/runtime_internals.jl). Julia FAQ: 'once a name is defined in a Julia session (technically, in module Main), it is always present' (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/faq/), so `removed` is structurally always empty in IJulia.
306	  - bash: bash_kernel drives one persistent bash via pexpect REPLWrapper (`pexpect.spawn("bash", ['--rcfile', bashrc], ...)`, `self.bashwrapper.run_command(code.rstrip(), timeout=None)`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/takluyver/bash_kernel/master/bash_kernel/kernel.py), so a `compgen -v` before/after is two extra REPL round trips. Bash auto-sets `_` ('expands to the last argument to the previous simple command'), `PIPESTATUS`, `REPLY`, `MAPFILE`, `COPROC`, `OLDPWD` as side effects (https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Bash-Variables.html); functions and aliases live in separate namespaces (`declare -F`, `alias`).
307	  - SQL: xeus-sql fronts 'DB2, Firebird, MySQL, ODBC (generic backend), Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQLite3' via SOCI (https://github.com/jupyter-xeus/xeus-sql); catalog introspection is per-backend (information_schema vs sqlite_master vs Oracle views), the catalog is shared with other sessions, and temp tables/CTEs are session-scoped, so a table-catalog diff is neither uniform nor guaranteed cheap or exclusive to this cell. Hex, the descendant with SQL cells, defines a SQL cell's output as a named dataframe variable, not the tables it touches (https://learn.hex.tech/docs/explore-data/cells/sql-cells/sql-cells-introduction; https://hex.tech/blog/dataframe-sql/). I could not verify that any Jupyter SQL kernel exposes a per-cell 'namespace' at all.

309	## [holds_with_caveats] Detecting 'rebound' names by object identity is either unreliable (id() values are recycled after garbage collection so a rebinding to a new object can be missed) or costly (holding strong references to every prior value during execution defers freeing replaced objects; weak references are unavailable for int, str, tuple, list, dict).
310	
311	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: The two horns are real, but the dichotomy is not exhaustive and the framing is Python-specific. (1) A hybrid, weakref where the type allows it (user-class instances, and, as far as I know but could not test here since numpy is not installed in the venv, numpy arrays and pandas DataFrames) plus (id, type) with strong references only for non-weak-referenceable builtins, confines the memory cost to list/dict/str/bytes values; it does not eliminate it, since lists and dicts can be large. (2) Reliable rebind detection exists via AST instrumentation (ipyflow/pyccolo) at CPU cost rather than memory cost, so 'reliable' and 'cheap' trade off differently than the claim states. (3) Identity is the wrong notion of rebinding for immutables regardless of gc: `x = 5` twice is indistinguishable from no rebinding. (4) In bash, variables are strings and value comparison is cheap and exact; in R and Julia, `identical()`/`===` compare values for immutables, so the identity argument does not transfer to the other kernels the design is meant to serve. (5) id reuse follows refcount deallocation, not only 'garbage collection', so it can happen within a single statement.
312	
313	MATTERS: The claim is the sole justification for dropping `rebound` from namespace_delta. If a hybrid or a per-language value comparison makes rebinding detection cheap enough in practice (bash, R, Julia immutables, weak-referenceable Python objects), then dropping the field is a design choice rather than a forced simplification, and the comparison between OLD and NEW should say so.
314	
315	EVIDENCE:
316	  - Python docs, id(): 'Two objects with non-overlapping lifetimes may have the same id() value.' (https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html). Local repro in the venv Python 3.14.6 with gc disabled: bytearray(10**6) freed then reallocated gets the identical id (True), i.e. reuse follows refcount deallocation, not a cyclic-GC pass; a small class instance did not get the same id in the same test (False), so misses are allocator-dependent, not systematic.
317	  - Python docs, weakref: 'Several built-in types such as list and dict do not directly support weak references but can add support through subclassing'; 'Other built-in types such as tuple and int do not support weak references even when subclassed.' (https://docs.python.org/3/library/weakref.html). Local check: weakref.ref raises TypeError for int, str, tuple, list, dict, float, bytes, bytearray and bare object(); succeeds for set, frozenset, user-class instances, functions.
318	  - Local check: rebinding to an equal immutable yields the same id: `x = 5; x = 5` (True), `s = 'hello'; s = 'hello'` (True), `a = 10**6; a = 10**6` (True, same-cell constant folding). Identity therefore cannot report a rebinding of a name to an equal immutable value, independent of id reuse.
319	  - ipyflow detects rebinding without identity comparison: it is built on pyccolo, 'a library for declarative instrumentation in Python ... general, event-emitting AST transformations', and 'Pyccolo instrumentation adds significant overhead to Python' (https://github.com/smacke/pyccolo). ipyflow 'peeks at runtime state in order to infer dependencies' (https://github.com/ipyflow/ipyflow). So the OLD design's 'ipyflow proves it works' is not evidence for identity diffing; it is evidence for tracing.
320	  - Cost mechanism: a shallow `dict(user_ns)` copy is O(n) and trivial in CPU; the cost is that every replaced object stays alive until the cell finishes, so `df = transform(df)` peaks at old+new, and objects whose cleanup relies on refcount deallocation (files, GPU buffers) are released late.

322	## [holds_with_caveats] Static analysis already reports which names a cell assigns, so rebinding information from the kernel adds nothing the reactive scheduler needs.
323	
324	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: True for a scheduler that trusts static analysis and enforces one definition per name, which is marimo's and Pluto's model and does not skip reruns on unchanged values. False for the two purposes the NEW design itself gives namespace_delta: validating static analysis (after the first run every name already exists, so mis-predicted or dynamic writes to existing names are invisible without `rebound`) and supplying defines for parser-less kernels (a bash cell that reassigns an existing variable shows an empty delta). Correction: 'rebinding information adds nothing the marimo-style scheduler consumes, but removing it makes the delta blind to dynamic writes to names owned by other cells and to redefinitions in kernels without analysis.'
325	
326	MATTERS: This claim, together with claim 2, is what lets the NEW design shrink namespace_delta to {added, removed}. If rebound is the only field that catches cross-cell dynamic writes and bash-style redefinitions, then the NEW field is weaker than the OLD {added, rebound, removed} for exactly the validation and fallback roles the NEW design advertises for it, and the comparison should credit the OLD design's field, minus its wrong 'ipyflow proves it works' justification.

328	EVIDENCE:
329	  - marimo: 'marimo statically analyzes each cell (i.e., without running it) to determine its references ... [and] definitions'; 'marimo requires that every global variable be defined by only one cell'; 'deleting a cell deletes its global variables from program memory'; 'marimo does not track mutations to objects' (https://docs.marimo.io/guides/reactivity/). The marimo scheduler reruns dependents whenever a defining cell re-executes; it does not consult runtime rebinds, so for the marimo model the claim holds.
330	  - Pluto: ExpressionExplorer 'ignores the arguments of macro calls. Macros can transform an expression into anything, so the output of ExpressionExplorer for expressions with a macro call is ambiguous' (https://github.com/JuliaPluto/ExpressionExplorer.jl); Pluto compensates by macroexpanding in the running workspace, a runtime step, not by diffing.
331	  - Dynamic writes static analysis cannot name, in the IPython dialect the kernel would analyze: `%run` does `self.shell.user_ns.update(prog_ns)` (IPython/core/magics/execution.py:876); `%store -r` does `ip.user_ns[arg] = obj` (IPython/extensions/storemagic.py:154); `exec`, `globals()[...] = `, `from m import *`. The NEW design's analyze_reply reduces these to a single `dynamic: true` flag with no names.

The pre-run `namespace_delete` does not help, since the frontend can only delete names static analysis predicted.
333	  - Parser-less kernels: for bash the NEW design says the delta gives 'the defines half of an edge for free', but after the first run a cell like `count=$((count+1))` produces added=[] and removed=[]; only rebinding (cheap by string comparison in bash) reports that the cell writes `count`.

352	## [holds_with_caveats] Whether the control channel is actually serviced concurrently with a running execution depends on the kernel: ipykernel uses a control thread; xeus kernels only if built on xeus-zmq's split server; IRkernel and IJulia service control in the same loop as shell.

354	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: Correct in substance, with two precision fixes. (1) IJulia does not run control 'in the same loop as shell': it runs two separate event loops as two `@async` Tasks on one OS thread. The practical effect the claim cares about holds (a CPU-bound execute that never yields blocks the control task), but control IS serviced during executions that yield (I/O, sleep, Julia's own task switches), unlike IRkernel where it is strictly sequential. (2) 'xeus kernels only if built on the split server' is right for the xeus-zmq family, but xeus kernels also ship on xeus-lite (WASM, no ZMQ, no threads) where neither control nor subshells are concurrent; and even with a split server, xeus-python's control handlers that need the GIL wait on the executing shell thread — the thread exists but concurrency for Python-level work is not guaranteed.
355	
356	MATTERS: This claim underpins the new design's argument that putting analyze_request on control (old design) buys nothing portable. It survives: control-thread concurrency is an ipykernel/xeus-python property, not a protocol guarantee. But the same caveat cuts against the new design's alternative too — subshells are also kernel-specific (only ipykernel advertises 'kernel subshells' here), so neither channel gives language-agnostic responsiveness.

378	## [holds_with_caveats] IPython's transform_cell output depends on the currently registered magics, so a magic registered by an earlier cell changes how a later cell is transformed; analyzing on the ordered shell channel therefore has a correctness benefit over the control channel.
379	
380	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: The dependency is real but narrower than 'how a later cell is transformed' suggests: explicit `%magic`/`%%magic` syntax transforms identically regardless of registration (the resolution happens at run time inside run_line_magic). Registration matters only for (a) single-line cells via automagic, which additionally depends on the live user namespace (shadowing), and (b) input transformers registered at runtime by extensions. Note also that with %%cell magics the body becomes a string literal, so registration state cannot change what analysis sees for the body anyway. More importantly, the 'correctness benefit' of shell ordering evaporates under the new design's own recommendation: sending analyze_request on a subshell for responsiveness (the design's stated plan) makes it concurrent with, not ordered after, the main shell's executions — the same ordering loss as the control channel. The benefit exists only when analysis goes on the main shell and queues behind execution, which is the responsiveness problem both designs were trying to avoid. And whole-notebook analysis before any cell runs is necessarily out of order with respect to magic registration regardless of channel.
381	
382	MATTERS: This is the new design's main technical argument for shell over control. It holds only for the main-shell case; as soon as the responsiveness workaround (subshell) is used, the old design's control placement and the new design's subshell placement have the same ordering semantics, and the choice reduces to the norms argument in claim 3 plus the dispatch-path convenience.

392	## [holds_with_caveats] Calling transform_cell from a control or subshell thread while the main shell thread executes user code is thread-safe in practice (or is not; check InputTransformerManager state and the magics registry).
393	
394	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: 'Thread-safe in practice' is the right characterization, with the honest qualifier that it is GIL-safe-by-accident rather than designed: (1) BuiltinTrap's nesting counter is a shared read-modify-write; a preemption between load and store could leave exit/quit/get_ipython builtins wrongly removed or wrongly present for the executing user code (low probability under the GIL, higher under free-threaded CPython). (2) `_last_input_line` races (harmless). (3) Under the GIL, a control- or subshell-thread transform_cell cannot run at all while the main thread is inside a C extension that holds the GIL, so 'responsiveness during a long run' is bounded by GIL release, not by channel choice. (4) The existing precedent is subshells (ipykernel's own do_execute path), not the control thread; running it on the control thread adds only the difference that control's asyncio loop is separate — no new shared state. Net: no evidence of a practical hazard, but no synchronization either; a JEP reviewer could reasonably ask for a lock around builtin_trap or for analysis to avoid the prefilter (multi-line static path only).
395	
396	MATTERS: If transform_cell were unsafe off the main thread, both the old design (control thread) and the new design (subshell) would need to serialize analysis onto the main shell, removing the responsiveness argument from both. Since ipykernel already does exactly this from subshell threads, neither design incurs a new hazard; the residual risks (builtin_trap counter, GIL-bound latency) apply equally to both.

451	## [holds_with_caveats] IPython's transform_cell output depends on the currently registered magics, so a magic registered by an earlier cell changes how a later cell is transformed; analyzing on the ordered shell channel therefore has a correctness benefit over the control channel.
452	
453	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: The premise is only partly true. For multi-line cells (the common case for analysis), transform_cell is purely lexical and does not depend on which magics are registered. The registry dependence exists only for single-line cells via automagic (and there it also depends on user_ns shadowing), plus the separate case of extensions that append input transformers at runtime. What does depend on the registry is not the transform but the analysis of cell-magic I/O (e.g. `%%R -i x -o y`, `%%sql res <<`), if the analyzer asks the magic object for declared inputs/outputs. The conclusion also has a hole the design does not address: ordering with executions holds only on the same subshell (the main shell); the moment analysis is sent on a subshell for responsiveness, as the new design recommends, it is no longer ordered with the user's executions and the 'correctness benefit' evaporates. And analysis is normally requested at edit time, before the earlier cell has run, so 'ordered after the cell that registers the magic' is not a property a frontend can rely on without explicitly re-analyzing after execution.
454	
455	MATTERS: If the ordering benefit is marginal (single-line automagic, runtime-added transformers) and is forfeited by the design's own responsiveness route, then shell-vs-control for analyze_request is decided by the threading/precedent arguments alone, not by correctness. That removes one of the three reasons the new design gives for the channel move; the remaining reasons (shared dispatch with complete/inspect, no threading requirement on kernel authors) stand on their own.

464	## [holds_with_caveats] Calling transform_cell from a control or subshell thread while the main shell thread executes user code is thread-safe in practice (or is not; check InputTransformerManager state and the magics registry).
465	
466	CAVEAT/CORRECTION: Thread-safe in practice for the static part (multi-line cells: tokenizer + regex rewrites, no shared mutable state) — and ipykernel's own subshell implementation already relies on exactly this. It is NOT strictly safe for the single-line dynamic path: `InteractiveShell.transform_cell` enters `builtin_trap` (an unsynchronised nesting counter also held by the executing thread) and consults `user_ns`, so a control- or subshell-thread call can, under an unlucky interleaving, remove `get_ipython` from builtins mid-execution on the main thread. A kernel-side analyze implementation should therefore call `shell.input_transformer_manager.transform_cell()` (the static TransformerManager, which ipykernel already uses off-thread for do_is_complete, ipkernel.py:654-661) rather than `shell.transform_cell()`, and skip prefilter/automagic. This is the same hazard on shell-subshell and on control, so it does not discriminate between the two designs; it argues for using the static manager in either.
467	
468	MATTERS: Both designs implement analysis as transform_cell + ast/symtable (kernel-design-notes.md §2a; new-design.md:51). If the old design's control-thread placement were unsafe while shell placement were safe, that would be a decisive point for the new design; the evidence shows the risk is identical for subshell threads (which the new design also uses) and is avoidable by choosing the static TransformerManager API. Channel choice is therefore not a thread-safety question in ipykernel; it remains a question of protocol precedent, ordering, and what other kernels can offer.

So with JEP 91 subshells, transform_cell (and run_cell) already execute concurrently on multiple threads against one InteractiveShell, with no IPython-side locking: `grep -n threading|Lock( IPython/core/interactiveshell.py` returns nothing.

<summary>Thinking</summary>

With all five lens analyses, 46 verification verdicts, and the critic's report in hand, I'm ready to draw conclusions. Now I need to write the comparison document as markdown, then build and publish the HTML artifact.

For the file writes I'll use Bash heredocs with a quoted EOF delimiter to avoid shell expansion issues with backticks and dollar signs in the content, which handles even a large HTML artifact fine. I also need to keep the document in Max's voice — plain, specific, first person where it fits, no tidy contrast pairs or signposting, no em-dashes.

Now I'm laying out the structure: a title framing this as a comparison of two kernel-protocol designs, an opening section explaining how the comparison was produced (comparing the notes' original design against the September 14 simplification, validated across five analyses and 46 adversarial claim checks against ipykernel, IPython, JupyterLab, the messaging spec, several JEPs, and various kernel implementations, with 45 claims holding and one refuted), then a side-by-side table of the two designs across key dimensions, followed by a section on what they share in common.

Now I'm detailing the shared ground between both designs — same goals, edge semantics, reused fields, prototyping approach, frontend responsibilities, and JEP path — plus areas where both were found to be wrong on the same points. Then I move into itemized differences, starting with the biggest one: dropping scopes, where the review found real soundness problems in how scopes were originally specified for Python (exec conflicts with ChainMap, dict copies breaking closures, functions retaining references to the original namespace causing leaks).

I move to the snapshots/clone decision, noting that restoring in place needs no protocol change since it fits within the existing provisioner/restart mechanism, while true cloning via CRIU on a single host isn't feasible without process and network namespace isolation since CRIU restores the same PID and ports — meaning the old design's assumption that the kernel rebinds ports was simply incorrect, and that replay serves as the practical, universal cloning approach on a standard install.

Then I turn to the namespace_request-as-field proposal: deleting it doesn't force a signature change if I use accepts_parameters, it enables atomic delete-then-run and cuts messages in half, but it introduces a silent-ignore failure mode instead of a hang, which I could mitigate by only advertising the capability when do_execute accepts it and verifying via delta.removed — though the abort semantics get tricky since stop_on_error aborting a queued purge is correct for rerun-purges but wrong for cell-removed purges.

I also want to weigh the field-vs-message tradeoff honestly: a field can't later be retired in favor of a message without leaving two ways to do the same thing, whereas a message can always be complemented by a convenience field later, so message is the more reversible choice on this axis even though field wins on atomicity and message count — I should present this tension and lean toward keeping the field while adding a reply slot for "not deleted" cases.

On the "set" decision, I'm reconsidering whether to drop it: the ambiguity is real across R/JS/Julia and tools like Pluto and marimo, the papermill comparison was misapplied since translators only concern syntax and don't resolve int/double, and the claim that it's "only needed for value edges" doesn't hold since input cells and parameters on kernels without widget libraries still need it or require frontend codegen.

For "delta," I'm noting added/removed variables are cheap to detect but only exact after per-language filtering of noise sources like user_ns_hidden, R's search path, Julia's using, and JS lexical scoping, plus concurrency contamination and unclear error-reply behavior. The rebound concept has real id-recycling and memory concerns, but the either/or framing isn't exhaustive since weak-reference hybrids or tracing could work, and dropping rebound would blind the design to validating dynamic writes and bash reassignments — plus the ipyflow citation in the old design was wrong. I'm concluding shrink is defensible but the state handling needs clarification.

Turning to the analyze_request channel question, I'm weighing JEP 91's caution against control channel use versus the fact that the spec doesn't actually reserve it, and ipykernel already accepts all shell messages there while its DAP handlers read user_ns from the control thread. Control concurrency and subshells are ipykernel/xeus-python-specific features, ordering benefits matter for Julia macros and C++ translation units but barely help IPython magics, thread-safety is identical either way, and shell remains the reversible direction with unknown message types hanging regardless of channel.

My verdict lands on shell being correct for both norms and reversibility, with responsiveness only honestly framed as an "ipykernel today" property, suggesting the right call is per-invocation: main shell for ordering guarantees, subshell for responsiveness. Then examining the analyze_reply shape, I'm flagging real problems: representing code as a list breaks string convention and would get rejected, folding imports loses R's library() and Julia's using bindings along with DAG UI info, a single dynamic flag collapses the define/reference distinction, per-cell error status seems right, reference semantics are ambiguous (free variables? inside functions? attribute writes?), and magic bodies as strings force re-parsing run_cell_magic args while leaving no declaration mechanism for something like %%R's -i/-o flags — plus open questions around top-level await and del.

Now I'm working through feature strings and advertising counts (3 vs roughly 4), JEP 92 conformance, the need for each string to have a testable contract, the fact that none are currently named, and versioning concerns. Then I'm looking at footprint and review cost using the JEP-91 vs JEP-92 timeline as evidence — cost scales with the semantics kernel authors must implement, and the real savings come from removing scopes rather than cutting message count.

I'm sketching out the plugin capability matrix (behaviors × old/new, ~10 compact rows), a language feasibility matrix (languages × analysis/delete/delta/scopes/set, 8 rows), and compiling a list of roughly 10 errors shared by both designs — including that user_expressions isn't universal, delete doesn't fully scrub, delta name sets, concurrency issues, stop_on_error, analyzer size, and snapshot capability version.

Pluto keeps\n  `using` statements as a separate class for this reason. A drawn-graph UI also wants\n  to hide import edges and not flag two branches that both `import numpy as np`. The\n  notes' separate `imports` list was load-bearing.\n- One `dynamic` flag forces the frontend to treat \"may define names I cannot see\" and\n  \"may reference names I cannot see\" identically. The notes' `has_unknown_references`\n  kept the distinction; a star-import cell and an NSE-heavy R cell should schedule\n  differently.\n- The per-cell error entry is the right shape; a syntax error must not fail the batch.\n- Neither design defines `references`: free variables only, or all names read;\n  whether reads inside function bodies count (marimo and Observable count them);\n  whether `obj.attr = 1` is a reference; whether `x += 1` is both.\n- Both designs' \"transform_cell then ast or symtable\" undercounts the analyzer.\n  `transform_cell` turns every cell-magic body into a string literal, so `%%time`\n  bodies must be re-parsed from the `run_cell_magic` argument, `%%capture out`\n  defines `out`, and `%%R -i x -o y` needs per-magic argument parsing with no\n  registry API to declare it. `$var` in `!` and line magics is expanded at run time.\n  `symtable` has no top-level-await flag, so the analyzer must wrap the cell in an\n  async scope. `del x` shows as an assignment. Measured cost is 2.5 ms per 200-line\n  cell, so batching a whole notebook is fine.\n\n### 3.8 Advertising and footprint\n\nJEP 92 explicitly allows a feature to be \"additional messages and/or additional fields\nin different existing messages\", so gating fields on strings is conformant, and\nJupyterLab already parses the list. Three strings for one message and two fields is a\nworse ratio than JEP 91 or the debugger, and a reviewer will accept it only if each\nstring has a testable contract: delete must specify per-name failure reporting; delta\nmust specify the name filter and the concurrency caveat; analysis must specify the\nreferences semantics. Neither design names its strings or versions them, and JEP 91\nitself says a version specifier is probably needed.\n\nOn cost, the review's strongest point: cost scales with semantics kernel authors must\nimplement, not with message count. JEP 92, one optional field, went from proposal to\nmerge in five months. JEP 91, new threading semantics, took 21 months to merge, 34 to\na shipped ipykernel 7.0, and has no xeus implementation yet. Scopes are in the JEP 91\nclass; `analyze_request` and `namespace_delete` are in the JEP 92 class. The\nsimplified design's real saving is removing the one JEP 91 class item, not shaving\nmessage pairs.\n\n## 4. What each plugin can do under each design\n\n| Behavior | notes' design | simplified design |\n|---|---|---|\n| Graph of a cold notebook before anything runs | one batch analyze; needs a running kernel | same |\n| Rewire on edit without running | analyze on control, live during a long run on ipykernel and xeus-python | analyze on shell; live during a long run on ipykernel via a subshell; queued elsewhere |\n| Stale markers | frontend | frontend |\n| Rerun descendants with partial failure | `stop_on_error` is coarser than needed under both; scheduler blocks descendants of an errored ancestor itself | same; plus delete-before-run means a failed cell has no bindings |\n| No hidden state on delete or rename | separate message; frontend may delete only after success | field; delete happens before the run |\n| Two branches defining `model` | run both, each in its own scope, concurrently on subshells (needs an IPython change to be real) | refuse, rename, serialize, or clone a kernel by replay |\n| Parameter sweep over one subgraph | N scopes, N sets, results collected per scope | sequential in one namespace with generated assignment code, or N kernels |\n| Input ports and parameters from the UI | one `set` message; kernel owns the JSON mapping | comms on kernels with a widget library; generated source elsewhere; translators live in the plugin |\n| Read a value out | `user_expressions`, plus a scope id | `user_expressions` |\n| Concurrent independent branches | scopes on subshells | subshells with proven-disjoint defines; GIL limits it to I/O-bound cells |\n| Kernels without analysis (bash, cling) | manual edges; delta including rebound | manual edges; delta reports first definitions only |\n| Reconcile analysis with what ran | delta with rebound catches dynamic writes to existing names | delta catches new names only |\n| Julia | delete via module bump under either | same; my \"Julia can advertise analysis without delete\" framed a choice as a limit |\n\nFor the reactive plugin alone, the simplified design is sufficient and simpler. For\nthe DAG plugin, it covers fan-out over disjoint names and defers genuine branching to\na tier outside the kernel that is replay on a plain install.\n\n## 5. Per-language feasibility\n\n| Language and kernel | analysis | delete | delta | scopes (notes) | set (notes) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Python, ipykernel | yes, with magic handling and a dynamic flag | yes; must decide whether `Out` and `_` are scrubbed | yes, with the hidden-name filter | fresh module per scope; concurrency needs an IPython change | exact |\n| R, IRkernel | yes; NSE makes many cells dynamic | `rm` from globalenv; `library()` not undoable by `rm` | yes if it also diffs the search path | `new.env(parent=)`, the cleanest substrate | ambiguous: integer vs double, vector vs list vs data frame |\n| Julia, IJulia | yes; macros must expand in the live module, so order matters | only by Pluto-style module bump plus method-table surgery | added only; `using` invisible before 1.12 | modules, but Pluto never forked them | ambiguous: Int64 vs Float64, Dict vs NamedTuple |\n| JavaScript, Deno and ijavascript | yes for Deno (swc in-kernel) | no: `let` and `const` cannot be removed; Deno allows redeclaration only | needs `Runtime.globalLexicalScopeNames` | `vm.createContext`; the only route to delete | number precision, BigInt |\n| bash | no | `unset` | `compgen -v` diff, noisy, two extra round trips | none | strings only |\n| C++, xeus-cpp | yes, order-dependent on the accumulated TU | no; clang-repl undo is LIFO and not exposed | new declarations per input | none | none |\n| SQL | dialect-specific; SQLite's authorizer is exact | `DROP`, which destroys data | catalog diff; not cheap on warehouses, not isolated from other sessions | none | none |\n| JVM, JShell | defines only | `drop(snippet)`, with dependents re-marked | eval events, exact | none | typed |\n\nDelete is exact in five of eight; set is exact in one. Factoring delete out of the\nnotes' namespace-ops bundle is the single biggest agnosticism gain in the simplified\ndesign. Delta is more universally implementable than analysis, but it never yields\nreferences and it must be normatively defined per language or two kernels\nadvertising the same string will disagree.\n\n## 6. What both designs got wrong\n\n- \"user_expressions already covers get.\" IRkernel returns an empty list, bash_kernel\n  and metakernel return `{}`, xeus-cpp ignores the argument. Get exists on ipykernel,\n  xeus-python, and IJulia.\n- Neither says what delete scrubs. A plain `del user_ns[name]` leaves the object\n  reachable through `Out[n]`, `_`, and `_N`, so a cell reading `_` sees stale data.\n- Neither defines the delta's name set, its presence on error replies, its relation\n  to the same request's delete, or its behavior under concurrent subshells.\n- Both treat `stop_on_error` as the partial-failure semantics a topological run\n  needs. It aborts everything queued on the same subshell, so it over-aborts\n  independent siblings when the scheduler pre-queues and does nothing when cells are\n  sent one at a time.\n- Both underestimate the analyzer (section 3.7) and gesture at cell magics\n  declaring their inputs and outputs without a mechanism.\n- Both misstate why snapshots would need messages: contract, not capability.\n- Both under-specify clone: the notes' \"kernel rebinds ports\" does not exist; my\n  \"a REST change\" hides the namespace requirement; neither mentions the restarter\n  race or the parent poller.\n- Both misuse Pluto in opposite directions: the notes as precedent for forkable\n  scopes, which Pluto never had; my design as \"only for delete\", when Pluto's delete\n  is a module bump plus method deletion plus re-imports, which a name list cannot\n  express.\n- Both cite ipyflow for namespace diffing; it traces.\n- Both leave the feature strings unnamed and unversioned, and both are silent on what\n  a kernel that advertises delete does when a name cannot be removed.\n- Both assume analysis is order-free enough to run out of order somewhere. For IPython\n  automagic, Julia macros, and C++ it is not, and neither tells the frontend to\n  re-analyze after execution.\n- Both describe `set` as the emulation route to value-carrying edges. Real value edges\n  need kernel-side handles for arbitrary objects; a JSON `set` emulates only\n  JSON-representable values.\n\n## 7. Gaps neither design covers\n\n- The ordinary execution path. Run Cell and Run All from the notebook view must go\n  through the plugin or the ledger diverges from the kernel at once. JupyterLab 4\n  exposes a replaceable `INotebookCellExecutor` token and only one provider can hold\n  it. Under the simplified design the replacement executor adds one field to the\n  request it already sends; under the notes' design it sequences two futures.\n- Multiple clients on one kernel. A console, a second tab, or a collaborator runs\n  `x = 5` outside the ledger. Neither design has a kernel-side owner of \"which cell\n  defined this name\". The ledger has to live in cell metadata in the shared model to\n  be RTC-safe.\n- Ledger persistence: reload, kernel restart, and opening a notebook whose kernel is\n  still running all need a reconciliation story; the actual namespace is recoverable\n  only by probing.\n- Temporaries under the one-definition rule. Ordinary Jupyter code reuses `i`, `df`,\n  `fig`, `ax`, `tmp` in many cells. marimo mangles underscore-prefixed names to\n  cell-local names in the kernel; neither design has a way to express cell-private\n  names. This will be the first complaint from any user of the reactive plugin.\n- The semantics of `references` (section 3.7) and the policy for `dynamic` cells:\n  run last, treat as defining everything downstream, refuse in reactive mode as\n  marimo does for star imports, or warn. The value of dropping rebound depends on\n  this policy.\n- Interrupt during a cascade: the scheduler must reconcile ran, aborted before run,\n  and, under the notes' message shape only, \"deleted but never ran\".\n- Which second kernel proves agnosticism. xeus-python drives an IPython\n  `InteractiveShell`, so it shares the analyzer, the delete, the name filter, and the\n  threading story with ipykernel and proves almost nothing. Deno, IRkernel, or IJulia\n  each exercise a divergence the review found.\n- Effort accounting. My table counts protocol items. The simplified design moves\n  work to the frontend: per-language literal generation for parameters, conflict\n  refusal or serialization, clone orchestration against an endpoint that does not\n  exist. The notes' design moves work the other way: scope lifecycle, re-forking\n  children when the prefix reruns, a scope id on every read.\n\n## 8. Decisions, with my recommendation\n\n1. May two branches of a user-drawn DAG define the same name? This is the decision\n   the whole scopes debate reduces to, and it is about the DAG plugin, not the\n   reactive one. Recommendation: no, for the first version. Enforce one definition per\n   name, flag conflicts from analysis, and offer clone-by-replay for real branching\n   later. If the answer is yes, the notes' scopes come back with a fresh-module\n   implementation and an IPython change for concurrency.\n2. Which plugin first. Recommendation: reactive. Its surface is analysis, delete, and\n   delta, and every shipped reactive notebook runs on that surface.\n3. Channel for analysis. Recommendation: shell, with a stated per-call policy: main\n   shell when ordering matters, a subshell when the kernel has them and the user is\n   waiting.\n4. Delete as a field or a message. Recommendation: the field, with the delete string\n   advertised only when `do_execute` accepts the parameter, removed names echoed in\n   the delta, and a `not_deleted` list on the reply.\n5. Delete before run or on success. Recommendation: before run, marimo's semantics,\n   with the scheduler recording names undefined because the run failed.\n6. Rebound. Recommendation: leave it out of the first version and reserve it as an\n   optional key; state plainly that the delta validates new names only.\n7. Set. Recommendation: leave it out, and say that inputs are authored as code cells\n   or ipywidgets in the first version, so the loss is named rather than hidden.\n8. Imports. Recommendation: put the `imports` list back as an optional key carrying\n   module names. It is load-bearing for R and Julia and cheap.\n9. One uncertainty flag or two. Recommendation: two, `unknown_defines` and\n   `unknown_references`.\n10. Feature strings. Recommendation: three, named, each with a testable contract\n    written before ipykernel ships them.\n11. The batch field. Recommendation: do not reuse `code` for a list; use a\n    differently named field.\n12. What to build before October 19 versus what to propose. Recommendation: build the\n    simplified surface over a comm target, and let the pre-proposal name scopes and\n    set as deferred with the reasons above, so the talk shows the small surface.\n13. Second kernel. Recommendation: IRkernel or Deno rather than xeus-python; either\n    exercises a real divergence (no `user_expressions` and invisible `library()` in\n    R; no delete for `let` in JavaScript).\n\n## 9. Conclusion\n\nThe simplified design is the one to propose, for a reason stronger than its message\ncount: it removes the only item that would be reviewed like subshells, and that item\nwas unsound as written. Its two irreversible commitments, shell channel and delete as\na field, are the ones with the cheaper reversal paths or the closable failure modes.\nEvery other cut is additive later.\n\nThe notes' design remains the more complete statement of what the DAG plugin was\nstarted for. Same-name branches, in-process sweeps, and language-agnostic input ports\nare real capabilities the simplified design gives up, and the \"server tier below\" I\npointed at is replay on any plain install. That trade is a product decision, and it\nshould be made explicitly rather than inherited from a protocol footprint argument.\n\nSeveral of my stated reasons were wrong even where the conclusion stands, and they\nshould not appear in a proposal: the Hex precedent, the IPython magic example for\nordering, \"no threading requirement\", \"for free\" on bash, \"only needed for value\nedges\", the papermill attribution, `copyToGlobals` as session-free, and\n`deletedCells` as a kernel-side precedent.\nMDEOF\nwc -w /Users/tel/git/jupyter-dag/.claude/artifacts/protocol-design-comparison.md /Users/tel/git/jupyter-dag/.claude/artifacts/protocol-design-simplified.md",

class=\"kicker\">jupyter-dag · kernel messaging protocol · September 14, 2026</p>\n  <h1>Two kernel-protocol designs for jupyter-dag, compared</h1>\n  <p class=\"lede\">The design in <code>kernel-design-notes.md</code> (sections 2 and 3, here <span style=\"color:var(--old);font-weight:500\">the notes' design</span>) against the simplification proposed the same day (here <span style=\"color:var(--new);font-weight:500\">the simplified design</span>). Five independent analyses, then forty-six adversarial checks of the simplified design's load-bearing claims against ipykernel 7.3, IPython 9.17, JupyterLab 4.7.0a1, the messaging spec, JEPs 47, 80, 91 and 92, and the sources of Pluto, marimo, papermill, Kishu, xeus, IRkernel, IJulia and Deno, with live experiments where a behavior could be exercised.</p>\n  <div class=\"tally\">\n    <span class=\"chip caveat\"><b>45</b> hold with caveats</span>\n    <span class=\"chip refuted\"><b>1</b> refuted</span>\n    <span class=\"chip holds\"><b>0</b> hold cleanly</span>\n    <span class=\"note\">The caveats are the content of this page.</span>\n  </div>\n</header>\n\n<nav class=\"toc\" aria-label=\"Contents\">\n  <p>Contents</p>\n  <ol>\n    <li><a href=\"#glance\">The two designs in one table</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#shared\">What they share</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#items\">Item by item</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#plugins\">What each plugin can do</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#languages\">Per-language feasibility</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#both-wrong\">What both got wrong</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#gaps\">Gaps neither covers</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#decisions\">Decisions, with recommendations</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#conclusion\">Conclusion</a></li>\n  </ol>\n</nav>\n\n<section id=\"glance\">\n  <h2><span class=\"num\">1</span>The two designs in one table</h2>\n  <div class=\"tablewrap\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th></th><th class=\"old\">notes' design</th><th class=\"new\">simplified design</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td>Edge analysis</td><td><code>analyze_request</code> on the <b>control</b> channel. Per cell: defines, references, imports, confidence, has_unknown_references.</td><td><code>analyze_request</code> on the <b>shell</b> channel, batch of code strings. Per cell: status, defines, references, one <code>dynamic</code> flag. Imports folded into defines.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Delete names</td><td>Standalone <code>namespace_request {delete}</code> on shell.</td><td><code>namespace_delete</code> list on <code>execute_request</code>, applied before the code runs. Purge without running = empty code with <code>silent</code>.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Set names from JSON</td><td><code>namespace_request {set: {name: value}}</code>.</td><td>None. Inputs arrive via comms or generated assignment code.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Read values</td><td><code>user_expressions</code>.</td><td><code>user_expressions</code>.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Runtime delta</td><td><code>execute_reply.namespace_delta {added, rebound, removed}</code>.</td><td><code>execute_reply.namespace_delta {added, removed}</code>, present whenever the kernel advertises it.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Branch isolation</td><td><code>create_scope</code>, <code>drop_scope</code>, <code>execute_request.scope</code>. Child is a shallow copy of or chain onto the parent.</td><td>None in the kernel. Frontend enforces one definition per name; isolation comes from a server-level clone.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Snapshots</td><td><code>snapshot</code>, <code>restore</code>, list, delete on shell, plus a CRIU provisioner tier and replay.</td><td>Nothing in the kernel protocol. CRIU provisioner and replay behind a server \"clone kernel\" operation.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Channels touched</td><td>shell and control</td><td>shell only; subshells for responsiveness</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>New message pairs</td><td>4, plus 4 for snapshots</td><td>1</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>New fields on existing messages</td><td>2</td><td>2</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Feature strings</td><td>one per feature, never named</td><td>3, never named</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Edge meaning</td><td>\"B runs after A in one namespace\"; value edges deferred</td><td>same</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n</section>\n\n<section id=\"shared\">\n  <h2><span class=\"num\">2</span>What the two designs share</h2>\n  <p>Both put the same work in the frontend: topological order, cycle detection, staleness, conflict detection, a per-cell ledger of the names defined at the last run, gating on feature strings, and fallback analysis providers for kernels without the feature. Both reuse <code>stop_on_error</code>, <code>silent</code>, <code>cellId</code>, comms, and JEP 92 <code>supported_features</code>. Both defer value-carrying edges.</p>\n  <p>Both plan to prototype over a comm target in ipykernel. A comm target carries either design unchanged, so the footprint question decides what the pre-proposal says, not what can be built before October 19. Both also make the same mistakes, listed in section 6.</p>\n</section>\n\n<section id=\"items\">\n  <h2><span class=\"num\">3</span>Item by item</h2>\n\n  <h3>3.1 Scopes</h3>\n  <div class=\"duel\">\n    <div class=\"side old\"><p class=\"label\">notes' design</p><p><code>create_scope(parent)</code>, a <code>scope</code> field on <code>execute_request</code>, <code>drop_scope</code>. Run a shared prefix once, fork branches that rebind the same names. Child is a shallow dict copy or a lookup chain. Isolation holds \"as long as cells rebind rather than mutate\". Composes with subshells for concurrent branches. Pluto's workspace modules cited as the Julia version.</p></div>\n    <div class=\"side new\"><p class=\"label\">simplified design</p><p>No scopes. The reactive plugin enforces one definition per name; the DAG plugin enforces or flags the same rule from analysis. Under the rebind contract, branches with disjoint definitions in one namespace cannot interfere. Isolation for mutating code comes from a server-level clone.</p></div>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"found\"><p class=\"label\">What the review found</p><ul>\n    <li>A lookup chain cannot be Python globals: <code>exec()</code> rejects a <code>ChainMap</code>. A bare dict copy assigned as <code>user_ns</code> breaks closures over cell-level names. A Python scope has to be a fresh module swapped into <code>shell.user_module</code> and <code>shell.user_ns</code> around each execute. Both reproduced in the venv.</li>\n    <li>Isolation is weaker than \"rebind, don't mutate\". Functions defined before the fork keep <code>__globals__</code> bound to the parent dict, so a child's rebinding is invisible to upstream code and later parent rebinds leak in. Pluto avoids this only by re-running every dependent cell in the new module.</li>\n    <li>Scopes do not compose with subshells as written. <code>InteractiveShell</code> has one <code>user_ns</code> shared by every subshell thread; concurrent per-branch scopes need a context-local namespace inside IPython. <code>%who</code>, the debugger's variable views, and <code>user_expressions</code> would each need a scope parameter.</li>\n    <li>Pluto never forks workspaces. Each <code>workspace#N</code> replaces the last in a linear chain. Pluto is precedent for delete by module migration, not for branch isolation.</li>\n    <li>What the simplified design gives up: two branches that both end in <code>model = fit(...)</code>; in-process parameter sweeps; and JavaScript's only route to \"no hidden state\", since a fresh context was the only way to make a <code>let</code> binding disappear.</li>\n    <li>The precedent I cited is narrower than I said. marimo, Pluto and Observable enforce one definer per name. No Hex document states such a rule, and Hex ships a fallback that runs cells in notebook order when it cannot infer dependencies.</li>\n    <li>Scopes never delivered isolation beyond the namespace level. RNG state, <code>pd.set_option</code>, the current matplotlib figure, <code>os.chdir</code>, and shared iterators leak through a shallow copy exactly as through one namespace.</li>\n  </ul></div>\n  <p class=\"verdict\"><b>Verdict</b>The cut is sound for the reactive plugin and for a proposal that has to land; scopes are the one item that would be reviewed the way subshells were, and they were unsound as written. It is a real loss for the DAG plugin, and it reduces to one product decision: may two branches of a user-drawn DAG define the same name?</p>\n\n  <h3>3.2 Snapshots and clone</h3>\n  <div class=\"duel\">\n    <div class=\"side old\"><p class=\"label\">notes' design</p><p><code>snapshot_request</code> and <code>restore_request</code> on shell, ordered with executions, plus list and delete. Manifest plus opaque blob; <code>fidelity</code> and <code>uncaptured</code> reporting. Tiers: replay, process-level CRIU via a provisioner (\"kernel rebinds ZMQ ports\"), language-native serialization. Clone preferred to restore for fan-out.</p></div>\n    <div class=\"side new\"><p class=\"label\">simplified design</p><p>Nothing in the kernel protocol. Replay needs nothing from the kernel; CRIU is a provisioner plus a Jupyter Server REST endpoint; the language-native tier is \"the only one that needs kernel messages\" and is Python-shaped. The DAG plugin codes against a server-level clone.</p></div>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"found\"><p class=\"label\">What the review found</p><ul>\n    <li>Restore in place needs no protocol change, if the provisioner uses <code>--tcp-close</code>, keeps jupyter_client's restarter from replacing the kernel during the gap (it polls <code>provisioner.poll()</code> every 3 seconds), keeps the parent pid stable (ipykernel's parent poller exits within a second if it changes), and routes the restore through the existing restart path so JupyterLab clears futures and comms.</li>\n    <li>Clone by \"restore one image twice\" does not exist on a plain host. CRIU restores the original pid and bound ports; a second copy needs its own pid and network namespace, or kernel-side rebind code. ipykernel binds ports once at startup with no retry when a port is specified; the notes' \"kernel rebinds ZMQ ports\" describes a mechanism that does not exist. On a plain install the only clone is replay.</li>\n    <li>The language-native tier needs no messages either. Kishu implements checkpoint and checkout with IPython <code>pre_run_cell</code> and <code>post_run_cell</code> hooks plus silent <code>execute_request</code> with <code>user_expressions</code>. Messages buy a language-neutral, advertised contract with fidelity reporting; that is the notes' argument, and it is the right framing.</li>\n    <li>The Kishu figures hold verbatim: CRIU-Incremental up to 36 times slower on checkout for the largest notebook, comparable on checkpoint, faster on 3 of 8 notebooks, failed on 2 of 8.</li>\n  </ul></div>\n  <p class=\"verdict\"><b>Verdict</b>Removing the four message pairs from the kernel protocol is right and costs kernel authors nothing. The consequence for the DAG plugin is that the \"isolation tier below\" is replay in practice, a full prefix re-run per branch. That raises the price of dropping scopes without reversing it.</p>\n\n  <h3>3.3 Delete</h3>\n  <div class=\"duel\">\n    <div class=\"side old\"><p class=\"label\">notes' design</p><p>A standalone <code>namespace_request {delete: [names]}</code> on the shell channel, before re-running a cell or when a cell is removed. No execution involved.</p></div>\n    <div class=\"side new\"><p class=\"label\">simplified design</p><p>An optional <code>namespace_delete</code> list on <code>execute_request</code>, applied before the code. Purge without running is an execute with empty code and <code>silent</code>. Advertised by a feature string; an unsupported list is silently ignored.</p></div>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"found\"><p class=\"label\">What the review found</p><ul>\n    <li>Verified against ipykernel 7.3.0: empty code with <code>silent: true</code> does not increment the counter, publishes no <code>execute_input</code>, stores no history, still publishes busy and idle, still evaluates <code>user_expressions</code>, replies <code>ok</code>. Empty code without <code>silent</code> publishes an <code>execute_input</code> with a counter IPython never consumes, so the next cell repeats the prompt number. Silent is mandatory.</li>\n    <li>JupyterLab's <code>CodeCell.execute</code> refuses empty code; purges must call <code>kernel.requestExecute</code> directly.</li>\n    <li>No forced signature change: kernelbase already inspects <code>do_execute</code> for <code>cell_meta</code> and <code>cell_id</code> and passes them only where accepted. <code>namespace_delete</code> slots into the same list; bash_kernel's five-argument <code>do_execute</code> keeps working.</li>\n    <li>Failure differs. The field is silently ignored on a kernel without the feature (verified: <code>x</code> survived) and the cell runs against stale bindings with an <code>ok</code> reply. The notes' unknown message gets no reply at all, so the future hangs. A hang is an availability failure a timeout detects; a skipped delete is a correctness failure nothing detects. Under a gating bug the message fails safe and the field fails unsafe. The fix stays inside the field shape: advertise the string only when <code>do_execute</code> accepts the parameter, and echo removed names in the delta.</li>\n    <li>Abort. <code>dispatch_shell</code> aborts only <code>execute_request</code> after a <code>stop_on_error</code> failure, so a queued silent purge is aborted with the queue: right for rerun purges, wrong for cell-removed purges. A queued <code>namespace_request</code> is never aborted, which is the reverse.</li>\n    <li>The field fixes delete-before-run: a cell that fails has already lost its previous bindings, which is marimo's semantics. The message leaves the choice to the frontend.</li>\n    <li>On this axis the message is the reversible shape: a message can later gain a convenience field; a field cannot be retired without leaving two ways to do one thing.</li>\n    <li>Neither shape says what happens to names that cannot be removed: <code>__builtins__</code>, <code>In</code>, <code>Out</code>, JS <code>let</code>, R locked bindings, Julia consts. <code>execute_reply</code> has no slot for it.</li>\n  </ul></div>\n  <p class=\"verdict\"><b>Verdict</b>The field is the cheaper and tighter shape for the reactive plugin's common path, and delete-then-rerun becomes one atomic message. Its two costs are closable without a new message. Recommendation: the field, with the two mitigations and a <code>not_deleted</code> list on the reply.</p>\n\n  <h3>3.4 Set <span class=\"chip refuted\" style=\"vertical-align:middle;margin-left:6px\">one claim refuted</span></h3>\n  <div class=\"duel\">\n    <div class=\"side old\"><p class=\"label\">notes' design</p><p><code>namespace_request {set: {name: json}}</code>: \"a language-agnostic way to bind a name to a JSON-ish value\", which is what widget-bound variables, papermill-style parameters, and DAG input ports all reduce to. Costs nothing extra. With <code>user_expressions</code>, emulates value-carrying edges.</p></div>\n    <div class=\"side new\"><p class=\"label\">simplified design</p><p>Dropped. JSON-to-binding is ambiguous in R, JavaScript and Julia, which is why papermill keeps per-language translators; comms already carry widget-bound values. It comes back only if value-carrying edges are chosen later.</p></div>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"found\"><p class=\"label\">What the review found</p><ul>\n    <li><b>Refuted:</b> \"only needed if we later choose value-carrying edges\". The notes listed three uses unrelated to value edges. Dropping <code>set</code> does not remove those needs; it moves them. An input cell or parameter on a kernel without a widget library becomes generated assignment source, papermill's translator layer living in the frontend, or does not exist.</li>\n    <li>What held: the ambiguity is real, and the two reactive notebooks that bind JSON values to names both shipped kernel-side conversion hooks for it (Pluto's <code>transform_value</code>, marimo's <code>_convert_value</code>).</li>\n    <li>papermill was the wrong witness. Its translators exist because it injects a source cell and needs each language's literal and assignment syntax; they hard-code one choice per language, do not resolve the numeric ambiguity, and there is no JavaScript translator at all.</li>\n    <li>\"Comms already carry widget-bound values\" is narrower than it sounds. Comms deliver a value to a trait on a kernel-side widget object, not to a name, and only on kernels with a widget library. Neither design covers Pluto's shape, a bound global name driven by a slider, without frontend bookkeeping from widget id to defining cell to name.</li>\n    <li>Real value-carrying edges need kernel-side handles for arbitrary objects; a JSON <code>set</code> emulates only JSON-representable values, so both designs overstate what <code>set</code> gives.</li>\n  </ul></div>\n  <p class=\"verdict\"><b>Verdict</b>Dropping <code>set</code> is a relocation, not a saving. It is still right for a first version whose thesis is reactive execution, because the spec burden of a per-language coercion table is real and the ambiguity undercuts the notes' \"costs nothing extra\" too. The decision is where the mapping lives, and it should be stated that way.</p>\n\n  <h3>3.5 The runtime delta</h3>\n  <div class=\"duel\">\n    <div class=\"side old\"><p class=\"label\">notes' design</p><p>Optional <code>namespace_delta: {added, rebound, removed}</code> on <code>execute_reply</code>, from diffing global names and object identity before and after. \"It works for languages with no parser support, and it's what ipyflow does inside ipykernel already.\"</p></div>\n    <div class=\"side new\"><p class=\"label\">simplified design</p><p><code>{added, removed}</code> only, exact set differences, present whenever advertised. Rebound dropped: identity comparison either keeps old values alive or compares recycled ids, and static analysis already reports which names a cell assigns. Gives parser-less kernels such as bash the defines half of an edge for free.</p></div>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"found\"><p class=\"label\">What the review found</p><ul>\n    <li>Added and removed are cheap (under 3 ms on a 100,000-name namespace). Both rebound problems are real and reproduced: <code>x = None; x = [9,9,9]</code> reports no rebind by id, and the pre-run copy keeps every replaced object alive until the reply.</li>\n    <li>\"Exact\" is exact only relative to a per-language enumeration the spec has to define. In ipykernel a raw key diff after one run reports <code>_1</code>, <code>_i</code>, <code>_i1</code>, <code>_ii</code>, <code>_iii</code>; the <code>user_ns_hidden</code> identity filter that <code>%who</code> uses is required. In R, <code>library()</code> changes the search path, not <code>globalenv</code>. In Julia, <code>using</code> is invisible before 1.12 and removed is always empty. In JavaScript, <code>let</code> and <code>const</code> are not properties of <code>globalThis</code>. In bash, <code>PIPESTATUS</code>, <code>_</code>, <code>RANDOM</code>, and <code>SECONDS</code> change on their own.</li>\n    <li>Subshells share one namespace, so a before-and-after diff attributes another subshell's assignments to this cell. The field must be present on <code>status: error</code> replies, since a failing cell can bind names before raising. Neither design says whether removed includes names removed by the same request's pre-run delete.</li>\n    <li>The dichotomy for rebound is not exhaustive: a weakref-where-possible hybrid bounds the memory cost, and instrumentation, which is what ipyflow actually does, detects rebinding exactly at CPU cost. Dropping rebound is a choice, not a necessity.</li>\n    <li>Dropping rebound blinds the two uses I gave the field. Cell A defines <code>x</code>; cell B runs <code>exec(\"x = 2\")</code>; B's delta is empty because <code>x</code> already exists. On bash, <code>count=$((count+1))</code> produces an empty delta after the first run, and bash_kernel needs two extra pexpect round trips per cell to get even first definitions.</li>\n    <li>The notes' \"ipyflow proves it works\" is wrong in the other direction: ipyflow traces with pyccolo; it does not diff namespaces.</li>\n  </ul></div>\n  <p class=\"verdict\"><b>Verdict</b>The shrink is defensible and additive; rebound can return as an optional key. The claims around it should be cut back: the field validates static analysis for new names only, and bash gets first definitions, not defines.</p>\n\n  <h3>3.6 Where analysis runs</h3>\n  <div class=\"duel\">\n    <div class=\"side old\"><p class=\"label\">notes' design</p><p>Control channel, \"like <code>debug_request</code>, which ipykernel services in a separate thread\", because static analysis needs no namespace and should not queue behind a busy shell.</p></div>\n    <div class=\"side new\"><p class=\"label\">simplified design</p><p>Shell channel: same dispatch path as <code>complete</code> and <code>inspect</code>, no threading requirement on kernel authors, ordered with executions (a magic registered by an earlier cell changes how a later cell parses). Responsiveness during a long run from a subshell where the kernel has them.</p></div>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"found\"><p class=\"label\">What the review found</p><ul>\n    <li>Norms. JEP 91 names completion, introspection, and variable inspection as things people put on control because it had its own thread, and says \"this is considered bad practice as it should only be used for control purposes\". Reviewers will quote it. The spec itself does not reserve control: it calls the channel \"identical to Shell\" on a separate socket, allows <code>kernel_info</code> there, and ipykernel accepts every shell message type on control. The notes' placement was against guidance, not against the spec.</li>\n    <li>Who is responsive today. A control thread exists in ipykernel and xeus-python. It does not in xeus-cpp or xeus-r, IRkernel, or in practice IJulia. Subshells exist in ipykernel 7 only; neither xeus nor xeus-zmq mentions them through their latest releases. On today's kernels the notes' route is responsive on a strict superset of kernels. The simplified design wins on direction and on what it asks of kernel authors, not on present capability.</li>\n    <li>Ordering. My IPython example was weak: <code>%%foo</code> and <code>%foo</code> rewrite textually whether or not the magic is registered; only single-line automagic and runtime-registered input transformers depend on live state. The requirement is real and strong elsewhere: Pluto expands macros in the live workspace module before resolving the topology, and a C++ cell cannot be parsed without the accumulated translation unit.</li>\n    <li>Ordering and responsiveness are mutually exclusive per request. A request sent to a subshell is ordered only within that subshell. The frontend picks per call, and the design should say so.</li>\n    <li>Thread safety does not discriminate. The single-line path enters <code>builtin_trap</code>, whose nesting counter is an unsynchronized read-modify-write shared with the executing thread. The hazard is identical for the control thread and a subshell thread, and ipykernel already runs <code>transform_cell</code> on subshell threads. The fix under either design is to call the static <code>input_transformer_manager.transform_cell()</code> and skip the prefilter.</li>\n    <li>An unknown message type on either channel gets no reply in ipykernel, and a message sent to a stale <code>subshell_id</code> is dropped with only a log line, so the frontend hangs rather than receiving the error JEP 91 promises.</li>\n    <li>Shell first is the reversible direction: <code>shutdown_request</code>'s move from shell to control took a deprecation cycle, and JEP 80 shows a message can later be allowed on both channels.</li>\n  </ul></div>\n  <p class=\"verdict\"><b>Verdict</b>Shell, for the norms and the reversal path, with an explicit per-call policy and the honest statement that responsive analysis is ipykernel-only for now.</p>\n\n  <h3>3.7 The shape of the analysis reply</h3>\n  <div class=\"duel\">\n    <div class=\"side old\"><p class=\"label\">notes' design</p><p>No schema. Per cell: <code>defines</code>, <code>references</code>, <code>imports</code>, <code>confidence</code>, <code>has_unknown_references</code>. Cell magics could declare their own inputs and outputs, as rpy2's <code>%%R -i x -o y</code> already says.</p></div>\n    <div class=\"side new\"><p class=\"label\">simplified design</p><pre><code>analyze_request  {\"code\": [\"df = pd.read_csv(path)\", \"df.head(\"]}\nanalyze_reply    {\"status\": \"ok\", \"cells\": [\n  {\"status\": \"ok\", \"defines\": [\"df\"],\n   \"references\": [\"pd\", \"path\"], \"dynamic\": false},\n  {\"status\": \"error\", \"ename\": \"SyntaxError\", \"evalue\": \"...\"}]}</code></pre></div>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"found\"><p class=\"label\">What the review found</p><ul>\n    <li><code>code</code> as a list conflicts with every other request, where <code>code</code> is a string. A spec maintainer would reject the reuse of the name with a different type.</li>\n    <li>Folding imports into defines is right for Python, JavaScript and C++ and wrong for R and Julia: <code>library(dplyr)</code> and <code>using Foo</code> bind nothing enumerable at top level yet must be ancestors of every cell that uses an exported name. Pluto keeps <code>using</code> as a separate class for this reason. A drawn-graph UI also wants to hide import edges. The notes' <code>imports</code> list was load-bearing.</li>\n    <li>One <code>dynamic</code> flag forces the frontend to treat \"may define names I cannot see\" and \"may reference names I cannot see\" identically; a star-import cell and an NSE-heavy R cell should schedule differently.</li>\n    <li>The per-cell error entry is the right shape; a syntax error must not fail the batch.</li>\n    <li>Neither design defines <code>references</code>: free variables only or all names read; whether reads inside function bodies count (marimo and Observable count them); whether <code>obj.attr = 1</code> is a reference; whether <code>x += 1</code> is both.</li>\n    <li>Both designs' \"transform_cell then ast or symtable\" undercounts the analyzer. <code>transform_cell</code> turns every cell-magic body into a string literal; <code>%%capture out</code> defines <code>out</code>; <code>%%R -i x -o y</code> needs per-magic argument parsing with no registry API to declare it; <code>$var</code> in <code>!</code> and line magics expands at run time; <code>symtable</code> has no top-level-await flag; <code>del x</code> shows as an assignment. Measured cost is 2.5 ms per 200-line cell, so batching a notebook is fine.</li>\n  </ul></div>\n\n  <h3>3.8 Advertising and footprint</h3>\n  <p>JEP 92 explicitly allows a feature to be \"additional messages and/or additional fields in different existing messages\", so gating fields on strings is conformant, and JupyterLab already parses the list. Three strings for one message and two fields is a worse ratio than JEP 91 or the debugger; a reviewer accepts it only if each string has a testable contract. Neither design names its strings or versions them, and JEP 91 itself says a version specifier is probably needed.</p>\n  <p>On cost, the review's strongest point: cost scales with the semantics kernel authors must implement, not with message count.</p>\n  <div class=\"tablewrap\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>Proposal</th><th>What it added</th><th>Opened</th><th>Merged</th><th>Shipped</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td>JEP 92, optional features</td><td>one optional field</td><td>January 2023</td><td>June 2023</td><td>ipykernel 7.3 advertises strings today</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>JEP 91, subshells</td><td>three control messages, a header field, new threading semantics</td><td>December 2022</td><td>September 2024</td><td>ipykernel 7.0 in October 2025; JupyterLab 4.4; no xeus implementation</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n  <p>Scopes are in the JEP 91 class. <code>analyze_request</code> and <code>namespace_delete</code> are in the JEP 92 class. The simplified design's real saving is removing the one JEP 91 class item, not shaving message pairs.</p>\n</section>\n\n<section id=\"plugins\">\n  <h2><span class=\"num\">4</span>What each plugin can do under each design</h2>\n  <div class=\"tablewrap\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>Behavior</th><th class=\"old\">notes' design</th><th class=\"new\">simplified design</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td>Graph of a cold notebook</td><td>one batch analyze; queued elsewhere</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Rerun descendants with partial failure</td><td><code>stop_on_error</code> is coarser than needed; scheduler blocks descendants itself</td><td>same, plus a failed cell has no bindings after delete-before-run</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>No hidden state on delete or rename</td><td>separate message; may delete only after success</td><td>field; delete happens before the run</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Two branches defining <code>model</code></td><td>run both in their own scopes, concurrently on subshells (needs an IPython change to be real)</td><td>refuse, rename, serialize, or clone a kernel by replay</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Parameter sweep over one subgraph</td><td>N scopes, N sets, results per scope</td><td>sequential in one namespace with generated assignment code, or N kernels</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Input ports and parameters from the UI</td><td>one <code>set</code> message; kernel owns the JSON mapping</td><td>comms where a widget library exists; generated source elsewhere; translators live in the plugin</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Concurrent independent branches</td><td>scopes on subshells</td><td>subshells with proven-disjoint defines; the GIL limits it to I/O-bound cells</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Kernels without analysis (bash, cling)</td><td>manual edges; delta with rebound</td><td>manual edges; delta reports first definitions only</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Reconcile analysis with what ran</td><td>rebound catches dynamic writes to existing names</td><td>catches new names only</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Julia</td><td>delete via module bump</td><td>same; \"Julia can advertise analysis without delete\" framed a choice as a limit</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n  <p>For the reactive plugin alone, the simplified design is sufficient and simpler. For the DAG plugin, it covers fan-out over disjoint names and defers genuine branching to a tier outside the kernel that is replay on a plain install.</p>\n</section>\n\n<section id=\"languages\">\n  <h2><span class=\"num\">5</span>Per-language feasibility</h2>\n  <div class=\"tablewrap\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>Language, kernel</th><th>analysis</th><th>delete</th><th>delta</th><th>scopes (notes)</th><th>set (notes)</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td>Python, ipykernel</td><td>yes, with magic handling and a dynamic flag</td><td>yes; decide whether <code>Out</code> and <code>_</code> are scrubbed</td><td>yes, with the hidden-name filter</td><td>fresh module per scope; concurrency needs an IPython change</td><td>exact</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>R, IRkernel</td><td>yes; NSE makes many cells dynamic</td><td><code>rm</code> from globalenv; <code>library()</code> not undoable</td><td>yes if it also diffs the search path</td><td><code>new.env(parent=)</code>, the cleanest substrate</td><td>integer vs double, vector vs list vs data frame</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>Julia, IJulia</td><td>yes; the only route to delete</td><td>number precision, BigInt</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>bash</td><td>no</td><td><code>unset</code></td><td><code>compgen -v</code> diff, noisy, two extra round trips</td><td>none</td><td>strings only</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>C++, xeus-cpp</td><td>yes, order-dependent on the accumulated TU</td><td>no; not cheap on warehouses</td><td>none</td><td>none</td></tr>\n      <tr><td>JVM, JShell</td><td>defines only</td><td><code>drop(snippet)</code>, dependents re-marked</td><td>eval events, exact</td><td>none</td><td>typed</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n  <p>Delete is exact in five of eight; set is exact in one. Factoring delete out of the notes' namespace-ops bundle is the single biggest agnosticism gain in the simplified design. Delta is more universally implementable than analysis, but it never yields references and must be normatively defined per language, or two kernels advertising the same string will disagree.</p>\n</section>\n\n<section id=\"both-wrong\">\n  <h2><span class=\"num\">6</span>What both designs got wrong</h2>\n  <ul>\n    <li>\"<code>user_expressions</code> already covers get.\" IRkernel returns an empty list, bash_kernel and metakernel return <code>{}</code>, xeus-cpp ignores the argument. A plain <code>del user_ns[name]</code> leaves the object reachable through <code>Out[n]</code>, <code>_</code>, and <code>_N</code>.</li>\n    <li>Neither defines the delta's name set, its presence on error replies, its relation to the same request's delete, or its behavior under concurrent subshells.</li>\n    <li>Both treat <code>stop_on_error</code> as the partial-failure semantics a topological run needs.
